## Opening

<a id="chapter-00"></a>

### N. The Universality of You

Where should we begin?

Can we at least agree that we exist as solitary minds? Reality manifests in each solitary mind.

$$
M_i \xrightarrow{\text{constructs}} R
$$

No, not abstractly. You can actually touch it, you can speak it, you can think it. I think, therefore I...

Ah, but there are things you cannot think. At least not yet. Your ability to think can change even when the thing in front of you does not.

Like this text. You may read the same sentence twice and find that it means something different the second time. The new material meets what you already know. You may misunderstand it, reject it, or connect it to an existing idea. So the new thing does not arrive alone. It arrives inside something already happening. The text didn't change. But something changed in you. 

Name this structure.

The questions, difficulties, expectations, and existing ideas already in play form a **problem situation**. New material is understood in relation to that situation. We will call that rebuilding **reconstruction**, as in reconstructing the problem situation.

The consequences are not limited by the place where we first encountered it or the form it takes. A theory may arrive in a physics class, an idea about evolution in a biology book, or a principle about knowledge under the heading *philosophy*.

But a field is not a fence. If an explanation says something is possible, other possibilities may follow from it. If two explanations apply to the same thing, they may fit together, collide, or reveal that the original question was badly formed. If an explanation developed in one field has consequences in another, the disciplinary border does not block those consequences.

Following an explanation through the consequences it entails will be called **taking explanations seriously**.

This does not mean believing the explanation, or pretending to know everything your explanation reaches. It means allowing its consequences to travel while remaining open to criticism. We travel to learn something about ourselves. Some explanations survive for a while. Some fail. Some do something more interesting. They make the original problem deeper.

Show me.

A mathematician can leave behind a proof that others continue to use. An engineer can leave behind a design that someone else can build. A scientific explanation can create problems for people not yet born when it was written.

Fine. But persistence is not enough. It can also change form.

A written explanation can be translated, a procedure can be programmed, and a design can be embodied in a bridge or instrument. What began in a person is now doing things without that person being present. Knowledge that exists objectively will be called **objective knowledge**.

The word *objective* is dangerous here. It sounds like *true*. 

Objective knowledge need not be true. A false theory can be written in a book. A bad law can be encoded in an institution. A broken program can be copied a million times. Objective knowledge can be wrong and still be objective.

But the same objective knowledge does not always produce the same reconstruction. One person may see a solution, another may see a contradiction, and a third may see nothing important at all. The idea enters different histories, memories, problems, and confronts existing explanations. The knowledge outside the mind can be common, while the processing inside the mind is solitary. No one can undergo this change in understanding for you.

Not all of that reconstruction is even clearly expressed. Some knowledge appears first in what you can do, notice, expect, or reject. You can catch a falling glass before you can explain the movement. A sentence can feel wrong before you can say why. You can recognize a face while being unable to describe what you recognized. Knowledge can be present before it can be stated. Only later, sometimes, can you explain it.

Knowledge that is present in action, recognition, expectation, or rejection before it can be stated clearly will be called **inexplicit knowledge**.

This is why communication is often hard. 

Shared knowledge does not require a shared framework or common machinery. It is not a literal meeting of the minds. But it is physical. It requires objective knowledge that can be recreated within minds, if only approximately.

So objective knowledge collides with reality, and comprises reality? How is this possible?

An explanation is not the thing it explains. But it can still change what happens in reality. A map is not the city, yet it can guide you through one. An equation describing an orbit is not the orbit, yet it can help place a spacecraft. A theory of light is not light, yet it can become part of a telescope.

Enough about maps and telescopes. People are part of that reality too. Whatever thought is, it must be physically possible.

Yes, knowledge has physical effects, and exists in physical forms. It is **physically instantiated**.

But how can knowledge be separate from the particular thing carrying it?

Consider the number three. It can appear as a numeral. It can appear as three stones. It can appear as a pattern of electrical states. None of those particular objects is what we mean by three.

A relation or structure that can remain recognizable across different instances, without being identical to any one of them, will be called an **abstraction**. The same is true of a problem, an algorithm, a legal rule, or an explanation. An abstraction can appear in different physical forms while preserving enough structure to be recognized, criticized, copied, or used again.

That gives us another problem. We have separated the carrier from the structure it carries. That simplification buys us something. But how can the same structure be embodied in different physical forms and still produce similar consequences?

Knowledge did not begin with explanation. It's much older. Reality contains solutions unexplained. Knowledge exists objectively without a knower.

Show me.

An eye focuses light. A wing permits controlled flight. A seed contains structures that participate in building a new organism. No ancestral organism needed to understand the problem these structures solved. Biological knowledge grows through variation and retention. Some variants fail. Some persist. What persists alters the starting point for what comes next. Over time, structures can accumulate that embody increasingly intricate solutions to problems of survival and reproduction.

Genes can therefore preserve workable solutions without containing an explanation of why those solutions work. So do minds.

Information retained through evolution that causes changes will be called **biological knowledge**. The process in which variation occurs, some variants are eliminated, and retained variants alter what can happen next will be called **evolution**, or more generally, an evolutionary process.

Evolution explains something profound. Knowledge does not require a goal in order to grow. It doesn't require an authority or justification. It requires only a knowledge processor or processing environment. But when we return from evolution to you, something new appears.

People introduce a different kind of variation. You can vary explanations, not merely inherit biological variants. And you do it much faster than biological evolution, so fast that you may not even be aware that you're doing it right now. You can imagine several explanations of the same event, notice that an explanation fails for a reason nobody has previously articulated, or decide that the original problem was badly framed.

This makes you a game-changer. Knowledge grows evolutionarily, through variation and selection. Some explanations are retained. Others are changed or rejected. New problems appear. An observation may conflict with what you thought was true. You may invent an explanation. Someone may criticize it and expose an assumption you did not know you were making.

Now the knowledge landscape has changed profoundly. Biological evolution does not need to know that it has a problem. But you can possess a problem. You can name it, share it, reformulate it, or decide that a different problem matters more. You can even turn on the question itself and ask whether it was worth asking in the first place. You are epistemically disobedient. That is a different kind of knowledge creation. It is vastly more complex, compounding, and accelerating than even our most powerful, obedient, and goal-seeking machines.

Can we shrink that idea without losing it? Start by keeping only the parts that change the next move.

A **problem** appears when something does not fit. It may resist explanation, create a contradiction, or block a change. A proposed explanation or response that might resolve a problem is a **tentative solution**. Criticism can expose weaknesses in a tentative solution. Rejecting, revising, or replacing the weak parts is **error elimination**. Criticism can also reveal another unresolved difficulty. That new difficulty is a **successor problem**.

That's still too much. Shrink it again.

A problem may lead to a tentative solution. The elimination of errors may lead to a new problem.

Shrink it again.

$$P_1 \rightarrow TS \rightarrow EE \rightarrow P_2 $$

That will suffice to carry it forward. But let's not forget what we've lost. The symbols are shorthand, not a script you recite internally. A mismatch can be felt before it becomes a conscious problem. A criticism can first appear as discomfort. The arrows change direction. A solution can be partly embodied in action before anyone can state it clearly.

The explanation about genes may already have created a new problem for you. Be selfish; embrace it. You may reject the claim that genes are knowledge. You may think the word knowledge is being stretched too far. You may react viscerally to the word evolution. Any of those responses may change your problem for the better.

Now shrink it again.

Useful representations preserve some structure and leave the rest out, to a reasonable approximation. A map leaves out almost everything. A category treats different things as the same for some purpose. A diagram preserves selected relations while discarding most of the object it represents.

Stop there. The examples all do the same thing. Keep the relation. Drop the incidental detail. We will call that **compression**.

Compression is indispensable. Without it, a map would need to reproduce the territory. A category would contain only one thing. A useful diagram would become as complicated as what it depicts. But compression can also inadvertently erase the very thing that matters. A map may omit a stairway that matters to a wheelchair user. A diagram may omit a connection that turns out to carry the cause. A model may predict an outcome while remaining silent about why it occurs.

The problem is not abstraction or compression. The problem is forgetting that abstraction is selective, and compression is lossy. What did this representation preserve? What did it make disappear? Those questions will accompany us on our journey for a long time.

Something important is lost if description and explanation are treated as the same thing. A regular pattern can be described precisely and still leave its cause unexplained. A description tells us what happened, or what regularly happens, or what statistically happened, or what probably happens. An explanation tries to tell us why.

A classification can be reliable without identifying a common cause. A prediction can succeed while we still do not know what produced the outcome. The causes that produce an outcome form its **causal structure**. Precision does not transform description into explanation. That distinction becomes easier to forget as the representation becomes more impressive. 

It feels like these explanations of knowledge keep moving underneath us, like trying to walk through a swamp.

Are you tired? This is effortful. Pace yourself. If you like, you can stop here. It will be waiting for when you return.

Press on.

Some explanations refuse to stay where we first found them. They continue to apply outside the problem that first produced them. Newton's explanations of motion did not apply only to the objects that first motivated them. Darwin's explanation of evolution did not remain confined to one species, or even biology itself. A rule-governed transformation can operate on cases no programmer inspected in advance.

Compress the examples into the common structure.

An explanation can continue to apply outside its original problem. We will say that explanations of this kind **travel**, and call the extent of that travel the **reach** of their constraints. 

Reach changes more than the number of cases an explanation covers. It changes which questions can be asked. Some explanations travel so far that they constrain entire classes of other explanations. Physics constrains what can happen physically. Evolution constrains the processes of complex things. Rules constrain what informational transformations can occur.

And what of people? Locate the most unique thing about people. Not the essence of people, but the exceptionality. Put your finger on it and don't let it go. What is the one thing that people do that no other thing in our known universe can do? It's not a noun, it's a verb. It's not knowledge, but it's also not knowing. It's something deep, mysterious, and swampy. Now name it.

Knowledge grows through conjecture and criticism without justification. The explanation of how knowledge grows will be called **epistemology**, and the things it reaches, **epistemic**.

Don't reduce it to a field or a fence. Let it travel.

When an explanation keeps applying beyond the original case and constrains whole classes of other explanations, its reach has become unusually broad. Follow them far enough and, eventually, they reach us. Some explanations reach everywhere. We will call that kind of reach **universality**.

Like gravity, computation does not belong to a particular machine. A represented state can be transformed into another state by rules, regardless of the particular machine that carries them out. Mechanical gears can carry out such transformations, electrical circuits can carry them out, and a person can follow a written procedure with pencil and paper.

Strip away gears, circuits, and pencil marks. Keep the rule-governed transformation, and call it **computation**.

Once a transformation is expressed precisely enough, a machine can then execute it without recreating the explanation that produced it. Long multiplication can be taught. A sorting procedure can be programmed. A proof-checking procedure can be automated. And given our best explanations of physics and computation, any physical process, even the mysterious processes within a human brain, can be simulated.

We don't have to wait. It's been happening for a very very long time. Once explained, the knowledge of a process can be moved outside a person. Parts of an inquiry can persist outside biological memory. Problems can be represented. Competing explanations can be preserved. Earlier states can be recovered and compared. Long explanatory trajectories can therefore exist outside biological memory.

Wait! I am not a gadget in some weird techno-fantasy!

You are computational, and physical, and evolved, and epistemic. You are not merely a computer, but whatever you are is constrained by these universal explanations. This does not mean that a computer has become a person. It does not mean that computation explains the mysteries of the person. If you take these explanations seriously, if you let them travel, they will reach even the most remote places. They reach the explanation of you. They participate universally, not reductively.

And if epistemology is one of those universal explanations, that reaches you too, within your epistemic mind. It also means the knowledge that explains your epistemic mind evolves, and may eventually become explicit enough to be embodied in tools.

When knowledge is embodied in a tool and performs a transformation, we will call it **technological knowledge**.

Objective knowledge participates directly in the journey. And as it travels, the boundary of the problem becomes more interesting. The architecture folds back on itself. Objective knowledge can change what later knowledge creation makes possible.

We don't know how it works, but we know it happens. Writing changed what people could preserve. Notation changed what people could calculate. Scientific instruments changed what could become observable.

That answer is hand-wavy. 

An explanation, argument, or proof that skips important details, logic, or evidence, will be called **hand-wavy**.

Stop that! Explain.

These are not merely new places to store old thoughts. They change what later thought can do. Using algebra, you can solve problems that would be  inaccessible without algebraic notation. Using a telescope, you can encounter observations unavailable to unaided vision. Using software, you can inspect systems too large to hold in biological memory. The products of knowledge creation can become inputs into later knowledge creation.

That gives us a reusable structure: an output can become part of the conditions for the next operation. Some of those products can even describe the process of knowledge creation itself. We can write about problems. We can model criticism. We can preserve explanatory history. Knowledge can become knowledge about knowledge. Then it can come back in strange loops.

Compress that loop.

When a process's output alters the conditions of its next operation, we have feedback. When a process applies its own explanatory methods to its own organization, a recursive relation can emerge. We will call this **recursion**.

You learn how you made a mistake, and that changes how you approach the next problem. A programmer creates a tool for inspecting programs, and the tool changes which programs can be built. Then the loop turns back toward you.

There is still a limit to what this architecture can give us. Knowing everything you already possess would leave something open. It would not tell us which genuinely new explanation you might create tomorrow. Can that be illustrated without pretending to predict the unpredictable?

Imagine that you have read every book available to you. Suppose you remember every argument, equation, and criticism that presently exists. That still would not reveal the next new explanation in advance. If an explanation is genuinely new, it is not latent in what came before. 

Once the explanation exists, we can reconstruct where it came from. We may identify earlier problems that prepared the ground. We may identify influences. We may identify tools without which it would have been impossible. But there is a difference between tracing a path after someone has walked it and knowing the path before it exists.

Separate those two operations.

The history from which an idea emerged is its **ancestry**. A procedure that would produce the idea from what came before would be a **derivation**. Ancestry does not by itself provide derivation. The future is not simply a hidden list of ideas waiting to be read out of the present.

You cannot create just anything at any time. You are situated in space and time. You may be creative, you may be imaginative, but you can't defy the laws of physics. Your future is open, but physically constrained. You have a body. You have finite time. You have limited attention and memory.

We're not talking about physics, we're talking about people!

Are you tired? This is effortful. Pace yourself. If you like, you can stop here...

Press on! Something remains stubbornly inside, unexplained.

The unexplained part concerns the creation of new explanatory knowledge. You may inherit earlier problems, tools, and theories. Every new explanation arises in a world already full of objective knowledge. Its ancestry can often be traced after it exists. An inventor used earlier technologies. An artist encountered earlier works. A scientist inherited previous theories.

But ancestry is not creation. Knowing the ingredients does not explain the new recipe. Knowing earlier theories does not explain why a particular new problem appeared. Knowing what entered your mind does not explain what you created from it. The new explanation was not already sitting there as a conclusion waiting to be unpacked. The machine runs out of data to extrapolate. Perhaps one day we will have an explanation of this. We do not have it now. We do not have it here.

But that ignorance is not an embarrassment to sweep away. It is one of the greatest problems ever created. Eventually the problem will reach the person who will explain it. The broad explanations developed so far will apply there too. It is not just abstract, it is abstracting. It is not just recursion, it is recursing. It is not just knowledge, it is knowing.

That's still not right. We don't yet have a name for it. But it reaches you and it is in you, even if you can't keep your finger on it.

Each explanation constrains what you can be. None of them, alone, is you. Put them within the same architecture and something changes. Now the word universality becomes a problem rather than a definition, a journey through a universe. Not humanity as a statistical population. Not a personality type. Not traits or tendencies.

You. A singular universe.

Our question is not whether you are important because you are human. The question is what you must be if all of these explanations are taken seriously at once. That question cannot be answered by extending the list. The list was useful. The list was curated into fields. The universe doesn't care, and neither do universal explanations.

Refactor. The architecture is now the problem. The architecture must be implemented and allowed to run. If we understand it, we can program it. If we don't, we'll learn a great deal in trying.

A biological organism produced by evolution can understand evolution. A physical system can create explanations of physics. A person can build a universal computer and use it to investigate computation. And despite all of this, we still do not know how you produce a genuinely new explanation. We still don't even have a name for it. That will come after it is explained. For now, the still-unexplained capacity to produce genuinely new explanations will be called **explanatory creativity**.

The phrase is compact. The problem it names is not. The scale of what has been explained is enormous. The remaining ignorance is infinite. That too is universal.

Ignorance can produce awe in the older sense of the word. Not fatalism. Not mysticism. Awe at what appears to be possible, at how much has already been explained, and at the infinite extent of what remains unexplained.

The category of *person* begins to look ordinary, our machines quaint, and the universality of you, extraordinary.

Are you tired? This is effortful. Pace yourself...

Absolutely not. Our problems are urgent. Allowing our best explanations to reach us as individuals may change us, our policies, and our technology. It may change what you seem to be, what seems possible, and sharpen what mysteries remain.

<a id="part-the-solitary-explainer"></a>

## The Solitary Explainer

<a id="chapter-01"></a>

### I. You Are Not A Geneget

Where does an inquiry into a person actually begin? 

One approach explains differences among people using genetics.

Personality genetics can combine large cohorts, genome-wide measurements, personality instruments, statistical models, and increasingly careful controls. It can detect patterns that would be invisible in a single life. It can test whether measured genetic differences covary with measured differences in personality, estimate how much variation in those measurements is associated with common genetic variation, and ask whether those relations survive across samples and methods.

Those are real achievements. The measurements can be precise, the associations reproducible, and the population patterns informative. Yet you still remain unexplained.

That is the first encounter. The problem is not that the observations are unreal. It appears when we ask what the observations are observations *of*.

Much of what we know about people is produced by comparison. We measure, classify, average, cluster, correlate, and compress. Those operations preserve relations among cases: where people differ, which differences tend to move together, and how those differences relate to other measurable features. An explanation of a person asks a different question: what produced this case?

A representation can therefore contain real knowledge about differences among people without explaining any particular person being compared. Comparison and singular causal explanation are different epistemic tasks. Personality genetics makes the difference unusually clear.

Heritability makes the boundary visible. If a personality score has a SNP heritability of 10 percent, that does not mean that 10 percent of an individual's personality is genetic.

Expand, no jargon.

It means that, within a specified population, historical period, measurement regime, and range of environments, some portion of the variance in that measured score covaries with measured common genetic variation. The estimate describes differences across cases; it does not decompose one case into genetic and non-genetic parts.

The boundary matters especially when major causal structures are shared across nearly everyone being measured. Participants in a contemporary cohort may share a language, legal institutions, schools, technologies, social conventions, scientific concepts, communication systems, and centuries of accumulated knowledge embodied outside any one person. Those shared structures may profoundly affect what people can think, notice, value, and do. Yet because they are shared, they may contribute relatively little to the variance being partitioned.

Stop. Abstract it.

**Variance contribution is not equivalent to total causal importance.** Some of the largest causes may contribute little to measured variance precisely because nearly everyone possesses them. That is not a defect in variance analysis. It marks the boundary of what variance analysis explains.

The problem begins even earlier, because personality research does not encounter “agreeableness” or “openness” directly. It encounters observations: what people report about themselves, what others report about them, and what their recorded actions show. Researchers then compress patterns of covariance among selected observations into dimensions.

Compression is indispensable because a useful representation must leave things out. A personality score preserves selected regularities while discarding much of the causal history that produced them. That allows the score to support comparison, prediction, and reuse across studies and institutions. The problem appears only when the regularity preserved by the representation is treated as the causal structure that produced it.

Two people can therefore receive similar agreeableness scores for different reasons. One may accommodate others because of religious duty, another because they value reciprocity, and a third because they fear conflict or act strategically. Similar observable outputs can be produced by different explanatory histories.

Compress it.

If different explanatory histories $E_i$ can produce the same observable $O_i$:

$$
[
E_1 \rightarrow O_1
]
[
E_2 \rightarrow O_2
]
$$

then
$$
[
O_1 \approx O_2
]
$$

does not establish
$$
[
E_1 \approx E_2.
]
$$

The similarity in observation is real, and the comparison may be useful. But the shared observable does not establish a shared underlying explanation. A representation built to compare people is not yet an explanation of the people being compared.

Yes, but these results are durable. They replicate across studies.

Replication can strengthen the representation without dissolving this distinction. Several personality instruments may converge; self-report and close-other report may agree; the same genetic associations may appear across multiple cohorts; within-family designs may reduce some forms of confounding. These procedures can eliminate many possible errors and show that a pattern is not merely an artifact of one questionnaire, one sample, or one analytical choice.

But replication within a representation does not by itself establish what the representation represents causally. More observations can make a compression more reliable. They cannot, without further explanation, turn the compression into the person. 

Name it.

**Replication can stabilize a compression without identifying its causal referent.** Precision, prediction, and replication can all improve a representation while leaving the represented object and the representation distinct.

Now let that distinction reach *you*.

You, too, can be measured, compared, classified, predicted, placed on dimensions, and described by patterns that remain stable for years. If those representations preserve only selected relations, however, a harder question appears:

> What would it mean to explain you?

Simply adding more variables does not answer it. A higher-dimensional profile is still a representation, a denser measurement is still a measurement, and a more precise prediction is still a prediction. The missing object is not merely more detail. It is the causal history by which you became you.

That causal history does not require opposing genes to knowledge. Genes are themselves a form of biological knowledge: products of evolutionary variation, selection, and retention, physically embodied in structures that help build and regulate organisms. Genetic variation can alter sensory systems, neural development, physiology, memory capacities, affective tendencies, and other conditions under which you develop.

The relevant distinction is therefore not nature versus nurture. It is between different forms of knowledge and different causal levels.

You inherit biological knowledge through genes. But you also enter a world containing knowledge that already exists outside any one mind: in language, technologies, institutions, arguments, mathematics, stories, laws, and scientific theories. Call this **objective knowledge**: knowledge embodied in transmissible structures and products that you can encounter without having created them.

The encounter is uneven. Some objective knowledge is taught, some inferred, some misunderstood or rejected. Some becomes skill that you can exercise without being able to state all the rules that make the skill possible; these are *inexplicit capacities*. Some encountered knowledge creates problems that did not previously exist for you. 

Compress it.

The sequence of problems you encounter, carry, and reformulate is your **individual problem history**. Some encountered knowledge is transformed into explanations that did not previously exist at all.

Your development is therefore not well represented by a simple chain such as

$$
\text{gene}
\rightarrow
\text{trait}
\rightarrow
\text{behavior}.
$$

A more faithful structure is closer to:

$$
\begin{gather*}
\text{biological knowledge}
+
\text{objective knowledge encountered}
\\
+
\text{individual problem history}
+
\text{inexplicit capacities}
\\
+
\text{criticism}
+
\text{new explanation}
\rightarrow
\text{action}.
\end{gather*}
$$

That seems a jumble. Explain.

Every part of this process is physical, but the terms are not interchangeable. It is a causal architecture of singular personal development and action.

Genes help construct the organism in which your later explanations will exist. They do not contain the language you later learn, the argument that changes your mind, the problem that becomes salient next year, or the explanation you may create tomorrow.

Historical change makes the distinction easier to see. Imagine a person regarded as highly agreeable five hundred years ago. That person might have been dutiful, compassionate, and socially respected while accepting punishments, hierarchies, or obligations that many people today would reject. The genome need not have changed appreciably for the meaning of socially admired conduct to change enormously.

What changed was knowledge.

Moral explanations were criticized, institutions changed, and new concepts became available. Practices once taken for granted became problems. Ideas about equality and rights, punishment and childhood, and political or religious legitimacy were revised and transmitted.

A biological disposition toward social accommodation might persist through such changes. Yet the actions through which it is expressed, the reasons given for those actions, and the moral meaning of the behavior can all change. Biological continuity therefore does not guarantee continuity in the explanatory meaning of behavior. You are not merely the stable bearer of a disposition; you also inhabit a changing world of objective knowledge and can alter the explanations through which that world is understood.

The same point applies to stability within one life. You may display the same behavioral regularity for twenty years. It does not, by itself, identify the causal structure responsible for the persistence.

The regularity may reflect a biological disposition, an explanation you have retained, an institution that has remained stable, a problem that you have never reformulated, or a habit that has never encountered effective criticism. Several of these causes may operate at once. Persistence alone does not tell us which causal history produced the persistence.

This matters especially because you are capable of creating knowledge.

A criticism can expose a weakness in an inherited explanation. A new distinction or tool can reorganize an old problem. Another person can change the framing under which the problem is understood. You may then create an explanation that was not previously present in either the genome or the surrounding culture.

After such a change, an old regularity may disappear. The earlier stability was real; what sustained it remained open. Human stability is retrospective: it tells us what persisted, not what had to persist.

We can now see more clearly what disappears when you are represented comparatively.

Missing from the representation may be which objective knowledge you encountered and how you interpreted it, which problems became salient, and which criticisms reorganized earlier explanations. It may also omit which inexplicit capacities shaped what you noticed or did, which institutions constrained the available alternatives, and which explanations you created or may create next.

The problem is therefore not merely that a population model has low resolution. Comparison and causal explanation are different epistemic tasks. A representation can become more detailed without becoming the history it represents.

Return to personality genetics.

Genetic differences among persons are real. Genes causally affect development. Common genetic variation can covary with measured differences in personality scores, and personality factors can capture reproducible regularities across populations. Those results can be scientifically useful.

But they do not, by themselves, explain the semantic content of your knowledge or why one criticism mattered and another did not. They do not identify which objective knowledge reorganized your understanding or contain the problem history through which you changed. They also do not determine whether a stable behavior is biologically constrained, culturally sustained, institutionally reinforced, inexplicitly learned, or maintained by an explanation you continue to accept. Nor do they specify which explanation you may create next.

Restate the comparison.

The genetics result concerns one explanatory object: variation across cases. The person concerns another: the causal organization of a singular knowledge-creating history. The two are related. They are not identical.

The danger appears when the boundary between them is crossed without supplying the additional explanation the crossing requires. The sequence can look like this:

this person often behaves this way  
→ this person receives a stable score on a dimension  
→ the score is treated as a trait the person possesses  
→ variation in the trait is associated with genetic variation  
→ the trait is treated as part of the person's biological psychological architecture.

Each step may sound small, but together they cross several explanatory boundaries. The first statement concerns observed behavior. The second concerns a measurement. The third converts a measurement dimension into an entity. The fourth relates variation in that measured entity to genetic variation across a population. The fifth imports the population relationship back into the causal organization of the individual.

The final statement may be true.

Yes, but it contains more explanatory content than the original observations supplied. That additional content requires its own explanation; it does not arrive automatically with the measurement.

Once this distinction is preserved, personality genetics need not be inflated or dismissed. The field may reveal biological contributions to variation, identify developmental conditions worth explaining, reveal regularities that persist across populations and instruments, and help locate parts of the biological architecture through which persons become possible. Those achievements still do not explain why you became you.

Such an explanation would require the singular causal history by which biological conditions, encountered objective knowledge, interpretations, problems, criticism, inexplicit capacities, and newly created explanations became organized in you. No alternative discipline follows automatically from that demand, and no new taxonomy of persons is required. The point is narrower: silently identifying a population construct with you adds explanatory content that the population construct itself does not supply.

The encounter with personality genetics began with a legitimate question:

> How much of the variation in measured personality is associated with genetic variation?

The answer can be informative on its own terms. But once the epistemic structure is taken seriously, another question appears.

The population and the person are not merely the same explanatory object viewed at different resolutions. One concerns variation across cases. The other concerns the causal organization of a singular knowledge-creating entity.

What is the new problem?

The problem is no longer how to construct a better trait model or measure individuality more finely. It is individuality itself: What is your individuality if it cannot be identified with the dimensions along which persons can be compared?

<a id="chapter-02"></a>

### II. Populations, Fast and Slow

What happens when psychological constructs built from populations are used to explain individual people? 

The constructs, formulated in research papers, enter psychology as a profession, a clinical practice, an institutional technology, and a way of talking about individuals.

The epistemic question changes with that move. It is no longer only whether a population-level construct corresponds to a stable psychological entity. It is whether knowledge created from relations among people can legitimately travel into explanations, diagnoses, interventions, and judgments about one particular person.

Compare it.

$$
\text{population regularity}
\neq
\text{individual causal explanation}.
$$

Population research can establish recurring differences, covariances, treatment-response averages, risks, and predictive regularities. 

State the new problem.

What structure is operating in this case, how did it come to operate, and what would have to change for the outcome to change?

The two forms of knowledge can bear on one another. They are not interchangeable. Something additional is needed to carry a result established among people into a causal claim about one person.

**Classification** is one way that transfer happens. A person is recognized as an instance of a researched category, and knowledge associated with the category is brought into the case. 

That move can be useful. It can also become circular when the category restates the person's actions in the vocabulary from which the category was built and then presents the restatement as a cause.

The problem is not that people have nothing in common. They plainly do. It is that commonality in what can be observed does not by itself establish commonality in the causal structures that matter to a person's present problem. Once that distinction is taken seriously, the person can no longer appear merely as the final recipient of population knowledge. The person remains the thing to be explained.

Outline and explain the steps.

<a id="chapter-02--1-from-population-knowledge-to-an-individual-case"></a>

#### 1. From population knowledge to an individual case

Conventional psychological research does not primarily produce biographies of persons. It produces standardized representations that can be reused across cases and institutions: diagnostic categories, trait dimensions, psychometric scales, normative distributions, developmental benchmarks, risk estimates, symptom clusters, treatment-response averages, standardized intervention protocols, actuarial decision rules, and population-level correlates.

These products are useful partly because they compress variation. A diagnostic class connects one patient to a large literature. A trait score permits comparison with a reference population. A symptom scale makes change measurable. A randomized trial estimates whether one intervention tends to outperform another for a defined class of participants.

Abstract it.

The practical architecture is therefore:

$$
\text{research population}
\rightarrow
\text{classification}
\rightarrow
\text{population expectation}
\rightarrow
\text{individual decision}.
$$

That architecture makes psychological observations reusable across schools, hospitals, insurers, courts, employers, clinics, and other institutions. A diagnosis may help a patient obtain care or accommodations. A risk estimate may draw attention to a danger. A treatment literature may identify an intervention worth trying. A measure may make otherwise vague change visible.

None of those uses requires the representation to be the cause of the case.

A diagnosis makes the distinction visible. The clinician observes a set of features and says, in effect:

> This person resembles the class of people represented by diagnostic category D.

The category then indexes accumulated knowledge:

$$
D
\rightarrow
\{\text{common course, common risks, common comorbidities, common treatment responses}\}.
$$

That can be practically important. The inflation occurs when

$$
\text{resembles category D}
$$

quietly becomes

$$
D \text{ explains this person}.
$$

Generalize it.

The same shift can occur outside diagnosis. A personality score can begin as a summary of responses and end as an explanation of why the person acts. An intelligence score can begin as standardized performance and end as a statement about the person's cognitive essence. A heritability estimate can begin as a property of population variance and end as a statement about what portion of the person was biologically determined.

The practical usefulness of a representation helps obscure the shift because the same term can perform two different jobs. It can identify a recurring pattern. It can also appear to name the mechanism producing that pattern. The classificatory procedure can establish the first. The second requires separate evidence.

Treatment selection shows why the distinction matters even when the practical inference is sound. Suppose a research literature shows that people in class $C$ improve, on average, with treatment $T$. A clinician encountering a new person who fits $C$ then has reason to consider $T$:

$$
C
\rightarrow
\text{evidence that }T\text{ is worth trying}.
$$

That does not establish:

$$
C
\rightarrow
\text{causal explanation of the person's problem}.
$$

A treatment can work across causally heterogeneous cases. If a breathing protocol reduces panic in many people, its efficacy does not show that every recipient's panic arose from the same explanatory history. If exposure reduces avoidance across many cases, successful exposure does not show that one psychological cause generated every avoidance pattern.

Case formulation moves closer to the individual because it asks a different question from diagnosis alone.

State the new problem.

Why does this person have this condition, in this form, at this time?

A formulation may include developmental history, current relationships, beliefs, habits, reinforcement patterns, trauma, coping strategies, physiological vulnerabilities, and environmental stressors. Yet its explanatory parts can still be imported from population-derived constructs such as avoidance, attachment style, core beliefs, rumination, maladaptive coping, trait anxiety, impulsivity, or perfectionism. The case is then individualized by recombining standardized pieces.

That is not necessarily an error. Shared mechanisms do exist. 

What licenses the transfer from a shared description to a shared causal structure?

Population knowledge can apply to an individual case only when the relevant mechanism is sufficiently stable across the people grouped together for the purpose at hand.

The implied sequence is:
$$
\begin{gathered}
\text{similar observable}
\rightarrow
\text{same construct}
\\
\rightarrow
\text{sufficiently similar causal mechanism}
\rightarrow
\text{population evidence applies}.
\end{gathered}
$$

The measurement rule may establish the first transition. The practical inference depends on the last. The step that still requires a causal warrant is the one between them:

$$
\text{same construct}
\rightarrow
\text{same relevant causal mechanism}.
$$

Name that missing structure.

Call that transition a claim of **local psychological homogenization**: members need not be psychologically identical generally, but must be causally homogeneous with respect to the mechanism being invoked. It does not say that all people are alike. It says that, for this explanatory or practical purpose, differences among them can be ignored because the category has captured the causally relevant commonality.

Sometimes that may be justified. A tightly characterized visual deficit may arise from a shared lesion. A specific pharmacological mechanism may be sufficiently invariant. A well-specified learning mechanism may transfer reliably. Broad personality constructs, diagnostic classes, and socially saturated behavioral categories leave more room for causally different lives to satisfy the same observational criteria.

Generalize the problem.

A result $R_P$ is established from variation among many people, while the practical claim concerns individual $i$:

$$
R_P \Rightarrow R_i.
$$

The problem of supplying such a warrant will be called the problem of **transportability**.

What makes that implication valid in this case? 

One reason the warrant cannot be assumed is that a relation among people and a process unfolding within one person are different objects. For example,

$$
\operatorname{Cov}_{persons}(X,Y) > 0
$$

does not imply

$$
X_i(t) \rightarrow Y_i(t+1).
$$

Explain.

If people differ in their dynamics, or if those dynamics change over time, a between-person average need not describe the dynamics of any particular individual. The formal conditions under which a structure estimated across persons also describes the structure unfolding within persons are discussed under the problem of **ergodicity**. The plain-language point comes first: averaging across people does not automatically recover the process occurring within one person.

That distinction exposes three separate transfers:

$$
\text{between-person structure}
\rightarrow
\text{within-person structure},
$$

then

$$
\text{within-person statistical structure}
\rightarrow
\text{causal structure},
$$

then

$$
\text{present causal structure}
\rightarrow
\text{future stability despite learning and criticism}.
$$

Ergodicity covers mainly the first transition. Causal inference concerns the second. The third transfer, from a present causal model to its future stability in a knowledge-creating person, completes the **three-transfer problem**.

Successful classification establishes none of these automatically.

What happens next?

<a id="chapter-02--2-you-become-the-explanatory-object"></a>

#### 2. You become the explanatory object

The transport problem changes character once you are no longer treated as the endpoint of the analysis but as the object that still needs explaining.

> Consider a psychologist observing a sustained conversation characterized by recursive criticism, abstraction, concern with classification, insistence on conceptual consistency, and repeated interrogation of the assumptions underlying psychological research.

From those observations, familiar hypotheses are available: high openness, intellectualization, obsessionality, perfectionism, rumination, need for cognition, or unusual autonomy needs.

Now flip the context:

> The conversation is part of a deliberate test of a software system the participant invented, specifically to observe how that system behaves when exposed to an intellectual environment that does not inherit from the same intellectual lineage.

The outward behavior has not changed. The problem situation has.

Many of the classificatory interpretations can become causally unnecessary because the behavior is now intelligible as part of a particular project.

Before that information:

$$
O
\rightarrow
\text{candidate trait or diagnosis}.
$$

After it:

$$
O
\leftarrow
\text{software-testing problem}.
$$

This is stronger than the claim that context matters.

The added information can remove the need for an entire class of psychological explanations while leaving the observable behavior untouched. The same outward pattern is therefore compatible with radically different causal histories.

The categorical interpretation can be preserved by saying:

> You wrote the software because you possess the very traits I identified.

But now the counterexample has been absorbed into the category.

Abstract the structure.

The invention becomes evidence of the trait, and the trait becomes the explanation of the invention:

$$
\text{novel achievement}
\rightarrow
\text{trait classification}
\rightarrow
\text{trait invoked as cause of novel achievement}.
$$

What disappears is the content of the achievement. What problem was being solved? Why this architecture? Why this intellectual lineage? Which prior explanations failed? Which criticism produced the new design? Why this solution rather than another?

The trait vocabulary does not answer those questions. It restates the creator using terms abstracted from population regularities. Novelty has been explained by commonality.

Once you are the explanatory object, a different sequence becomes necessary. The inquiry has to recover the particular difficulty as you encountered it, the understanding through which it became a problem, the possibilities then available, the tentative solutions attempted, the criticisms that altered them, and the organization that resulted.

That whole concrete configuration—the circumstances, your understanding of them, the knowledge already available, and the possibilities you can conceive—will be called your **problem situation**.

The same external event can therefore constitute different psychological problems for different people. The event enters a different history of explanations, expectations, skills, habits, and unresolved difficulties. What it means for you, and what responses become possible, depends partly on your history.

Compress it.

An individual-first explanation can be compressed as:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\text{particular problem situation}
\rightarrow
\text{relevant knowledge history}
\\
\rightarrow
\text{candidate causal explanation}
\rightarrow
\text{criticism against the case}.
\end{gathered}
$$

This differs from a classification-first sequence:

$$
\text{individual observations}
\rightarrow
\text{population category}
\rightarrow
\text{likely mechanism}
\rightarrow
\text{protocol}.
$$

The contrast is not that one sequence uses general knowledge and the other rejects it. The difference is where the causal claim is earned. In the first sequence, general findings become candidates whose relevance has to survive criticism against the case. In the second, the category can too easily stand in for the mechanism.

Individuality now becomes a **positive explanatory problem** rather than the **residue left after regularities have been extracted**. To explain you is to reconstruct how a particular structure came to exist: which problems became salient, which explanations were retained, which criticisms altered them, and which changes reorganized what you could subsequently perceive or do.

Not all of the relevant knowledge need be available as a sentence you can report. Some appears in habits, expectations, skills, sensitivities, or ways of interpreting a situation without being fully articulated. Knowledge that operates in this way will be called **inexplicit knowledge**. Its importance is causal, not mystical: conduct can depend on retained capacities and expectations that are expressed in action without first being stated as propositions.

Neither explicit self-description nor an observed inexplicit regularity is automatically an explanation. Both are evidence from which a causal structure may be conjectured and criticized.

You, on this account, are neither an opaque exception nor a bundle of measurements. You are a **historically developing causal organization** whose present responses depend partly on the problems encountered, the explanations and habits retained, the criticisms that changed them, and the possibilities you can now conceive.

Generality does not disappear. It changes location.

What generalizes need not be the psychological content of every person. The recurring element may instead be the explanatory method: recover the problem, reconstruct the relevant knowledge, propose causal dependencies, expose them to criticism, and revise them when the case resists.

Shared cognitive and biological mechanisms remain part of the explanation's background. Two people may share language competence, memory architecture, perception, and many physiological capacities while interpreting the same criticism in opposite ways because their explanatory histories differ. The shared mechanisms make many responses possible. They do not by themselves determine the individual meaning of the event.

Nor does individuality imply that you require a private science with no recurring mechanisms. Recurrence has to be established at the level at which the causal claim is made. A population category can suggest where to look. Satisfying its observational rule does not by itself settle what is operating in you.

Right. So population knowledge like classification, scales, averages, traits, diagnoses, risk estimates and generalization moves fast, but knowledge of individuals, the causal reconstruction of their history, problem situation, the mechanisms of conjecture, criticism, and revision moves slow.

Return to the population knowledge and restate within this framework.

<a id="chapter-02--3-returning-to-population-knowledge"></a>

#### 3. Returning to population knowledge

With you now treated as the explanatory object, familiar population findings can be reconsidered without discarding what they actually establish.

Suppose a study finds that measured variation in parenting explains relatively little variation in some adult characteristic. That result answers a question about differences within the studied population: how much of the observed variation among people is associated with measured differences in parenting? It does not by itself answer the larger causal question of how parenting contributed to producing the phenomenon at all.

A cause can be nearly constant across a population and therefore explain little variance within that population while remaining indispensable to the phenomenon.

Language makes the distinction clear. Among native Japanese speakers, exposure to Japanese may explain almost none of the variance in who speaks Japanese. Yet Japanese linguistic culture remains central to explaining why they speak Japanese at all.

Compare that structure.

The distinction is:

$$
\text{explanation of residual variation}
\neq
\text{explanation of the phenomenon itself}.
$$

An imagined society makes the consequence concrete. Suppose "Agreeablestan" transmits, through language, institutions, norms, parenting, peers, law, ritual, and education, an unusually strong cultural system of agreeable conduct. A child whose genotype would weakly predict lower agreeableness in a Western dataset might nevertheless develop into an entirely ordinary Agreeablestan citizen. Even if subtle biological differences remained, the developed social and psychological organization could be overwhelmingly shaped by common cultural knowledge.

A behavioral-genetic result could still accurately describe residual differences among members of that population. What it would not contain by itself is an explanation of you as a whole. Explaining variation after common developmental structures have done much of the work is not the same as explaining those structures.

This distinction also clarifies the recurrent qualifications attached to heritability claims. Statements such as personality is heritable, intelligence is heritable, or particular traits have genetic correlates are often accompanied by reminders that heritability is not determinism, genes are not destiny, environment still matters, and population statistics do not determine individuals. Those qualifications matter because the underlying quantities concern relations in populations, not a partition of the causal composition of a person.

The slippage appears when a population relation is summarized in language that sounds like a claim about what the trait itself is. "Genetic basis of personality" sounds like a statement about the constitution of personality. "Genetic covariance with variance in a psychometric phenotype" states a narrower relation. The second says less because the evidence establishes less.

No hidden ideological motive is needed for the stronger reading to appear. Once a research program provides

$$
\text{trait}
\rightarrow
\text{heritability}
\rightarrow
\text{associated loci}
\rightarrow
\text{polygenic prediction},
$$

a parent, clinician, institution, or policymaker can begin to treat the represented trait as though its future expression were already partly contained in the genetic description. The practical form of the result makes that interpretation easy to imagine even when the population evidence does not license it.

Classification has another property that becomes visible only after returning from the person-level inquiry: the representation can enter the causal system it represents. A score, diagnosis, or risk classification can affect access to treatment, educational placement, disability status, insurance decisions, institutional credibility, legal judgments, employment, and self-conception.

A diagnosis can provide relief and useful language while also becoming part of identity. A trait can provide concise description while also becoming a presumed limit. A genetic association can describe population variance while also becoming a story about what a child is destined to be.

People can encounter the theory applied to them, incorporate it into self-understanding, resist it, exploit it, or have their opportunities reorganized by institutions that use it. The classification can therefore become one of the causes shaping what happens next.

That reflexivity is methodological as well as ethical. If applying a representation changes the self-understanding or institutional conditions of the person being represented, a later causal explanation may have to include the effects of the representation itself.

Nothing in this argument removes the practical value of population knowledge. It narrows the kind of claim that has been established. Population evidence can reveal risks, common responses, useful interventions, recurring patterns, and possibilities that deserve attention. By itself, it does not complete the causal explanation of the person to whom the evidence is applied.

Now point that population knowledge at the individual.

<a id="chapter-02--4-individual-explanation-under-criticism"></a>

#### 4. Individual explanation under criticism

Turning to you creates a symmetrical danger. If your case is treated as so particular that no general standard can touch it, explanation collapses into storytelling. Any narrative could be protected from criticism by declaring you unique.

An explanation of you therefore has to expose its causal commitments. It needs to identify the problem being solved and the relevant knowledge, including both what you can state and what appears through habits or expectations. It also has to specify the proposed dependencies, the observations those dependencies account for, the counterfactuals they imply, the evidence that would defeat them, and a rival explanation capable of replacing them.

Neither intimacy nor classification supplies causal authority.

There is no such thing as causal authority. Restate the mechanism.

A clinician's statement that they understand you does not establish an explanation. Your own self-description may be corrected. A population category does not become a mechanism merely because you satisfy the category. All three remain open to criticism.

Several established problems in psychological inference fit inside this reciprocal demand. Relations estimated across many people need not describe the process unfolding within you; this is the familiar contrast between nomothetic and idiographic description and the formal problem of non-ergodicity. But intensive individual measurement does not finish the job either. A high-resolution time series remains a statistical description until its causal interpretation is independently explained.

Stop! We're trying to explain *you*, not psychology! Focus on the constraints.

Variation across situations adds another constraint. Stable tendencies can appear as conditional patterns rather than invariant outputs. But for you, the relevant situation is not always exhausted by the external stimulus configuration. The **same event can become a different problem when different knowledge makes it intelligible in a different way**.

Historical and reflexive approaches add a further complication. Psychological regularities can change when culture changes, and psychological knowledge can itself alter behavior. At the level of your own case, the causal point is that you can acquire, criticize, and create knowledge. **New knowledge can reorganize the system that generated the earlier behavior**.

Statistical sophistication does not remove that explanatory burden. Statistics can perform excellent error elimination while leaving open what causal structure a construct name refers to. The problem is not quantification. It is **using quantification to answer a causal question before the explanatory object has been established**.

These criticisms also have limits. Descriptive regularity does not disappear merely because a trait is not a deep causal primitive. Cultural explanation does not imply a biological blank slate. Ordinary genetic variation may alter affect, attention, arousal, perception, or other conditions under which problems arise. The narrower claim is:

> Biological difference cannot be promoted into a limit on explanatory possibility without a mechanism establishing that limit.

Nor does an individual-first approach license unaided clinical intuition. Statistical prediction can outperform unaided professional judgment. Population evidence can still generate possibilities, identify risks, and prioritize interventions. The distinction concerns inferential role, not whether population knowledge is allowed into the case.

Historical or social construction does not imply unreality either. A psychological category can be historically constructed and still track something causally real. Every scientific category is invented in the sense that the classification is made by people. The relevant question is whether the proposed causal structure can be altered freely without losing what it explains. A structure that cannot be varied in that way will be called here a **hard-to-vary explanation**.

Good enough. But we need some structure to carry it. Compress these ideas algorithmically.

<a id="chapter-02--5-four-tests"></a>

#### 5. Four tests

The argument can now be compressed into four tests. Each asks for a warrant that either population classification or person-specific explanation can fail to provide.

First: has a relation estimated across people actually been shown to describe a process within you? This is the **Ergodicity Test**:

> When population evidence is applied to you, what establishes that the relevant between-person relationship corresponds to a process within you?

Without that demonstration, the population structure remains population evidence rather than an individual mechanism.

Second: has a name for a recurring statistical pattern been mistaken for the causal structure that generates it? This is the **Reification Test**:

> When a psychological construct names a recurring covariance pattern, what independently established causal structure does the construct refer to?

A stable factor solution is not itself the answer. The construct may summarize the observations successfully while leaving open what produces them.

Third: could an apparently stable limitation be reorganized if you acquired an effective criticism of the knowledge producing the behavior? This is the **Epistemic Plasticity Test**:

> What would have to be true for explanatory revision to reorganize this pattern, and what mechanism would prevent that reorganization if the constraint is claimed to be fixed?

A claim of fixed constraint therefore carries a causal burden. Stability observed so far does not establish stability under knowledge not yet acquired.

Fourth: what could show the account of you to be false? This is the **Idiographic Discipline Test**:

> What observation or counterfactual would defeat the explanation?

If no possible finding could count against the account, individuality has become a shield against criticism rather than an explanatory object.

The four tests impose reciprocal discipline. Population models have to earn individual applicability. Individual explanations have to earn causal status.

The contrast is therefore not statistics versus stories, quantitative versus qualitative, general versus unique, or objective versus subjective. The relevant distinction is between representations whose evidential reach is known and explanations whose causal claims have survived criticism at the level where they are being applied.

I find it ironic that we're categorizing and systemizing the thing that we first criticized as categorical and systemic. But let's wrap this up with a tentative solution to our problem.

<a id="chapter-02--6-what-can-population-knowledge-reveal-about-you"></a>

#### 6. What can population knowledge reveal about you?

The inquiry can now return to its starting point. Conventional psychology produces knowledge about population differentiation, behavioral measurement, classification, prediction, intervention efficacy, and institutional decision support. Those are substantial achievements and can produce useful, sometimes life-improving technologies.

The explanatory error begins only when success at those tasks is treated as though it automatically supplied a causal account of you.

Once you enter as the explanatory object, two questions that had been allowed to collapse into one have to be kept distinct:

> Which known structure do you instantiate?

and

> What structure is actually operating here, how did it come to operate, and what would show that we are wrong about it?

The first question can narrow possibilities, surface risks, and connect the case to accumulated knowledge. The second asks whether any of those possibilities actually explain you. Classification can begin that investigation. Naming the resemblance cannot complete it.

The deeper contrast is therefore not between generality and uniqueness. It is between **classification-first explanation** and **individual-first explanation**.

Classification-first explanation is fast. It begins with a representation whose meaning was stabilized across a population and asks how you fit it. Individual-first explanation is slow. It begins with your actual problem situation and asks which general findings, if any, survive criticism when transported into your case.

That change of direction also changes what population knowledge can mean personally. A population result may show that people resembling you in some measured respect have often followed a certain course, responded to a certain intervention, or displayed a certain risk. That is information about possibilities that may deserve attention. It is not yet an explanation of why you are as you are.

A causal explanation requires the organization particular to the case to be reconstructed: the relevant problems, the knowledge through which they are understood, the explicit and inexplicit expectations that shape action, the criticisms already encountered, and the changes that remain possible.

That reconstruction illuminates the next problem. If you can acquire criticism, create new explanations, and reorganize the knowledge through which a situation is understood, then the object being explained is not merely particular. You can change the very structure from which your previous regularities were generated.

The remaining question is therefore harder than how to model an individual more accurately:

> How can a causal explanation of you remain testable while taking seriously that you can acquire new knowledge that changes the causal organization being explained?

<a id="chapter-03"></a>

### III. The Anxious Authorities

At the social level, the problem of *you* changes because society is not merely a distant influence. It supplies much of the material with which you think: language, rules, roles, expectations, explanations, institutions, laws, stories, technologies, and inherited ways of framing problems. Call it **social objective knowledge**, or social knowledge.

Social knowledge can therefore act on you far more directly than a statistical relation between genetic variation and behavior. That makes the social case both stronger and more dangerous.

The error is not that society has little causal effect. The error appears when knowledge about a social regularity is treated as knowledge of the kind of person who participates in it.

Abstract that idea.

The conventional movement is familiar:

$$
\text{group regularity}
\rightarrow
\text{group property}
\rightarrow
\text{individual explanation}.
$$

A bureaucracy exists. A legal system exists. A language exists. A political doctrine exists. The social object can be real, and the regularity measured across it can also be real. But the reality of the object does not make the category naming it an explanation of the individual who encounters it.

Locate the pattern in politics.

A political survey makes the distinction unusually clear. Suppose two people both endorse proposition $Q$:

$$
P_1 \rightarrow Q
$$

and

$$
P_2 \rightarrow Q.
$$

The survey may have discovered something straightforward: both people presently endorse the same proposition. What it has not discovered is why either person endorses it. One may have reached it through moral reasoning, another through personal experience, economic argument, trust in an authority, or failure to consider an alternative.

Compare it.

The important relation is:

$$
\text{same expressed knowledge}
\neq
\text{same explanatory history}.
$$

The group description can represent something real while leaving the person unexplained.

The social case goes further because many social objects are themselves shareable structures that survive any one person's participation in them. A language can be learned by different speakers. A constitution can be read, criticized, amended, obeyed, or ignored by different citizens. A professional code can constrain people who disagree about its justification. A moral tradition can be inherited before you can state the principles it contains.

Call these publicly available structures **objective knowledge**: knowledge embodied in forms that can be evaluated across solitary minds. You do not begin by inventing the language, law, institution, or tradition. You encounter it already there.

That encounter changes what becomes thinkable and actionable. A rule can close an option. A norm can make one action intelligible and another shameful. A hierarchy can attach sanctions to disagreement. A doctrine can supply an explanation before you have encountered a criticism of it.

A gene cannot tell a child that adults know better. A culture can. A gene cannot tell an employee that managers are entitled to decide. An institution can. A gene cannot tell a citizen that obedience to authority is virtuous. A political tradition can.

Society therefore does not simply surround you. It helps constitute the field of problems, expectations, explanations, and constraints within which you act.

Call that surrounding structure your **problem situation**: the problems you can see, the knowledge you have inherited, the options you believe are available, the sanctions you anticipate, the explanations you can presently use, and the criticisms you can presently formulate.

If social knowledge enters your problem situation, what explains your action?

Take a bureaucrat. At work, the person may be formal, procedural, risk-averse, deferential to hierarchy, and emotionally restrained. At home, the same person may be playful, spontaneous, irreverent, affectionate, and improvisational.

Labels such as role, organizational culture, situational norm, or identity activation can mark real regularities. But they do not yet tell us what this person understands themselves to be doing.

The person may understand the workplace as a system in which procedure defines admissible action, disagreement carries career costs, success means avoiding unauthorized risk, and superiors possess legitimate decision rights. At home, those problems may disappear. Other obligations, possibilities, and expectations become active.

Abstract that structure.

The causal structure is closer to:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\text{socially inherited knowledge}
+
\text{individual problem situation}
\\
\rightarrow
\text{interpretation}
\rightarrow
\text{action}.
\end{gathered}
$$

The same mind can behave differently because different knowledge and different problems become active in different circumstances. No contradiction in personality is required.

This does not make the institutional regularity unreal. If an organization gives many people similar procedures, incentives, sanctions, vocabularies, and decision rights, similar behavior is unsurprising. The regularity may explain something important about the institution. The point is narrower: the causal route into action still passes through a person who interprets what those conditions mean.

Nor is interpretation unconstrained. Institutions can alter the actual possibility space around you. Law changes which actions are permitted. Censorship changes which criticism can circulate. Employment hierarchy changes who possesses formal decision rights.

Social conditions can also remove conditions needed for the normal exercise of explanatory agency. Solitary confinement, for example, can remove ordinary social interaction and contribute to psychological deterioration. That does not make the mind a lesser kind of mind. It shows that explanatory agency has enabling conditions: a universal capacity can be impaired when conditions required for its exercise are removed.

Compare it.

The distinction is therefore not between social causation and individual freedom. It is between two different explanatory claims:

$$
\text{restricted action space}
\neq
\text{restricted explanatory capacity}.
$$

You may act cautiously because criticism is punished. An employee may defer because formal authority is backed by sanctions. A bureaucrat may follow procedure because procedure determines what counts as an admissible move. Those conditions can explain recurring behavior without becoming an intrinsic property of the people who behave that way.

This is where social essentialism enters. 

Stop. There's no such thing as an essence. Reverse the definition.

Behavior produced under conditions is redescribed as a property of the people who inhabit them: bureaucrats are rigid, members of hierarchical societies are deferential, children are suggestible.

Compress it.

The observation may summarize a distribution. The explanatory inflation occurs when:

$$
\text{behavior under conditions}
$$

becomes

$$
\text{property of person}.
$$

A social category can tell us which roles exist, what sanctions are likely, which propositions are widely shared, or which actions are formally possible. It does not by itself tell us which of those things this person accepts, fears, misunderstands, criticizes, combines, or rejects. That requires your explanatory history.

Much of that history need not be explicit. A child can learn who is allowed to interrupt whom before possessing a theory of hierarchy. An employee can learn which disagreements are career-limiting without formulating a doctrine of managerial authority. A student can learn which questions count as challenges before being able to describe the rule being enforced.

Because this is knowledge rather than essence, it can conflict with other knowledge. You can retain one rule in one domain and reject it in another. An inherited norm can remain invisible until criticism exposes it. An explanation can be revised without you becoming a different kind of mind.

Knowledge learned this way can remain inexplicit: operative in action before you can state the rule being followed.

You are therefore not merely the endpoint of social causation. You are where inherited social knowledge is interpreted, combined, criticized, and sometimes changed.

Authority makes the structure especially visible.

A persistent social pattern can be understood as a network of propositions, norms, habits, and institutional arrangements concerning who is entitled to decide for whom. It need not be a collective mind or a hidden social trait. Its content may be learned through recurring relations: parents over children, teachers over students, managers over employees, experts over non-experts, rulers over citizens.

These relations do not merely recur independently. They can persist as inherited knowledge, reproduced through explicit propositions, inexplicit habits, recurring practices, and institutions. Call such a transmissible unit of social knowledge a **meme**. Where several such memes support and reproduce one another, they form a **memeplex**.
