The recurring knowledge concerning who is entitled to decide for whom can therefore be treated as an **authority memeplex**.

Abstract it again.

The relation can become familiar before anyone states it as a doctrine:

$$
\text{higher-status actor}
\rightarrow
\text{greater decision authority}.
$$

Modern liberal societies also inherit a newer memeplex organized around autonomy, equality, freedom of speech, democratic participation, freedom of conscience, informed consent, and individual rights. This newer knowledge can coexist with the older authority memeplex inside the same society and inside the same person. The newer vocabulary can therefore sit on top of older authority relations without fully replacing them. The older structure may reappear when applying the newer principle would dissolve an established authority relation.

One relation says:

$$
\text{person}
\rightarrow
\text{presumptive autonomy}.
$$

Another says:

$$
\text{authority differential}
\rightarrow
\text{legitimate control}.
$$

You may defend freedom of judgment in politics while treating obedience as obvious at work. An employee may resent managerial control and reproduce the same authority relation with a child. A professional may affirm autonomy while regarding expertise as sufficient grounds to override another person's interpretation.

A hidden trait called authoritarianism is not required to make those conflicts intelligible. Partially incompatible bodies of inherited knowledge may become active in different problem situations.

The personal question is then, which knowledge is active here, what problem does it appear to solve, and what criticism could expose the conflict?

Children put unusual pressure on this question because differences in knowledge and practical competence are obvious.

The familiar argument is:

> children know less, therefore adults should decide for them.

The first proposition is often true. The second introduces a stronger relation:

$$
\text{less knowledge}
\rightarrow
\text{less epistemic sovereignty}.
$$

Once stated in that form, the principle is not logically confined to childhood. It can be extended wherever one person or institution judges another to know less: patients, students, employees, voters, or populations regarded as vulnerable to misinformation.

When differences in knowledge are used to justify differences in your authority over your own judgment, the result is a doctrine of **graded epistemic personhood**.

The child case is relatively easy because unequal knowledge is visible. But unequal knowledge and unequal kinds of mind are not the same claim.

A pilot may know more than a passenger about landing an aircraft. A doctor may know more than a patient about a disease. An adult may know more than a child about traffic. These differences concern knowledge possessed in a domain. They do not establish a different capacity for creating knowledge.

Abstract it.

The distinction is:

$$
\text{knowledge possessed}
$$

versus

$$
\text{capacity for knowledge creation}.
$$

A child begins with less knowledge, fewer experiences, fewer available explanations, and less practical control over circumstances. Those are real features of the child's problem situation. Yet the child still has to interpret what happens. The child forms expectations, notices anomalies, invents explanations, imitates, asks questions, misunderstands, tests, criticizes, and revises.

Authority can therefore change more than what the child is allowed to do. It can change which problems the child is permitted to pursue, which explanations are available, and which criticisms survive long enough to develop.

Media makes that change easy to see.

One common model treats the child as a passive recipient. The medium acts; the child absorbs. Its causal structure is:

$$
\text{content}
\rightarrow
\text{mind}.
$$

We will call this **the bucket theory of mind**. Once the child is pictured as a container, controlling inputs looks like a direct way of controlling what enters the mind.

But the child cannot receive a medium without interpreting it. A child looking at a screen must conjecture what is happening, what matters, what another person intends, what will happen next, and which rules govern the situation.

Abstract it again.

The structure is closer to:

$$
\text{media environment}
\rightarrow
\text{problems encountered}
\rightarrow
\text{child's conjectures and criticism}.
$$

Removing a screen therefore does not merely remove content. It may terminate an active problem environment selected by the child. A parent may imagine that "go outside and play" moves the child into a richer world. The child may experience the opposite: a move from a dense unresolved problem space into one containing nothing presently salient.

The physical medium does not settle that difference. The explanation depends on what problem this child is pursuing through it.

That same distinction helps with recurring concern about new media. Reading, radio, television, the internet, social media, and generative AI differ technically and can generate different harms. Any specific criticism may turn out to be correct. But as one medium becomes ordinary infrastructure, concern can migrate to the next. That recurrence does not show that the specific criticisms are false. It suggests that the changing technical criticism may not exhaust the explanation. Each medium also changes the routes by which you encounter knowledge and who or what controls your next epistemic encounter.

Social media changes association. A rare interest once constrained by geography can become a searchable community:

$$
\text{rare interest}
+
\text{geographic dispersion}
\rightarrow
\text{searchable community}.
$$

That same structure can support ideological reinforcement, specialist collaboration, support networks, or scientific exchange. "Polarization" can describe one outcome without exhausting the architectural change.

Let's introduce AI as a new medium and contrast it with older forms of media.

Generative AI changes something else. Social media helps you find others already organized around an interest. A search engine retrieves from an existing informational landscape. A generative system can recombine inherited knowledge around a problem that may not yet correspond to an existing document, course, community, or established query. It can therefore create a responsive interaction around your present problem:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\text{individual problem}
\rightarrow
\text{generative system}
\\
\rightarrow
\text{candidate explanation}
\rightarrow
\text{criticism}
\rightarrow
\text{new problem}.
\end{gathered}
$$

Call it an **application of epistemic processing**.

For a child pursuing an unusual scientific, technical, philosophical, or artistic problem, the former bottleneck may have been the accidental availability of an adult or institution able to respond. A generative system can alter that bottleneck by making a candidate explanatory response immediately available.

That does not establish that the response is true, reliable, or worth retaining. It changes the problem situation. It changes what can be asked next and how quickly a candidate explanation can be produced, criticized, and replaced.

This is why opposite complaints about media need not identify one mechanism. Social media can be criticized for excessive differentiation; AI for excessive commonality; unusually capable AI for threatening human distinctiveness. Those claims concern different possible effects. What the media can share is a transfer of some **control over the next epistemic encounter** away from incumbent curators, away from the incumbent authorities.

And the authorities become anxious.

That transfer is not, by itself, a judgment about whether the change is good or bad. It identifies a change in the distribution of epistemic control.

Now return to the original social-scientific problem. This personal analysis changes its significance.

A theory about society can become part of society. A claim that children are vulnerable to media can alter parental behavior, school rules, platform policy, regulation, and public norms. Claims that workers require supervision, voters are irrational, social media polarizes, or AI causes dependence can likewise be built into institutions.

Once institutionalized, such claims cease to be mere descriptions. They become causal inputs into the lives of the people described.

Abstract it.

The sequence can be:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\text{population observation}
\rightarrow
\text{social category}
\rightarrow
\\
\text{policy interpretation}
\rightarrow
\text{institutional rule}
\rightarrow
\text{individual problem environment}.
\end{gathered}
$$

Suppose an association between media use and distress in a population of children is redescribed as "children are vulnerable to media," and that description then supports rules controlling children's access. Whether the policy works is a separate empirical question. The epistemic transition has already occurred: a class-level observation has been translated into an authority relation over particular people.

The social sciences therefore contain a reflexive causal route:

$$
\text{theory of society}
\rightarrow
\text{policy}
\rightarrow
\text{social structure}
\rightarrow
\text{individual problem environment}.
$$

A weak explanatory category can become a strong institutional constraint.

That return also clarifies what the original social knowledge can genuinely tell us. Social categories can identify distributions, shared propositions, institutional rules, recurring behavior, authority structures, legal restrictions, communication networks, and changes in information environments. Some social structures provide direct causal explanations of constraints: a law prohibits an action, a hierarchy allocates a decision right, censorship removes a channel of criticism.

What the category does not contain merely by naming the group or regularity is the explanatory history of the individual.

The conventional movement tends to be:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\text{group}
\rightarrow
\text{regularity}
\\
\rightarrow
\text{social category}
\rightarrow
\text{individual expectation}
\rightarrow
\text{policy}.
\end{gathered}
$$

The epistemic movement keeps the social knowledge but relocates you inside the causal chain:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\text{socially inherited knowledge}
+
\text{individual problem situation}
\\
\rightarrow
\text{interpretation}
\rightarrow
\text{criticism or retention}
\rightarrow
\text{action}.
\end{gathered}
$$

Society changes the concepts available to you, the problems that become salient, the explanations encountered before criticism begins, the sanctions attached to dissent, the criticism that can circulate, and the actions that are possible. You may accept that inherited knowledge, misunderstand it, combine incompatible parts of it, reproduce it elsewhere, criticize it, or replace it with a new explanation.

That is how the same social knowledge can produce regularities without producing identical minds. It is also how you can participate in a regularity without being explained by the category that records it.

The deeper distinction is not simply between a group statistic and an individual case. It is between social knowledge and the explanatory history of the person who encounters that knowledge. The first can describe real institutions, propositions, constraints, and distributions outside you. The second explains how you encounter that world and what happens next.

Confusing them turns social knowledge into a substitute for you.

The alternative is not to imagine yourself outside society. Societal knowledge is close to the content of individual minds precisely because it is inherited through language, institutions, norms, laws, roles, media, technologies, and authority relations. It can constrain action, alter which criticism is available, and determine which problems become visible first.

Its causal power is why classificatory overreach matters. But none of those transitions requires a lesser kind of person beneath the constraint.

I feel an abstraction coming on.

The negative distinction remains:

$$
\text{social constraint}
\not\Rightarrow
\text{lesser explanatory person}.
$$

The positive relation is more important:

$$
\begin{gather*}
\text{socially inherited knowledge} \\
\downarrow \\
\text{person-specific problems} \\
\downarrow \\
\text{possible criticism and new knowledge}.
\end{gather*}
$$

You can inherit norms of autonomy and hierarchy at the same time. A child can know less without being a lesser kind of knower. A medium can change a child's epistemic landscape without mechanically writing content into the mind. An institution can restrict action without defining the explanatory capacity of the person subject to it.

The social world enters you as a field of inherited explanations, constraints, and problems. It does not enter as a completed psychological essence.

There's no such thing as an essence. What's the next problem?

If social knowledge acts through individual problem situations, where is the society that appears to know, decide, and command?

<a id="chapter-04"></a>

### IV. The Wisdom Between The Crowd

*You* remain the locus of explanation. Here, that commitment is applied to society itself.

Wait. That sounds like a contradiction. The individual is the locus of society?

The conventional language of social life is saturated with collective subjects: society believes; the government knows; the market decides; science says; the church teaches; the company wants; the public demands. These expressions are useful shorthand, but the shorthand can become an ontology.

Speak clearly.

A stable social pattern begins to sound like a subject that sees, judges, intends, and knows. There is no social mind in the explanation developed here. There are individual minds. Each person is a distinct locus of experience, conjecture, interpretation, criticism, and action. Each knows only part of what other people know and only part of the social world in which they act. Communication can connect these minds without merging them. Institutions can coordinate them without creating a superordinate knower.

Explain.

What persists between people is not a shared subjectivity but knowledge made objective. Call it **objective knowledge**. Explanations, rules, classifications, procedures, records, software, texts, and standards can outlast the persons who created them and later be reconstructed by others. Such structures can have enormous causal effects without possessing experience of their own.

A law can constrain you without knowing you. A holy book can reorganize a life without possessing a mind. A bureaucracy can preserve procedures without understanding them. An artificial intelligence system can transform and recombine objective knowledge without thereby establishing that it is a knowing subject.

The problem is therefore narrower than a complete theory of cultural transmission, collective coordination, or machine cognition. Two explanatory frames are in conflict. The conventional frame permits societies, institutions, technologies, and fields of knowledge to appear as superordinate epistemic actors.

Abstract it.

The epistemic cycle requires every such appearance to decompose into the same universal process of knowledge creation:

$$
P_1
\rightarrow
TS
\rightarrow
EE
\rightarrow
P_2
$$

Problem, tentative solution, error elimination, and new problem, instantiated in the minds of individual explainers.

If society requires a special collective process of knowing, this epistemology is not universal and therefore false. Applying the explanation recursively is therefore not an optional extension of the theory. It is a consistency test.

Where do we begin?

<a id="chapter-04--1-the-solitary-standpoint"></a>

#### 1. The solitary standpoint

Knowledge can be objective. Experience cannot.

A scientific paper may exist independently of any present reader. A law may remain in force after everyone who drafted it is dead. A computer program may encode knowledge that no current user could recreate. An institution may preserve procedures across generations.

But every encounter with any of these structures still occurs from one subjective standpoint.

You do not experience society as a whole. You experience particular conversations, rules, media, institutions, sanctions, documents, and other people. From those fragments, you construct an understanding of a social world that is never directly available in its entirety.

That understanding is partial, but partiality is only the first difficulty. What reaches you must also be interpreted. You form conjectures about what others believe, what institutions intend, which norms apply, who has authority, which actions are permitted, what consequences are likely, and what “society” expects.

Those conjectures may be accurate. They may also be wrong.

Nothing unusual has to happen for the error to arise. No class, profession, institution, or historical period has to be especially confused. The possibility follows from the structure of individual experience itself: no person occupies the standpoint of society.

That creates the first explanatory problem. If nobody encounters the social whole directly, how does social life acquire the appearance of unity at all?

Communication seems to offer an answer. One person has an idea, expresses it, and another receives it. Yet that description already assumes the thing that needs explaining: that the same knowledge has somehow crossed from one mind into another.

A speaker has some internal explanatory structure and externalizes part of it through language, gesture, artifact, or action. Another person encounters that expression. The second person does not receive the speaker’s mental state. They reconstruct meaning using their own prior knowledge, language, expectations, current problems, and criticism.

Even successful communication therefore produces overlap rather than identity. Two people can use the same words while possessing different explanatory structures. They can also converge on the same proposition through very different histories.

The important result is not that communication fails. It is that coordination does not require mental identity. Enough overlap can sustain a legal system, laboratory, company, church, school, or family across time. Stable social patterns can emerge from many individual minds reconstructing sufficiently compatible models of one another and of the objective structures through which they act.

The appearance of a social whole begins to dissolve. The next question is whether institutions put it back together at a higher level.

<a id="chapter-04--2-institutions-without-an-institutional-mind"></a>

#### 2. Institutions without an institutional mind

Institutions can look as though they escape individual ignorance. A government may contain intelligence agencies, statistical offices, ministries, databases, advisers, courts, and bureaucracies. A corporation may contain finance, legal, engineering, operations, sales, and executive divisions. A university may contain hundreds of disciplines.

The larger the structure, the more knowledge it appears to contain. But the knowledge is distributed. No single mind has access to all of it.

The institution coordinates partial perspectives through reports, forms, meetings, databases, procedures, chains of command, software, policies, and other objective structures. These let people who do not share the same knowledge, and may not even know one another, participate in a stable pattern of action.

That produces a functional whole without producing an epistemic whole.

A government may “know” a statistic in the sense that the statistic exists somewhere in its records. That does not imply that any person making a relevant decision has encountered it, understood it, or interpreted it correctly. A corporation may “decide” to pursue a strategy, but the decision resolves into individual judgments, communications, delegated authority, procedures, and recorded actions.

The institution is causally real. What has not appeared is a new subject of experience.

This distinction matters because objective knowledge can act without awareness. A contract can bind an employee. A diagnostic manual can alter how a clinician interprets a patient. Software can block access to a service. An algorithm can route information. An LLM can produce a candidate explanation. None of these effects requires the artifact itself to possess subjective experience.

The distinction avoids two opposite mistakes. If only persons experience, it does not follow that objective structures are causally unimportant. If objective structures have powerful effects, it does not follow that they are minds.

You are still where the structure becomes lived: encountered, interpreted, criticized, obeyed, resisted, or reconstructed.

That return to *you* makes coercion less abstract.

A rule can alter another person’s action space through force, threat, punishment, exclusion, loss of resources, legal restriction, surveillance, censorship, or denial of access. An institution can scale the effect, but the causal chain still runs through persons creating, maintaining, or enforcing objective structures that change what other persons can do. A law does not arrest anyone by itself. A school rule does not remove a child from a classroom by itself. A corporate policy does not dismiss an employee by itself.

Constraint can also survive after the enforcing person disappears from the immediate scene. Someone may act within propositions such as: I must obey; people like me should not do this; the expert knows better; this question is inappropriate; this authority is entitled to decide; there is no alternative.

Calling this internalization can make it sound as though “society” has entered you. The more exact sequence is simpler. You encounter socially inherited objective knowledge, reconstruct it, and later use that reconstruction in your own reasoning. The social structure becomes causally effective through your own explanatory system.

External and internal constraint therefore meet at the same point. One changes the available action space. The other can change which alternatives you can see as available at all.

What does this imply about freedom?

<a id="chapter-04--3-freedom-authority-and-error-correction"></a>

#### 3. Freedom, authority, and error correction

Once constraint is described in those terms, freedom acquires a specifically epistemic role.

Error correction requires alternatives. You need some possibility of formulating a problem, considering rival explanations, encountering criticism, testing conjectures through action, and revising conclusions. Coercion can interfere with any of these steps. A censor can restrict rival explanations. A school can forbid a question. A manager can punish dissent. A government can constrain association.

The effect is not exhausted by suffering or domination. Restricting problems, criticisms, associations, or tests can prevent errors from becoming visible and can stabilize false knowledge.

In this inquiry, freedom therefore names more than the absence of restraint. It names a condition in which no other person has unilateral control over the problems you may formulate, the criticisms you may encounter, or the actions through which you may test a conjecture.

That formulation immediately encounters an apparent objection. People do not know equally much about every problem. A patient may rely on a surgeon. A passenger may rely on a pilot. A student may rely on a specialist. Local asymmetries of knowledge are ordinary and often indispensable.

Generalize it.

The difficulty appears when a local asymmetry is transformed into a general rule:

$$
\text{less knowledge}
\rightarrow
\text{less decision authority}
$$

The person granted authority remains another partial and fallible mind. A manager may know more about one organizational problem and less about another. An expert may know more about a technical domain and little about the other person’s own goals. A government department may possess aggregated data while misunderstanding the local problem of an individual citizen.

Authority can redistribute decision power. It cannot create an omniscient node.

The solitary standpoint therefore survives every institutional level. The relevant question is no longer whether one person sometimes knows more than another. It is what happens when partial knowledge is converted into durable control over another person’s problem situation.

Can we make this more specific?

Psychology provides a compact case because the whole social structure can return to one person through a single professional encounter.

<a id="chapter-04--4-who-knows-you"></a>

#### 4. Who knows you?

Psychology is a field, but more tangibly a vast network of researchers, clinicians, reviewers, editors, students, research participants, journals, databases, statistical conventions, professional bodies, diagnostic systems, and institutional rules. Each participant knows only part of the field. What appears as disciplinary knowledge is distributed across individual minds and objective knowledge.

And knowledge moves.

A theory may originate in one person, be revised by another, encoded in a questionnaire, standardized in a manual, taught in a textbook, implemented in software, and applied by a clinician. At each transition, somebody reconstructs what was inherited or transferred.

This explains how a discipline can display more continuity than any individual mind within it. Knowledge persists because it has been externalized. Without that persistence, each generation would have to rediscover everything.

But persistence is neutral about truth. The same machinery can preserve an error. A questionnaire may survive because it is standardized. A construct may persist because journals recognize it. A diagnostic category may remain because reimbursement systems require it. A statistical method may become conventional because software implements it.

Persistence therefore does not imply continued explanatory adequacy. A field can preserve an inherited problem formulation after the reasons for adopting it have become obscure.

Now return to *you*.

A patient does not encounter “psychology.” The patient encounters one clinician, one questionnaire, one report, one diagnosis, one treatment protocol. The clinician carries compressed objective knowledge inherited from a much larger disciplinary network, but the macro structure becomes locally effective in a relation between particular persons.

The diagnosis can then return to the patient as new objective knowledge. The patient may reconstruct it and begin to interpret themselves through it. A theory used to describe a person can therefore become part of the phenomenon it later measures.

That is the reflexive power of social knowledge.

The claim is not that a field should stop classifying, measuring, or preserving knowledge. The narrower point is explanatory. A disciplinary representation can contain information about a person without containing the whole explanatory history of the person who encounters and reconstructs it.

The same distributed structure also explains how claims can expand while moving through a network.

A researcher reports that a measure correlates with outcome $X$. Another reports a genetic association. A clinician learns that a construct helps classify patients. Later, a journalist says that characteristic $X$ is partly genetic, and a parent concludes that a child is naturally like this.

No single person has to traverse the whole inferential chain. Successive local reconstructions can transform the claim until the public or professional conclusion substantially exceeds the original evidence, even when each participant regards their own step as reasonable.

Isn't that why we have meta-analyses and replicable studies?

Meta-analysis cannot automatically correct this kind of inheritance. Different studies may use independent samples while sharing the same psychometric ontology, trait definitions, measurement assumptions, and statistical framework. Meta-analysis can reduce random sampling error. It cannot, merely by aggregating samples, criticize the common frame inherited by all of them.

Replication across samples is therefore not the same thing as replication across problem formulations.

A field can repeatedly corroborate a result inside one inherited frame while leaving that frame itself largely untouched. When you later encounter the result, you usually do not encounter this history of construction and criticism. You encounter a compressed representation whose apparent authority may exceed the criticism that produced it.

The pattern becomes still clearer when the representation leaves the discipline and becomes policy.

Abstract the structure.

Individual observations can be aggregated into a social category. The category can become policy knowledge, and policy can be implemented through institutions. The institutional action can then return as a constraint on an individual:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\text{individual observations}
\rightarrow
\text{aggregate representation} \\
\rightarrow
\text{policy knowledge}
\rightarrow
\text{institutional action}
\rightarrow
\text{individual constraint}.
\end{gathered}
$$

A category may begin as description and end as a rule governing a person. A population is judged vulnerable and access is restricted. A group is judged irrational and an authority structure is introduced. A demographic category becomes a risk class.

No social mind is required. Researchers, administrators, policymakers, and professionals act through objective structures, each seeing only part of the chain. Yet the chain can become stable enough to act back upon the individual from whom the original category was abstracted.

What does the aggregate contain when it returns?

It may contain regularities, risks, correlations, administrative categories, or predictive information. It does not thereby contain the person’s entire problem situation, knowledge history, interpretations, criticisms, goals, or capacity to create explanations not represented in the category. The aggregate can describe something about a person without becoming the person’s explanatory standpoint.

Then the medium really is the message after all?

<a id="chapter-04--5-media-and-control-of-the-next-encounter"></a>

#### 5. Media and control of the next encounter

The same decomposition changes what “media” means. A medium changes the conditions under which you can encounter, reconstruct, criticize, and continue knowledge.

Explain.

Media are technologies through which objective knowledge is stored, transmitted, selected, or generated. Their history can be read as an expansion of the epistemic functions available to individual minds. Print makes knowledge durable and reproducible. Broadcast lets one communication reach many recipients simultaneously. The internet makes a large body of knowledge individually navigable. Social media reduces geographic and temporal barriers between persons. Generative AI makes objective knowledge responsive to your current problem.

Compress the structure.

The sequence is not a progression toward a social mind. It is a change in how individual minds can encounter objective knowledge.

This becomes important when media effects are compressed into a direct causal shorthand:

$$
medium
\rightarrow
child.
$$

Television influences the child. Social media polarizes the child. AI teaches or manipulates the child.

Abstract it.

The shorthand removes the epistemic middle. A more exact sequence is:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\text{knowledge created by persons}
\rightarrow
\text{technological instantiation} \\
\rightarrow
\text{routing / selection / generation}
\rightarrow
\text{child’s individual reconstruction}.
\end{gathered}
$$

The medium changes what can reach the child, how quickly it can arrive, how it can be selected, and what forms of response are possible. It does not replace the child’s conjectural actions.

The same physical device can therefore mediate activities with very different epistemic structures: passive viewing, conversation, coding, research, argument, art, technical collaboration, tutoring, or problem solving. “Screen time” compresses all of them into one physical exposure variable.

Does this explain our collective anxieties?

Historical anxieties around new media can now be stated more precisely. The specific concern changes: print can corrupt; radio distracts; television makes passive; the internet exposes; social media fragments; AI homogenizes, replaces, deceives, or overpowers. The recurrence does not show that every concern is false. Each technology has real causal properties.

What persists across the transitions is a change in who can control the next epistemic encounter.

Print weakens local oral gatekeeping. Broadcast weakens geographic information boundaries. Search weakens institutional scarcity. Social media weakens the scarcity of rare-interest communities. AI weakens the scarcity of responsive explanation.

The authority problem survives the technological change because the routing of knowledge changes the problems and criticisms you can encounter.

Social media makes one side of this especially visible. The same network relation that can produce polarization under some conditions can also make highly specialized association possible. Rare interests that were previously geographically isolated can become viable communities. What appears as fragmentation at an aggregate level may, from your standpoint, be increased ability to find other people organized around unusually specific problems.

That does not establish that every resulting community is epistemically healthy. It establishes something narrower: an aggregate category such as “polarization” can hide changes in the topology of association experienced by particular persons.

So the medium is not a subject acting directly on a population. It changes the structure of possible encounters. The consequence still occurs when particular people reconstruct what reaches them and carry that reconstruction into the next problem.

This seems to magnify, not diminish, the stakes with AI.

Generative AI changes this structure again, because the objective knowledge no longer merely waits to be retrieved.

<a id="chapter-04--6-interactive-objective-knowledge"></a>

#### 6. Interactive objective knowledge

A search engine retrieves from an existing landscape. A generative model can recombine inherited knowledge around a problem that may not yet correspond to a document, course, or community.

You can therefore move through repeated cycles of problem, tentative solution, criticism, and successor problem while using a technological system as a rapid generator of conjectural material. The system can propose explanations, translate concepts, generate counterexamples, compare theories, critique arguments, produce code, expose hidden assumptions, and suggest rival formulations.

Yes, we're doing it now.

The important change is not that an artificial social mind has appeared. It is that objective knowledge has become interactive.

That interactivity makes the old distinction harder to keep in view. A book contains explanations but does not answer back. A calculator computes but does not converse. An LLM can produce explanations, arguments, code, criticism, plans, stories, and novel combinations. Ordinary language therefore slides easily into claims that AI knows, believes, understands, wants, or is smarter than humans.

Some of that may be harmless shorthand. The ontology remains unsettled.

Structure the problem so we can criticize it more clearly.

Three claims have to stay separate:

1. AI instantiates objective knowledge.
2. AI dynamically transforms objective knowledge.
3. AI is a knowing subject.

The first two can be true without the third having been explained.

The distinction becomes concrete during use. A system can greatly expand the candidate space of explanations without settling which problem matters, which criticism is decisive, or which successor problem should be pursued. You can reject the system’s proposed trajectory and substitute another problem.

Current human-AI knowledge creation is therefore deeply coupled to individual problem selection. This does not prove that AI can never become an autonomous explainer. It identifies a difficult **problem of problems** within the present explanatory boundary.

The boundary is deeper than anthropomorphism. We still do not possess an explanation of how people create genuinely new explanatory knowledge. We can describe conjecture, criticism, problem selection, error elimination, recombination, analogy, and search. The mechanism by which you produce a genuinely new explanatory idea remains incompletely understood.

That incompleteness changes what can be claimed about machines. If explanatory knowledge creation itself is not yet explained, how can we assert that it exists in machines?

We can identify large stores of objective knowledge, linguistic and statistical structure, search, recombination, planning, problem-responsive generation, and criticism-like procedures. Whether those operations comprise the same universal epistemic process found in persons remains open.

Powerful output in adjacent areas therefore does not establish artificial explanatory knowledge. The limitation is not that AI is weak. The limitation is that the theory of knowledge creation is incomplete. Given the theory, the implementation would follow quickly thereafter. And once explained, the epistemology we're applying here would be revealed as false.

“Superhuman” performance does not remove the gap. A telescope sees farther than a person. A calculator computes faster. A database stores more. A search engine retrieves across scales impossible for one mind. Generative AI extends this familiar pattern into tasks that were previously treated as close proxies for cognition.

A brief digression may be warranted. The superhuman capabilities of AI presently envelope fields that have been conventionally associated with super intelligence. A mathematician may look with despair on the progress of AI and conclude the singularity has arrived. It is still incumbent upon them to explain why. It is insufficient to point to the observations of mathematical proofs and induce from that proof of superhuman creativity. That would merely replicate the problem we've been discussing here. This problem of induction may inform the conjecture that AGI has arrived, we may conjecture AGI in the inductive direction, but it doesn't explain it.

A system can outperform an individual at a task without that performance, by itself, explaining a superior explanatory person. The artifact may do something astonishing. That performance still does not settle what kind of epistemic entity produced it, or how

Technology also makes the earlier political structure easier to scale. A censor once had to act repeatedly; a technical system can encode the censorship rule. A teacher once had to control access manually; a platform can automate restriction. A government once had to distribute instructions through officials; software can implement them instantly.

The same machinery that expands access to explanation can therefore expand constraint. Technology amplifies objective knowledge, including both explanatory and coercive knowledge. The relevant question is which knowledge has been encoded, by whom, and how that encoding changes the problem and action spaces available to particular persons.

The same technology can widen one person’s field of possible criticism while narrowing another’s. It can weaken one gatekeeper and create another. Once again, the explanatory unit is not “technology” acting as a subject. It is the relation between individual minds and the objective structures through which their possible encounters and actions are changed.

<a id="chapter-04--7-the-recursive-test"></a>

#### 7. The recursive test

The argument can now be turned back on itself.

If the epistemology is universal, every apparent social mind must decompose to individuals. Psychology resolves into psychologists and objective disciplinary knowledge. A government resolves into officials, citizens, laws, records, technologies, and communications. A religion resolves into persons, texts, institutions, rituals, and inherited explanations. A corporation resolves into employees, managers, procedures, contracts, software, and capital structures. Science resolves into scientists, instruments, papers, datasets, methods, and criticism.

AI must also decompose into technology, objective knowledge, training processes, system design, and interactions with individual people unless and until an independent explanation establishes a new epistemic subject.

If any one of these cases requires a special collective mind, then this universal account has failed. That is what makes recursion a test rather than an illustration.

The conventional frame can say that society believes, science knows, institutions decide, or AI understands because aggregate descriptions are useful. The epistemic frame keeps asking what the shorthand has compressed: Which individuals know what? Which objective structures preserve what? How is that knowledge communicated? Where is it reconstructed? Which person acts? Which structure changes the action space?

Some might call this intellectual dishonesty, or moving the goalposts, or denial of reality. We would say, reality is common sense, but epistemology is not, and universality provides the grounds.

Collective phenomena remain. What disappears is the need to add a collective subject merely because the pattern is stable or powerful. Society can be causally real, institutionally durable, and epistemically powerful without becoming a mind above the persons who compose and encounter it.

The epistemic frame can be compressed to three elements: individual knowers, objective knowledge, and fallible coordination between them. It's not a wisdom *of* the crowds, because crowds can't possess wisdom. It is a wisdom *between* the crowds, in the objective knowledge and interfaces through which individual minds exchange, preserve, criticize, route, and reconstruct knowledge.

Every social structure in this account must be explainable in those terms. If one cannot be, the universality of epistemology has failed.

But survival produces a harder question. If society has no mind of its own, how does knowledge created by particular people become socially persistent? How is it reconstructed by people who did not create it, preserved across generations, transformed as it moves, and stabilized strongly enough to shape the problems of persons not yet born?

And if freedom or coercion changes which reconstructions remain possible, how does that alter the evolution of socially persistent knowledge?

<a id="part-one-reality-many-worlds"></a>

## One Reality, Many Worlds

<a id="chapter-05"></a>

### V. The Popperian Heckle

You've been largely defensive. *You* should not be confused with genetic covariance, a psychometric category, a social class, an institutional role, or a collective abstraction. Genes matter. Psychological regularities matter. Social knowledge, institutions, and technology matter. But none of them is you.

Lots get positive then. What is the positive claim?

*You* is where objective knowledge can become a problem, where a problem can produce a conjecture, where a conjecture can be criticized, and where criticism can make a different problem possible. The schematic is:

$$
P_1 \rightarrow TS \rightarrow EE \rightarrow P_2.
$$

That doesn't sound hard. In fact, it sounds simplistic.

That's the problem with compressions: we're apt to lose the underlying explanation.

So what's hard about it?

The schematic $P_1 \rightarrow TS \rightarrow EE \rightarrow P_2$ is simple, the underlying epistemic schema is not. The schematic is useful because it describes the evolutionary logic of knowledge growth without pretending to explain its mechanism.

Like the familiar hard problem of consciousness, where describing neural and functional processes does not by itself explain qualia, this schematic leaves its own explanatory residue. We can name a creative problem, a creative tentative solution, a creative criticism, and the successor problem that results, but the letters conceal almost everything important about how those states are instantiated and how the transformations between them occur. We do not yet understand, even in general, how you come to have this problem rather than another, create this explanation rather than one already available, or produce the criticism that changes an evaluation of the problem itself.

The underlying schema is therefore closer to an evolutionary state machine: it identifies a system (not a sequence) of epistemic configurations whose operation can be reconstructed historically, while leaving the generative content of those states and transitions largely unexplained.

Call that epistemic mystery **the Popperian heckle**. Richard Dawkins invented the term to describe pedantic philosophical arguments that are advanced to conceal manifest truth. Here we take that criticism seriously.

You're being defensive again.

If that epistemic cycle is not merely something we use to describe science or culture, but something that also occurs within your epistemic mind, what does it say about you. The question is no longer only what goes wrong when you are reduced to a category.

> **What becomes possible when you are treated as an open-ended creator of knowledge?**

That question leads to freedom, but not first to freedom as the absence of physical constraint, an exemption from causality, or a political doctrine. A more primitive possibility appears earlier: your present knowledge does not contain all the knowledge you may later create.

A problem can become visible that is not visible now. A criticism can destroy an explanation that presently feels obvious. A distinction can appear that changes what you think the problem was. A future self can understand something the present self cannot yet think.

Your Popperian heckle is much more powerful than your selfish genes. Most of it remains unexplained. Some of it hides from criticism behind authorities of observation and manifest truth. That is the nature of universal explanations. They collide, they make us uncomfortable, even confrontational. But they don't care what we believe.

Your future self is still physically constrained, historically situated, biologically instantiated, and immersed in inherited objective knowledge. But no present description of what you know can also contain the explanations you have not yet created.

<a id="chapter-05--1-the-open-future"></a>

#### 1. The Open Future

It offers us a different way to reflect on two old problems: If people move uniquely through evolving problem situations, how might free will and consciousness appear inside that movement?

The answer remains conjectural, as always. But the conjecture may reveal how much of freedom is not choice among already known alternatives, and how much of consciousness may not be a common container holding different contents. The epistemic individual may be more individual than that.

The explanation of *you* first appeared as something that had to be protected from explanatory substitution. But you are not merely what remains after false abstractions are removed. You are generative. You can encounter knowledge that already exists and produce knowledge that does not. You can inherit a problem and reformulate it, inherit an explanation and reject it, or inherit a value, institution, or category and discover that the problem it once organized has changed.

None of this implies infallibility. You also create errors. You misunderstand, become dogmatic, and construct explanations that make your own problem space smaller. The optimism lies elsewhere: if an error can be created, it can also become a problem. The present state is not final.

This gives freedom an epistemic structure. Freedom is often discussed as permission: permission to speak, leave, associate, or choose. Those freedoms matter because they affect what you can do. They also affect what you can come to know.

Your future depends partly on whether present explanations can still become problems. If an explanation cannot be questioned, a problem cannot be reformulated, rival knowledge cannot be encountered, or an unusable environment cannot be left, some epistemic transitions become unavailable. The same is true when you cannot try something whose value no authority can presently recognize.

> **Freedom preserves the possibility of movement into epistemic states that cannot be specified completely from the present one.**

This is broader than choosing from a menu. A menu contains known options. An epistemic future can contain alternatives that do not yet exist because criticism can change the problem itself. You may eventually reject every alternative you can presently name and create another.

Freedom is therefore not only a question of which available path may be chosen. It is also a question of whether the landscape of possible paths can continue to change.

That claim immediately creates a physical problem. The cycle

$$
P_1 \rightarrow TS \rightarrow EE \rightarrow P_2
$$

compresses relations in the growth of knowledge. It does not imply that the brain contains a problem compartment, a tentative-solution compartment, an error-elimination compartment, and a successor-problem compartment. The symbols describe what states are doing in an epistemic process; they do not identify the mechanism that does it.

But the relations cannot float outside reality. If your state functions as a problem, that state must be physically instantiated somehow. The same is true of conjecture, criticism, and the transition by which one problem gives way to another. The implementation may be distributed, partly inexplicit, different across people, and badly aligned with the conceptual boundaries imposed by our notation.

The epistemology therefore does not give us a cognitive mechanism. It gives us a constraint:

> **if epistemic transformations occur, physically possible processes must instantiate them.**

The distinction matters because it lets epistemology generate questions about the mind without turning epistemic vocabulary into imaginary brain machinery.

Theory-laden observation gives one concrete clue about what such dependence can look like.

No jargon, please.

You do not first receive a neutral observation and only later attach an interpretation. What can be noticed already depends upon knowledge. A radiologist can see a structure in an image that another person cannot. A chess player sees a threat where a novice sees pieces. A mechanic hears a problem in an engine sound that another listener hears only as noise.

Abstract it.

$$
T(O) \rightarrow O'.
$$

The theory need not be an explicit sentence, and you may not know what objective knowledge is doing the work. The point is functional: prior knowledge changes what can become observable.

Now extend that structure cautiously. Let $O_i$ denote, not a bare observation, but a physically instantiated epistemic state organized by the person's existing knowledge. Then we can write:

$$
P_1(O_1)
\rightarrow
TS(O_2)
\rightarrow
EE(O_3)
\rightarrow
P_2(O_4).
$$

The notation does not say that $O_1$ contains a little object called a problem. It says that this state functions as problematic for this person: something does not fit, attracts attention, or resists the current explanation. Likewise, $O_2$ is a state in which a conjectural relation has become available, and $O_3$ is a state in which criticism has changed what can be retained.

The arrows remain schematic, and they also contain unexplained content. They tell us that transformation occurs, not how it occurs. Something moves you from confusion into a problem, from a problem toward a conjecture, from a conjecture toward criticism, and from criticism toward another problem. Sometimes that movement is explicit. Often it is not. The arrows may point in many directions at once. A sentence can feel wrong before the criticism can be stated; a solution can appear before its ancestry can be reconstructed; a criticism that seemed weak yesterday can become decisive today.

We do not yet possess an explanation of those transitions. But the ignorance is now more precise. The problem is not to find an uncaused mental event. It is to explain physically instantiated transformations whose epistemic role cannot be read off from a description of the present state alone.

That physical problem gives us a different entry into free will. 

<a id="chapter-05--2-freedom-inside-a-mind"></a>

#### 2. Freedom Inside a Mind

The traditional question often asks whether you could have chosen otherwise under the same physical conditions. That problem can remain where it is. The narrower epistemic question is:

> **what might free will look like inside a mind whose activity includes movement through changing explanatory states?**

Start with something ordinary. You can act in ways that change the conditions under which later thought occurs. You can redirect attention or ask a question, enter or leave an environment, consult an artifact, create one, or withhold one. These actions alter what you are likely to encounter next.

The plain relation comes first: you can change part of the environment that will later participate in changing you. Call that function **Choice**. The name does not refer to a proposed brain module or a little agent inside your mind. It compresses one relation: altering the epistemic conditions under which what happens next will occur.

An altered environment can change what becomes salient, which problem appears, which criticism becomes available, and which conjecture can be constructed. New knowledge can then alter later action.

Abstract it.

$$
\Delta E
\rightarrow
\Delta K
\rightarrow
\Delta A
\rightarrow
\Delta W
\rightarrow
\Delta E',
$$

where $E$ is the person's epistemic environment, $K$ their knowledge, $A$ the actions that become available, and $W$ the wider physical environment. The changed world becomes part of the next epistemic environment, and the loop continues.

Under this conjecture, free will may concern a causal process in which newly created explanations become new causes of later action. The explanation was not present before it was created. Once it exists, it can change what you notice, criticize, attempt, avoid, build, or seek.

The conjecture can therefore be stated cautiously:

> **Free will may be the evolving organization of epistemic openness: your capacity to participate in transformations that alter the conditions of your own future knowing and acting.**

This does not explain how explanatory novelty is produced. It changes the location of the problem. Instead of asking how freedom escapes causality or physical determinism, the inquiry asks how new knowledge can be physically created and then become causally relevant to what happens next.

Continuous evolving development makes the conjecture more individual. A capacity to alter epistemic conditions would not remain historically untouched, because every successful or failed attempt changes you before you attempt the next one.

People can therefore develop different architectures for performing related epistemic work. One person learns to decide by writing or speaking until a problem becomes explicit. Another builds rules or trained intuitions that reduce what must be reconsidered each time. Another learns to delay choice, seek disagreement, or interrupt the felt need to choose until the problem itself changes.

Abstract this choice architecture.

Call the developed form for individual $i$:

$$
Choice_i(t).
$$

The notation does not imply a discrete mechanism. It marks a possibility: the epistemic function may be shared while the developed architecture through which it is instantiated becomes highly individual.

This matters because the experience of choosing can vary. You may experience decision as forceful conscious authorship: *I chose this.* Training can change that experience. Meditation, for example, can make thoughts and intentions appear less like commands issued by an explicit chooser and more like events that become available to awareness. That phenomenological change does not by itself show that epistemic freedom has disappeared. The organization of choosing may have changed.

Injury can also alter forms of agency that had become central to one person's developed organization. Neurodiversity makes the observation universal. The point here is conceptual rather than clinical. Similar reports of choosing may arise from **different evolved architectures**, while different reports may arise from architectures performing related epistemic functions.

Free will, on this conjecture, would therefore not be one uniform inner object distributed across otherwise unique people. It would name related forms of epistemic movement whose mature organization becomes particular to a life.

That possibility creates the next problem. If choosing can become developmentally individual, perhaps conscious availability can too.

<a id="chapter-05--3-consciousness-and-the-evolving-architecture"></a>

#### 3. Consciousness and the Evolving Architecture

You embody and use far more knowledge than appears in your explicit consciousness. Biological knowledge, perceptual expectations, motor skills, language, memories, learned salience, emotional associations, habits, unfinished problems, and inexplicit criticisms can all affect what happens without first appearing as explicit objects of awareness.

Some of this becomes conscious. Much does not. Consciousness therefore cannot simply be identical to all the knowledge operating you.

The narrower epistemic question is:

> **what changes when some part of your larger epistemic organization becomes available in a form that can participate differently in criticism, comparison, communication, or reconstruction?**

A pain can become a problem rather than only a disturbance. A memory can become something that is compared with evidence rather than merely something that biases action. An intention can become something that is inspected and criticized before it is acted upon. Inexplicit unease can become a sentence: *something does not fit.*

Perhaps consciousness includes transformations through which parts of a much larger epistemic organization become available for forms of error correction that would otherwise be unavailable. That is a conjecture about what conscious availability may do in the epistemic cycle.

Development now returns. Shared biological capacities do not imply identical mature or static epistemic organization. People acquire different languages and distinctions, practice different forms of attention, inherit different social explanations, and turn different skills into inexplicit competence. Those histories change what later becomes salient and what criticism can reach.

Why assume that conscious organization is exempt from that history or that the process ever stops?

Perhaps people do not merely have different contents inside one common conscious processor. Perhaps some of the organization through which content becomes consciously available also develops. One person may rely heavily on inner speech while another reports little of it. One may organize thought visually or spatially while another relies more on bodily salience or explicit conceptual chains. One may experience agency as a strong internal act while another experiences an intention as something that seems to arrive.

These differences support a narrower conjecture:

> **evolving consciousness may be a shared biological possibility expressed through individually developing epistemic architectures.**

If so, the familiar hard problem remains. Nothing here explains why physical processes are accompanied by subjective experience at all. But another problem becomes visible beside it: Are you carrying the implicit assumption that the conscious organization whose subjectivity you are trying to explain is one uniform object across evolving persons?

The opacity of another mind may therefore arise not only because experience is private. It may also arise because the structures through which experience becomes epistemically available have been shaped by a history no other person shares. This does not solve the mystery. It makes one part of the mystery more local and more individual.

The free will and consciousness conjectures meet at one correction. Freedom cannot require complete conscious control over the causes of thought. You do not explicitly choose every problem that becomes interesting, command every useful memory to appear, or issue an internal instruction that generates each conjecture. You can know that something is wrong before knowing what, and the next thought can surprise you.

If freedom required a conscious executive directing every epistemically relevant transition, the epistemic mind would appear mostly unfree. But the conjecture developed here requires less: *You* can participate in changing the conditions of future thought without controlling every transformation that follows.

You can learn, externalize a problem, practice a skill, seek criticism, build a tool, alter a relationship, or change what you expose yourself to. Or you could choose not to. Each intervention modifies part of the environment in which later cognition occurs. The altered environment changes what you encounter; what you encounter changes what becomes salient; what becomes salient can change your next problem.

The mind changes the environment. The changed environment returns to the mind. You change.

Epistemic freedom may therefore operate recursively across explicit and inexplicit processes. You need not be transparent to yourself to remain the locus of epistemic development. Self-opacity and agency are not opposites.

That result is interesting because your environment is not made only of physical objects. It is already full of explanations created by other people.

<a id="chapter-05--4-when-social-knowledge-enters"></a>

#### 4. When Social Knowledge Enters

You enter a world already filled with knowledge embodied in language, family explanations, institutions, media, laws, moral concepts, role descriptions, categories, and technologies. This is objective knowledge in the earlier sense: knowledge that can exist outside any one person's present awareness and be encountered, reconstructed, criticized, or reused.

You do not receive this knowledge as a neutral object. You reconstruct it through an existing epistemic organization. Once reconstructed, social knowledge can participate in your own problem situation. It can open problems, but it can also close them.

Consider explanations such as *this is what I am*, *this failure reveals something permanent*, or *this problem has no alternative solution*. Each can become internally causal without subsuming you. An inherited explanation can affect what you notice, which alternatives you consider, what criticism feels available, and which successor problems can even be formulated.

This gives social knowledge a concrete route into individual life. The damage need not be a mysterious social force acting from outside. An explanation enters your epistemic environment and reorganizes what movement appears possible from inside it. The same mechanism also explains how social knowledge can heal: a new explanation can reopen the landscape.

Consider someone who explains their situation this way:

> I am defective because I lack conventional social success.

The explanation locates the problem in a fixed property of the person. It also constrains what can follow. If the cause is an essential defect, many possible next questions disappear before they are asked.

Now consider a different explanation:

> I have not yet solved the problem of finding relationships in which the things that matter to me can be shared.

The outward condition may be identical. The epistemic condition is not. The second explanation creates different successor problems: where are such people, what forms of communication could make connection possible, which inherited expectations misdescribe the problem, and what kind of community might not yet exist?

A better explanation need not remove loneliness. It changes what loneliness can lead to. You occupy a different problem space because different successor problems have become available.

Objective social knowledge can enter your mind and alter the sequence of epistemic transitions that follows. You can inherit an explanation that closes movement. You can also encounter one that makes movement possible again.

Once freedom is conceptualized this way, flourishing need not produce greater psychological convergence. The opposite can occur because expanding objective knowledge gives people access to more specialized epistemic environments: unusual disciplines and technical subcultures, distant communities and languages, new artistic forms and explanatory traditions.

The reachable epistemic landscape becomes larger, but individuals need not distribute themselves through it in the same way. Greater opportunity can therefore generate greater divergence. You may become increasingly unlike the people nearest you in interests, knowledge, language, explanatory commitments, skills, and problems.

From the perspective of an aggregate, divergence may look like fragmentation. From your perspective, it may be flourishing. Divergence itself settles neither interpretation. You can diverge into error, isolation, dogma, or obsession.

The narrower claim is:

> **distance from the mean cannot tell us whether an epistemic trajectory is flourishing or failing.**

That requires criticism of the trajectory itself. The same conclusion now reaches inward. If epistemic histories diverge, the architectures produced through those histories may diverge too. Different people may not merely think different things. They may differ in how problems become salient, how choice is organized, how criticism is experienced, and how parts of the mind become consciously available.

You become hardest to infer from the population precisely where your history has done the most work.

Divergence then creates a practical problem for anyone responsible for another person. A parent may watch a child enter technological environments the parent does not understand. The child develops interests, friendships, language, and problems that no longer overlap neatly with the parent's world. The uncertainty is real, and so is the loss of legibility.

The epistemic error begins when one explanation is substituted for another:

> I no longer understand the child's world

becomes:

> the child's world is harmful.

Sometimes it is harmful. Sometimes restriction is necessary. But unfamiliarity and harm are different claims. Restoring an environment the parent recognizes can restore parental legibility without necessarily improving the child's epistemic condition.

The same structure can appear in schools, workplaces, institutions, and governments. When another person's trajectory becomes difficult to interpret, control becomes attractive because control reduces variation. Reduced variation makes the system easier for the controller to see. That is an observable effect. It does not by itself tell us what happened to the controlled person's problem space.

Legibility and flourishing can therefore come apart. Once they do, the problem is no longer merely interpersonal. It becomes a problem about coordination, authority, and the preservation of criticism.

<a id="chapter-05--5-freedom-legibility-and-epistemic-closure"></a>

#### 5. Freedom, Legibility, and Epistemic Closure

Authority can solve real coordination problems. It can act quickly, concentrate expertise, set standards, and prevent local actions from imposing unacceptable costs on others. Nothing in  epistemology eliminates those functions.

The problem begins when responsibility for a problem is mistaken for possession of its uniquely correct solution. The epistemic cycle is:

$$
P_1 \rightarrow TS \rightarrow EE \rightarrow P_2.
$$

An authority can instead produce:

$$
P_1 \rightarrow TS_A \rightarrow \text{control}.
$$

The danger is not authority as such. It is closure. A problem definition becomes mandatory, alternative conjectures disappear, criticism becomes disobedience, and a successor problem is reinterpreted as refusal to accept the solution.

The immediate system may become easier to coordinate while becoming less able to discover errors in the explanation governing that coordination. Coordination and criticizability are therefore not opposites. A coordinated response can still preserve routes through which dissent, revision, exit, competing experiments, or replacement can occur.

It is not only whether anyone is in charge. It is whether the explanation governing the intervention can itself still become a problem.

Pressure sharpens the tension. The more serious a problem appears, the stronger the temptation to close the epistemic cycle. High stakes make variation look dangerous, delay irresponsible, and criticism obstructive. But urgency does not transform a tentative solution into infallible knowledge.

That creates an asymmetry between effects that exist after an intervention and alternatives prevented from existing. A restriction may reduce a measured exposure, a rule may increase compliance, or a ban may stop a particular action. Those effects can often be observed. The suppressed alternative is different.

If you are prevented from pursuing a problem, the conjecture you would have created does not exist. If an institution suppresses a criticism, the successor problem that criticism would have produced may never become visible. If a child is prevented from entering an unfamiliar domain, a later skill or relationship that might have emerged cannot appear in the data.

Compress it.

Coercion can produce:

$$
\text{known compliance}
+
\text{unknown epistemic loss}.
$$

The second term cannot be inventoried in advance because it refers partly to knowledge that was never created. That does not imply that every restriction is wrong or that emergencies require decentralization. Sometimes rapid coordination is indispensable.

The narrower point is epistemic:

> **severity increases the cost of error in the imposed solution as well as the cost of error in failing to act.**

A system can therefore gain coordination while losing some of the mechanisms through which errors in that coordination would have been discovered. The loss is hardest to measure when the prevented future never becomes actual.

<a id="chapter-05--6-the-expanding-epistemic-environment"></a>

#### 6. The Expanding Epistemic Environment

The same open-future argument applies to physical constraints. Matter, energy, time, and infrastructure are real. You cannot explain scarcity away. But the practical meaning of a physical constraint depends partly on knowledge.

Oil existed before people knew how to use it as an energy resource. Uranium existed before people knew how to release useful energy from it. Silicon existed before people knew how to build computational systems from it. In each case, the material world set constraints while knowledge changed which possibilities inside those constraints became reachable.

Abstractly:

$$
\text{present constraint}
\neq
\text{permanent possibility boundary}.
$$

The climate and energy demands associated with artificial intelligence provide an immediate example. AI infrastructure consumes real electricity and materials, creating real problems. But a description based only on current energy technology cannot contain every future way of responding to those problems. Compute demand can create pressure for better hardware and software efficiency, different cooling and storage, changes in generation and transmission, or technologies not yet available.

Innovation may fail, arrive too slowly, or create new problems. Nothing in epistemic openness guarantees rescue. The narrower claim is that the future resource landscape depends partly on explanations that do not yet exist. Present scarcity is evidence about present constraints. It is not a complete inventory of future practical possibility.

Artificial intelligence matters here for another reason. It can change not only the resources available to society, but the problems you can reach. You can use it to cross unfamiliar technical vocabularies, generate and test candidate models or code, and revisit bodies of objective knowledge at scales unavailable to unaided memory. You can use it to cross unfamiliar technical vocabularies, generate and test candidate models or code, and revisit bodies of objective knowledge at scales unavailable to unaided memory.

We're doing it now, for better or worse.

The relevant consequence here is immediate: the technology changes your epistemic environment.

You can reach problems you previously could not practically enter and encounter rival explanations faster. You can construct tentative solutions with tools you did not possess and expose a conjecture to forms of criticism that were previously too costly or inaccessible. That enlarged reach can produce error, but it can also expose error.

Abstract it.

The technology therefore enters the reciprocal process:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\text{objective knowledge}
\rightarrow
\text{individual reconstruction} \\
\rightarrow
\text{criticism and creation}
\rightarrow
\text{new objective knowledge}.
\end{gathered}
$$

You remain the locus at which inherited knowledge becomes a live problem and at which a generated output is accepted, rejected, misunderstood, corrected, or transformed. AI changes the reachable landscape. It does not displace the epistemic mind.

This reciprocity prevents the argument from becoming individual against society. You do not create from nothing. You begin inside objective knowledge created by others: language, mathematics, crafts, moral vocabularies, scientific explanations, stories, legal concepts, technologies, and ways of naming experience.

You may suffer partly because the explanations available to you are poor. A new distinction can then reorganize the problem. A failure can become a learning problem rather than a verdict on worth. A relationship can become a coordination problem rather than proof of defect. A diagnosis can become one useful description rather than a complete identity.

The physical world may not change immediately. Your problem space does. That is one way social knowledge can heal.

The recursion moves outward.

Changed, you can criticize inherited knowledge and externalize something new: a distinction, tool, explanation, institution, method, or previously unformulated problem. Social knowledge can therefore be changed by precisely the kind of person that existing categories do not yet describe well.

The dissenter, eccentric, difficult student, lonely outsider, unconventional researcher, obsessive engineer, or misunderstood artist may ask why something has to be the way it is. Most such questions will not produce important objective knowledge by conventional measures. That does not negate the opportunity. An important criticism cannot always be identified before it is created.

You are therefore not outside social knowledge. You are a place where social knowledge can change.

This is also why more freedom need not make people more alike. More objective knowledge need not produce one common epistemic landscape. Better communication need not eliminate deep disagreement, and greater technological reach can increase differentiation.

You can find collaborators around an interest nobody nearby understands. A child can encounter a discipline unknown to the family. A researcher can combine fields whose institutional boundaries previously kept them apart. These developments can produce fragmentation, but they can also produce flourishing.

Uniformity can arise from shared good explanations or from restricted possibility. Divergence can arise from error or from expanded possibility. Neither convergence nor divergence therefore settles the epistemic question.

The trajectory has to be criticized at the level of the problems, explanations, errors, and consequences actually involved. No population metric can automatically tell us whether your epistemic path is flourishing merely because it is common or uncommon. Freedom preserves variation partly because future knowledge cannot be identified in advance by conformity to present knowledge.

That returns us to the boundary no abstraction can cross for us: another person.

<a id="chapter-05--7-another-person"></a>

#### 7. Another Person

We cannot leave our own minds, directly occupy another person's epistemic state, or inspect their conscious organization from inside. We encounter speech, action, artifacts, silence, expression, and history. From that surface we construct an explanation.

Understanding another person is conjectural. The explanatory questions become concrete: what problem are they trying to solve? Which distinctions matter to them, and what history made those distinctions salient? What alternatives do they think are available? What knowledge or transition am I failing to see?

Then the other person can criticize our model.

> No. That is not me.

An error becomes visible, and the model changes. That is progress. The goal is not fusion. Two minds do not need to become the same to understand one another better. The distance can remain while the bridge improves.

That distance can itself become epistemically useful. A person whose world overlaps heavily with ours may leave many of our assumptions invisible. A person who is very different can expose them. They may reject a distinction we never thought to question, notice a problem we cannot see, or misunderstand us in a way that reveals how poorly we explained ourselves.

Difference therefore has epistemic value even when agreement never arrives. It creates surprise, and surprise can create a problem. The stranger can reveal the invisible boundaries of our own landscape. Interpersonal distance is then more than a communication obstacle. It can become an engine of error discovery.

If choice and conscious availability are partly shaped by individual epistemic development, the distance may run deeper than disagreement over beliefs. People may differ in some of the structures through which salience, choosing, criticism, and conscious availability are organized.

That possibility weakens the assumption that your own internal form can serve as a universal template for another person. It also completes the initial movement of this series. You first had to be protected from explanatory substitution. You then became a positive epistemic object: a physically instantiated, socially embedded, historically developed locus at which inherited objective knowledge can become problematic and new knowledge can appear.

The same account that makes you generative also makes another individual difficult to compress.

Every person inherits different objective knowledge, encounters different problems, develops different inexplicit expectations, and follows different epistemic transitions.
