Imagine working through a problem over days. You jump between notes. Return to old arguments. Introduce examples. Reject them. Recover something from another project. Change terminology. Reformulate the problem. To another human following synchronously, the trajectory may be exhausting.

AI can preserve much more of the evolving context. It can recover earlier states, make transitions explicit, compact repetition, and reorganize a highly dynamic process into a stable artifact.

You do not need to become more state-like. The interface becomes better at preserving the movement.

This does not make the AI the originator of your epistemic direction. It performs an objective-knowledge function. You move. The technology helps preserve the trail.

Abstract it.

This can transform a difficult-to-follow epistemic journey into something another mind can reconstruct:

$$
M_A
\rightarrow
\text{epistemic movement}
\rightarrow
O
\rightarrow
M_B'.
$$

The objective artifact $O$ may be an essay, a diagram, a piece of software, or a theory.

The recipient does not have to reproduce the creator's entire journey. That has always been true of objective knowledge. AI can make the transformation from private movement to stable surface cheaper and more continuous.

That may have a moral consequence. People whose cognitive transitions were historically expensive for others to follow may gain new ways to make those transitions legible without suppressing them. The playing field changes not by normalizing the person but by improving the bridge.

<a id="chapter-17--9-institutions-route-the-arrows-of-persons"></a>

#### 9. Institutions Route the Arrows of Persons

Groups do not possess a collective subjective arrow. Society does not think. The corporation does not become curious. The bureaucracy does not experience boredom.

People do.

Institutions nevertheless create structures that route our arrows. They specify which problems count, who may define them, which tentative solutions are admissible, what criticism is permitted, when the discussion is over, and which successor problems receive resources.

This is unavoidable to some extent. Coordination requires interfaces. A hospital cannot allow every worker to reinterpret a safety protocol during an emergency. A flight crew cannot spontaneously reinvent landing procedure. A factory cannot permit every operator to change product specifications. Constraints can enlarge freedom by making complex cooperation possible.

The epistemic criterion remains:

> which constraints make more independent explanatory lives possible?

Arrows suggest a dynamic version:

> **Which constraints coordinate necessary states while leaving arrows open?**

Top-down systems are attractive because they simplify coordination. The authority defines the problem, selects the solution, assigns roles, specifies sequence, and measures compliance. Where the required transformation is already known, this can work extremely well. Known transformations can be standardized, and objective knowledge can be embodied in procedure.

But knowledge creation introduces another problem. The authority does not merely need the correct state. It must know where the system should move next. That requires knowledge the authority may not possess. 

Worse, the relevant knowledge may not yet exist. A worker may notice a problem no manager has formulated. A scientist may challenge the premise of the research program. A dissenter may expose a problem in the official explanation.

Command-and-control can therefore fail for a reason deeper than incomplete information. It can suppress the process by which missing knowledge would have been created. It imposes not only static structure on a dynamic epistemic landscape. It can impose static arrows on the persons capable of changing that landscape.

Organizations often recognize the resulting disorientation. Employees seem disengaged. Teams lack alignment. People resist change.

The proposed solution is frequently more communication. Leadership must explain the reality, share the facts, clarify priorities, align everyone around the problem. Sometimes this is exactly what is needed. Miscommunication is real. Missing objective knowledge can create unnecessary conflict.

But the solution can reproduce the original mistake. 

It assumes:

$$
\text{shared information}
\rightarrow
\text{shared problem}
\rightarrow
\text{shared direction}.
$$

The same objective knowledge enters different $M_i$. People reconstruct it through different histories, problems, skills, obligations, fears, interests, and inexplicit criteria.

Corporate facts do not comprise a corporate mind. More information can improve coordination without producing the arrows management wants. When leadership interprets continued divergence as failure to understand reality, the system begins to confuse its own problem formulation with reality itself.

The same issue appears in economic and political institutions. Free markets remain an interesting epistemic conjecture not because markets are infallible, prices explain everything, or economic value equals epistemic value. Markets can concentrate power. Exit can be expensive. Competition can reward triviality. Firms operating inside markets can be profoundly hierarchical.

The narrower observation is that decentralized economic systems can permit many problem situations and many arrows to coexist. One person sees a problem, another sees a different one, a third builds a substitute, and another changes the problem entirely. No central authority needs to know in advance which transition will matter.

The epistemic content of the arrows strengthens an old criticism of command economies. The difficulty is not merely that the planner lacks distributed information. The planner lacks **uncreated knowledge**. If the planning system tightly controls which problems may be pursued, which experiments may occur, and which criticisms may alter direction, it can impair the generation of the very knowledge it lacks.

This does not prove liberal economics. It identifies another point of consilience between decentralized institutions and an epistemology of fallible, problem-generating persons.

The same idea applies more broadly to liberal institutions. Freedom of speech matters partly because criticism must be able to enter. Freedom of association matters partly because people need to form new problem-solving arrangements. Exit matters because you may need to leave one imposed problem situation for another. Freedom of conscience matters because inherited explanations must remain criticizable inside you. Political liberty matters because authorities are fallible.

Liberty is therefore not merely permission to occupy different states. It is also permission to move.

To change your mind.
To abandon a theory.
To form a new problem.
To pursue an interest others find strange.
To criticize the official sequence.
To become someone whose future problem situation was not predictable from the present one.

That does not eliminate coordination. It changes the problem from:

> how do we make everyone follow the right arrows?

To:

> how do we build interfaces through which many different arrows can coexist without destroying the shared conditions that make movement possible?

<a id="chapter-17--10-the-open-future-arrives-one-arrow-at-a-time"></a>

#### 10. The Open Future Arrives One Arrow at a Time

The failure of forced arrows is not only economic. It can be psychological, moral, and creative.

If you are repeatedly required to follow prescribed transitions, you may become less able to recognize your own. The signals become inconvenient. Boredom must be ignored. Curiosity must wait. Criticism must be softened. The alternative problem must be suppressed.

Eventually you may become good at staying in the permitted state. That can look like maturity, professionalism, discipline, or reliability. Sometimes it is. Sometimes it is the successful internalization of epistemic control.

The distinction cannot be read from compliance alone. An institution may obtain predictable behavior while reducing the number of independent explanatory trajectories available inside it. That tradeoff may be necessary. It may also be far more expensive than the institution can see.

Lost knowledge does not produce a report. The problem that was never formed leaves no metric. The conjecture that never became explicit cannot appear in the retrospective. Suppressed arrows are difficult to count because their products do not exist. That is precisely why they are hard to value.

Freedom preserves an open future. Arrows give that abstraction a local form. The open future is not encountered all at once. It arrives through proximate transitions. This problem becomes that conjecture. This criticism becomes that new problem. This interest becomes that skill. This mistake becomes that explanation.

Your future remains open because the next arrow is not fully specified by the present state. Causal history, biology, objective knowledge, institutions, and physical possibility all matter. But the explanatory future is not already contained as a semantic script inside any of them.

> The next problem may not yet exist.
> The next criterion may not yet exist.
> The next explanation may not yet exist.

The next person you become may depend upon arrows nobody could presently name.

That is one reason control should make us epistemically cautious. To prescribe every arrow is to presume knowledge of a future that has not been created.

The same point appears in the ordinary experience of being stuck. You cannot think. Nothing is moving. So you stop trying to force a destination. You walk. The mind drifts. A memory appears; something unrelated becomes irritating; a connection forms. Perhaps nothing useful happens. Perhaps the entire afternoon is wasted. Or perhaps the successor problem appears.

The important point is not that wandering is secretly efficient. That would convert freedom into another productivity technique.

The point is that sometimes you know only this:

> **The current state is not where I should remain.**

That is already an epistemic orientation. The arrow can become consilient before the destination does. Movement itself can be the next thing that makes sense.

<a id="chapter-17--11-coordinate-the-interface-not-the-arrows"></a>

#### 11. Coordinate the Interface, Not the Arrows

This clarifies why the institutional problem is so difficult. A command system is not merely trying to coordinate many people. It is trying to coordinate many moving epistemic worlds.

Abstract it:

$$
M_1(t), M_2(t), \ldots, M_n(t).
$$

Each epistemic mind contains different problems, histories, inexplicit structures, transitions, rhythms, and ways of becoming stuck or interested and of externalizing what has changed.

The system then imposes:

$$
P_A \rightarrow TS_A \rightarrow EE_A \rightarrow P_B.
$$

The mismatch is structural. A static representation of the organization is applied to dynamic explanatory agents. The more complex the problem environment becomes, the more expensive that mismatch can become.

The irony is that the system may respond by increasing control: more process, more reporting, more standardized problem definitions, more prescribed arrows. The attempted solution can intensify the original epistemic failure. People become easier to administer and less able to generate the knowledge the system cannot anticipate.

Perhaps coordination does not require a mind above minds. Perhaps it requires better bridges among them. Arrows strengthen the point. The bridge must accommodate movement.

It is not enough to connect static representations of people. People will change. Their problems will change. Their criteria will change. Their explanations will change. Their next useful direction may not yet be knowable.

Objective knowledge can help. Contracts can define thin interfaces. Standards can stabilize what must remain shared. Markets can coordinate differently motivated agents. Liberal institutions can preserve criticism and exit. AI can reduce the cost of following complicated epistemic trajectories.

None solves the problem. But all suggest a direction:

> **Coordinate the interface without trying to own the arrows.**

That may be one of the deepest design principles available to a civilization of solitary, changing explainers.

<a id="chapter-17--12-the-arrows-between-people"></a>

#### 12. The Arrows Between People

There is also a gentler version of the same problem. One person speaks. Another listens. The first person's explanation moves somewhere unexpected. The second becomes lost.

Ordinarily, this is frustrating. But if you are to take another person's explanation seriously, sometimes you must reconstruct not only the state but the transition.

Why did that objection follow? Why did that memory become relevant? Why did they abandon the previous line?

You may never know fully. The road through another $M_i$ remains partial. But asking about the arrow changes the interaction.

Instead of:

> you're off topic,

you can sometimes ask:

> what moved for you there?

Not because every transition deserves indulgence. Because it may contain the problem you are missing.

This is not only intellectual. To know another person over years is partly to learn their arrows: the subjects that light them up, the problems they cannot release, the criticisms that wound, the bait that rages, the silences that mean a transition is occurring, the need to remain, the need to leave.

You still do not occupy their mind. The solitude remains. But familiarity can reduce the reconstruction cost. A loved one's strange transition becomes less strange because you know more of the landscape.

Perhaps this is one meaning of being known. Not that another person possesses your internal state. They begin to recognize your arrows. A form sees the state. A relationship can sometimes intuit the arrow.

<a id="chapter-17--13-what-arrows-do-not-explain"></a>

#### 13. What Arrows Do Not Explain

The abstraction of arrows should not be mistaken for biology. Nothing here establishes that the brain contains discrete epistemic components connected by literal transition mechanisms corresponding to the notation.

The states are abstractions. The arrows are abstractions. Even the distinction between state and transition may carve the underlying physical process in a way that is useful for epistemology without mapping neatly onto biological machinery.

That is acceptable. An explanation need not instantiate the vocabulary of a different level. But it must not pretend the physical mechanism has already been explained.

So the position remains deliberately modest:

> people appear to move among distinguishable epistemic states;
> those movements carry epistemic significance;
> the causal machinery remains inexplicit and unexplained.

The abstraction earns its place if making the movement visible creates better problems.

Observations of arrows has not explained the causal machinery that moves people among epistemic states. It has not explained attention, ADHD, creativity, or fun. It has not shown that decentralized systems always outperform centralized ones or that every spontaneous transition deserves protection.

You remain vast and solitary. Other people reconstruct you incompletely. Institutions see interfaces. Even you may notice the direction only after it has begun to change. But the transition need not be treated as empty space between the states we name.

There may be knowledge in the arrow. And sometimes, the only thing you know is that it is time to move.

So how do we know where to go next?

If future knowledge depends on creative transitions that have not yet occurred, what can we possibly know about the person you will become?

<a id="chapter-18"></a>

### XVIII. Unpredictable You

Creativity appears throughout the epistemic cycle: in problems, tentative solutions, criticism, successor problems, and the transitions among them.

Fallibility travels with it. A creative problem can be a bad problem. A creative criticism can be mistaken. A transformed evaluative criterion can make an explanation worse. A novel transition can move you into a more epistemically closed world.

Creativity is not a guarantee of progress. It is the capacity to bring new explanatory structure into the world.

That capacity suggests a problem: If genuinely new explanatory knowledge can appear, then the future epistemic landscape does not yet exist. We can know an enormous amount about the present. But the knowledge that will change the world is not yet available.

The problem is therefore deeper than uncertainty. The future is not merely hidden; it is open. And if people create the knowledge from which later history will be made, then we are not merely living inside an unpredictable world. We are among the causes of its inherent unpredictability.

<a id="chapter-18--1-creativity-is-distributed-through-the-cycle"></a>

#### 1. Creativity Is Distributed Through the Cycle

The schematic can tempt us into assigning creativity to one place:

$$
P_1 \rightarrow \mathbf{TS} \rightarrow EE \rightarrow P_2.
$$

The problem is given, you invent a solution, the solution is criticized, and the cycle continues. That picture is too simple.

You can live for years inside an inherited problem and then realize that the problem was badly formed. The question changes. The evaluative criteria change. What once counted as progress becomes irrelevant. You have not merely produced another answer; you have created a new region in which answers can exist.

Criticism can do the same. It need not merely eliminate a tentative solution. It can reveal that the original opposition was false or expose an assumption that neither side had noticed. It can also connect two previously distant explanations and create a contradiction that did not previously exist for either participant. The successor problem is then not simply the old problem with one bad answer removed. It is new knowledge.

The arrows matter too. You can move from one problem to another without a complete explicit account of why. A memory becomes relevant, a distinction becomes salient, an old irritation becomes a problem, or something that had seemed settled becomes unstable. We do not yet possess a complete causal explanation of these transitions. But we can already reject one simplifying picture: creativity is not a module that activates when you need an idea. Nor is it a special mode reserved for artists, scientists, inventors, or children. It is implicated in the entire growth of knowledge.

That also means creativity does not always lead to progress. You can invent a better explanation or a better rationalization. You can create a criticism that exposes error or one whose function is to prevent another criticism from being heard. You can create a moral category that enlarges sympathy or one that makes exclusion easier. You can invent a tool for freedom or a tool for surveillance. The epistemic capacity is the same. The direction differs.

<a id="chapter-18--2-the-future-knowledge-problem"></a>

#### 2. The Future Knowledge Problem

Suppose someone asks:

> What will people know fifty years from now?

The question sounds ordinary. We may list likely technologies, extrapolate scientific trends, forecast political arrangements, or describe future cities, medicine, education, artificial intelligence, energy systems, relationships, and institutions. We may give probabilities or construct scenarios.

But the deepest problem appears before any of those exercises begin. If the future knowledge is genuinely new, then we do not yet possess the explanation that would make it available for prediction. To specify the explanatory content of the future discovery now would be, in the relevant sense, to have already created it.

This is not merely a shortage of data, insufficient computing power, or the complexity of the future. The future explanation does not yet exist as objective knowledge. That is why the growth of knowledge is intrinsically unpredictable.

A new explanation has a causal history. You can struggle with a problem for months while your skills change, your attention shifts, a criticism weakens an old explanation, and a new abstraction slowly becomes available. Several apparently unrelated regions of your epistemic mind can change incrementally. Then you say:

> I just realized something.

The explicit appearance can be discontinuous even when the causal preparation is not.

The same structure can appear outside your solitary mind. A scientific revolution may later be narrated as a leap. A technological platform may seem to arrive suddenly. A moral transformation may be attached to one speech, one book, one court decision, one protest, or one invention.

Yet the visible event can emerge from countless smaller changes distributed among many loosely coordinated persons. Someone invents a tool. Someone else develops a notation. Someone elsewhere creates a criticism. An institution changes, a technical constraint disappears, a concept becomes culturally legible, or a problem that once seemed local becomes general. Eventually one visible artifact reorganizes the landscape.

The historical surface looks discontinuous because the causal history is distributed. Openness therefore does not require magic. It requires only that genuinely new explanatory structures can be created through causally continuous processes.

<a id="chapter-18--3-how-prediction-closes-the-world"></a>

#### 3. How Prediction Closes the World

The impossibility of predicting future knowledge is easy to state and difficult to inhabit because common sense pulls in the other direction. We look backward, see patterns, extend them, and call this experience. History seems to teach us how history behaves.

The familiar phrase is:

> History does not repeat, but it rhymes.

The phrase denies crude repetition, but the deeper epistemic structure remains:

$$
\text{past pattern} \rightarrow \text{future pattern}.
$$

The rhyme is still supposed to be available in the past. The future remains a transformed continuation of an already represented possibility space.

Modern predictive reasoning can look as though it escapes that structure. Instead of saying, "This happened before, therefore it will happen again," we now say something more precise: "This happened before, so the posterior probability should increase." The formal tools are more powerful too. The epistemic move can nevertheless remain the same: represent a possibility space, assign probabilities within it, and use new observations to update those probabilities.

This can be extremely useful inside a closed enough world. The problem begins when the representation is promoted into an account of knowledge creation itself. A probability distribution operates over represented possibilities, while knowledge creation can alter what the possibilities are. You can create a new option, reject the original categories, or redefine the problem. You can invent a criterion that makes the previous ranking meaningless or produce an explanation showing that the original possibility space was badly formed.

The progression becomes more sophisticated: from "history repeats" to "history rhymes," then to probabilistic resemblance and updating credence as confirming observations arrive. The problem remains.

The same inversion appears when a useful model becomes a theory of the mind using it. The Bayesian model becomes the Bayesian brain. A person who can employ a probabilistic representation is redescribed as though their epistemic life consists of assigning and updating weights over an already specified world. The categorical error: a psychometric compression becomes personality, a diagnostic compression becomes the person, a statistical regularity becomes a causal ontology. Now a probabilistic model of represented uncertainty becomes a model of knowledge creation itself.

The tool is real, and so is its usefulness. The promotion is the error.

Once a projected future exists, observations can begin to accumulate around it. A predicted trend continues, so confidence increases. An event resembles the scenario, so the model appears corroborated. A contrary observation arrives and is classified as noise, temporary deviation, or an exception anticipated by another branch of the model. The representational structure grows more elaborate, and its apparent credibility increases because it can absorb more of what happens.

Abstract it.

The sequence can become:

$$
\text{extrapolation}
\rightarrow
\text{future model}
\rightarrow
\text{credence}
\rightarrow
\text{confirming observations}
\rightarrow
\text{greater credence}.
$$

This is deeper than confirmation bias as a psychological tendency. The future model has been granted the epistemic status of a space within which later observations are interpreted. The closed world becomes the frame. You then move through imagined histories, updating priors and counting confirmations inside a representation whose most important omission is the knowledge that does not yet exist.

Such a model may be mathematically sophisticated. It may generate precise outputs, survive many observations, and support useful decisions. None of that changes the status of the represented possibility space itself: it remains conjectural. A new technology can invalidate the category by which a trend was represented. A moral criticism can transform what later people regard as an acceptable outcome. A new institution can change the relevant action space. A scientific explanation can show that the variables in the original model were badly chosen.

The failure, then, need not be that the forecast was slightly wrong. The represented future can cease to be the relevant future.

<a id="chapter-18--4-you-are-not-a-projection-of-your-present-compression"></a>

#### 4. You Are Not a Projection of Your Present Compression

The argument becomes more intimate when we return to you and your solitary mind. That mind includes explicit explanations, but also inexplicit knowledge, memory, skill, salience, affect, expectation, perceptual organization, concepts, language, social knowledge, unfinished problems, and changing evaluative criteria. No outside observer possesses direct access to this vast universe, and you do not possess explicit access to it either.

Yet we regularly compress the epistemic mind, $M_i$. We call someone conscientious, anxious, agreeable, gifted, difficult, traditional, impulsive, depressed, creative, uncreative, a leader, a follower, a risk, or a type. Some of these compressions can be useful. The epistemic error appears when compression becomes projection:

$$
M_{i,t_0}
\rightarrow
\hat{M}_{i,t_0}
\rightarrow
\hat{M}_{i,t_1}
\rightarrow
\hat{M}_{i,t_2}.
$$

You are first made simple in state and then simple in evolution. Your future is predicted from the compression.

The problem is not only that categories fail to capture everything about you. **The dimensions discarded by the category may include the very knowledge creation through which you become different.** You become predictable in the model because the model first makes you smaller—not smaller in reality, but smaller in the representation.

The moral consequence becomes clearer when the compression concerns another person. Imagine that I construct an explanation of them: selfish, unreliable, ideological, anxious, narcissistic, timid, ambitious. Perhaps the description captures something observable. But once the category becomes stable, it begins to travel forward. A generous act becomes strategic. A disagreement becomes diagnostic. A change of mind becomes inconsistency. A surprising action becomes evidence for a deeper version of the same trait.

The model begins to absorb its own criticism. The other person becomes increasingly predictable because the explanation has become increasingly difficult to escape. The problem is not merely that I may be wrong. I have reduced the other person's epistemic openness before encountering it.

A broader approach begins by keeping the explanation exposed to failure. Suppose the person acts in a way I do not understand. Instead of asking:

> What kind of person behaves like this?

I can ask:

> What problem would make this action intelligible?

That question produces several tentative reconstructions:

$$
A \rightarrow \{P_1,P_2,P_3,\ldots,P_n\}.
$$

Perhaps the person is solving a status problem, a safety problem, or a loyalty problem. Perhaps they are responding to a moral problem I do not yet recognize. Perhaps my description of the action is itself wrong. One of these models need not secretly be the true one. Their value here is that the wider representational surface creates more opportunities for my explanation to fail.

This is **the rationality principle** used as a surrogate rather than a prophecy. The model says:

> If this were the person's problem situation, the action would make sense.

It does not say:

> Therefore this is what the person will do next.

Its epistemic value comes from becoming criticizable. The observed person remains able to destroy the reconstruction. To explore another person's mind in this way is therefore also a moral practice. It refuses premature closure and treats the other person as a universe that cannot be exhausted by the compression through which they first became legible to us.

<a id="chapter-18--5-how-openness-gets-recruited-against-itself"></a>

#### 5. How Openness Gets Recruited Against Itself

Children make epistemic openness difficult to ignore. A child can turn a chair into a spacecraft. A question about an insect can become a question about death. A game can change its criteria halfway through. A child can ask a question that exposes an assumption adults stopped noticing years ago.

The claim is not that childhood is a mystical state of pure creativity. Children are fallible. Their problems can be confused, their explanations wrong, their criticisms arbitrary, and their inventions unable to survive contact with reality. What childhood makes conspicuous is open-ended epistemic movement.

Coordination changes the environment in which that movement occurs. Schools need schedules, curricula, assessments, standards, classrooms, roles, and expected outputs. Organizations need employees to perform identifiable tasks. Professions need credentials. Bureaucracies need forms. Coordination therefore requires compression.

A child who freely creates problems enters environments in which the problem is often supplied in advance. The solution space narrows, the evaluation criteria become externally legible, and the transition schedule is imposed. 

Abstract it.

The sequence can become:

$$
\text{assigned problem}
\rightarrow
\text{permitted solution}
\rightarrow
\text{authorized criticism}
\rightarrow
\text{next assigned problem}.
$$

This does not eliminate creativity. If it did, communication itself would become impossible. You still have to interpret instructions, reconstruct meanings, resolve ambiguities, form expectations, and integrate new information into an epistemic mind no institution possesses. The creative process continues, but its direction can be constrained and recruited.

Creativity can even be used to impede further creativity. A manager can invent a more sophisticated performance system that makes dissent harder. A bureaucracy can create increasingly elaborate categories through which people must become legible. A political movement can create a vocabulary that turns criticism into evidence of disloyalty. An institution can create procedures whose complexity makes responsibility difficult to locate. Objective knowledge can preserve and scale these creative attempts to suppress further creativity.

The same structure can operate inwardly. You encounter an inherited explanation of what a successful person should be. You do not merely submit mechanically; you can creatively reconstruct yourself within it. You explain why your interests are impractical and reinterpret dissatisfaction as immaturity. You explain away a problem that threatens an identity and invent reasons that the life expected of you is the life you really wanted. The resulting self-explanation may become extraordinarily elaborate.

Creativity has not disappeared. It has been recruited into epistemic closure.

That is why saying "I am not creative" can distort what is happening. If personhood involves creating problems, explanations, criticisms, interpretations, and transitions among epistemic states, then artistic creativity is one conspicuous expression of a more general epistemic capacity. The issue is not that everyone is secretly an artist. It is that your epistemic life already depends upon forms of creation that a narrow cultural category of creativity may fail to name.

<a id="chapter-18--6-the-geometry-of-openness"></a>

#### 6. The Geometry of Openness

The distinction between compression and openness now recurs at several scales. The error has the same shape each time: compress an open present, project the compression, and mistake continuity in the model for knowledge of what will become.

Abstract it.

At the level of civilization:

$$
K_{t_0}
\rightarrow
\text{compress}
\rightarrow
\text{project deeply}
$$

vs:

$$
K_{t_0}
\rightarrow
\text{expand broadly}
\rightarrow
\text{seek contradiction}.
$$

At the level of a field:

$$
E_{t_0}
\rightarrow
\text{narrow model}
\rightarrow
\text{forecast}
$$

vs:

$$
E_{t_0}
\rightarrow
\text{connect explanations}
\rightarrow
\text{consilience}
\rightarrow
\text{new problem}.
$$

At the level of a person:

$$
M_{i,t_0}
\rightarrow
\text{trait / category / profile}
\rightarrow
\text{behavioral prediction}
$$

vs:

$$
M_{i,t_0}
\rightarrow
\text{multiple tentative reconstructions}
\rightarrow
\text{criticism}
\rightarrow
\text{deeper encounter}.
$$

At the level of the self:

$$
M_{\text{self}}
\rightarrow
\text{identity compression}
\rightarrow
\text{expected future self}
$$

vs:

$$
M_{\text{self}}
\rightarrow
\text{new problems}
\rightarrow
\text{new criticism}
\rightarrow
\text{open future self}.
$$

That recurring geometry sharpens the question we can ask of objective knowledge. At $t_0$, our representational surface is extraordinarily broad. We possess objective knowledge about physical systems, biological processes, technologies, institutions, laws, markets, languages, software, mathematics, scientific explanations, engineering systems, historical records, norms, organizational processes, and innumerable local causal structures.

The breadth is vast, but the depth of legitimate causal projection into an epistemically open future is comparatively shallow. We can represent many things near the present. We cannot represent the future knowledge that will later reorganize them. The epistemic landscape may therefore look less like a narrow road extending far into the future. It may look more like an enormous surface lying close to the present: very broad, relatively shallow.

Much of our representational activity points in the opposite direction. We build narrow explanatory surfaces and project them many steps forward. Economic forecasts, political forecasts, technology forecasts, demographic forecasts, market forecasts, risk scenarios, strategic roadmaps, and histories of the future all take this form. The representation has depth; the causal basis may not. The farther the projection travels through domains saturated by human knowledge creation, the more opportunities there are for explanatory novelty to alter the path. The future representation grows thick while the epistemic foundation grows thin.

Consilience points across the broad surface instead. If there is one reality, explanations developed in different domains cannot remain permanently incompatible. A biological explanation can collide with a psychological explanation. A computational explanation can collide with a theory of mind. A moral explanation can collide with an institutional practice. A statistical model can collide with an explanation of the person. The collision creates a problem.

This is one reason creating a genuinely good explanation is difficult. An explanation may look excellent inside the narrow surface where it was invented; its weakness becomes visible only when its consequences reach another domain. The breadth of objective knowledge therefore creates an enormous error-elimination surface. More knowledge does not merely mean more facts. It means more opportunities for explanations to collide.

The direction of epistemic progress is therefore not necessarily:

$$
\text{deeper projection}.
$$

It may be:

$$
\text{greater breadth}
\rightarrow
\text{greater consilience}
\rightarrow
\text{more contradiction}
\rightarrow
\text{better problems}.
$$

This is not a retreat from explanation. It is a different use of explanatory reach. Present categories receive less authority over the distant future, while present explanations face more pressure to survive contact with everything else we already know.

<a id="chapter-18--7-ai-depth-or-breadth"></a>

#### 7. AI Depth or Breadth

Modern computation gives us extraordinary representational scale. A machine can retrieve, transform, compare, and preserve more objective knowledge than one biological mind can hold explicitly, and artificial intelligence extends that scale dramatically.

One obvious use of that capacity is to project represented structure forward. We ask machines to forecast, rank, score, predict, estimate, assign probability, generate scenarios, project trends, and model future behavior. The machine receives a possibility space, extends it, assigns weights, elaborates consequences, and generates a future that appears increasingly detailed. This can make epistemic thinness look like knowledge.

A model begins with a few assumptions. The machine produces ten pages of consequences. The output is coherent, specific, internally connected, perhaps quantitative. The original assumptions disappear beneath the representational richness. A thin future looks thick.

Generative AI is unusually well matched to this operation because continuation is one of its conspicuous abilities. Give it a sequence and it can continue the sequence. Give it a trend and it can extend the trend. Give it a set of political assumptions and it can generate future political scenarios. Give it a technological roadmap and it can populate the decades around it. Give it a profile of a person and it can produce imagined future behavior.

The output can be compelling because it resembles the structure of historical explanation. Events lead to events. Causes accumulate. Institutions respond. People adapt. Technology advances. The future becomes narratively legible. But narrative legibility is not future knowledge.

The machine has extended inherited structure. It has not thereby created the explanatory knowledge that future persons will later create. This is the external analogue of predicting the compressed person: a narrow representation is projected forward, the generative system fills the empty surface, and openness disappears inside prose.

Probabilistic machinery can make the projection look firmer still. Scenario A receives 50%, Scenario B 30%, Scenario C 20%. The imagined future now has numerical credence as well as narrative detail. New events can be interpreted as movement toward one scenario or another, and the future is progressively redescribed as though it had always been contained in the original model. The history of the future is closed.

But computation need not be used primarily for depth. A model can make an explanation precise, expose a dependency, show what would follow if a conjecture were correct, and make criticism easier. The rationality principle is useful for exactly this reason. A model of another person can say:

> If this were their problem situation, this action would make sense.

Reality can contradict that reconstruction. The same logic can operate at larger scales. A model of an institution can say:

> If these constraints are operative, this outcome should follow.

A model of a technology can say:

> If this causal architecture is correct, this intervention should produce that effect.

The model is useful because it creates a surface for error elimination. The mistake is to promote that surface into prophecy.

This changes the computational problem. Instead of asking which represented future is most probable, the machine can help expose which presently available explanations cannot all be true together. Instead of predicting what another person will do, it can generate several problem situations that would make an action intelligible. It can then identify what would disconfirm each reconstruction. Instead of asking which technology will dominate in 2040, it can expose the present constraints, explanations, and unresolved contradictions that make current trajectories unstable. Instead of narrating the future of education, it can place explanations of learning, authority, childhood, measurement, and knowledge creation beside one another and reveal where they conflict.

This does not make the future more predictable. It makes the present more criticizable.

Artificial intelligence may be particularly useful here because biological cognition is narrow at the explicit surface. You cannot simultaneously hold every relevant theory, paper, institutional rule, historical example, technical constraint, philosophical implication, and conflicting explanation. Objective knowledge already extends you beyond those limits: writing extends memory, mathematics extends representation, libraries extend retrieval, scientific institutions extend specialization, and computers extend calculation.

AI can extend comparison. It can place explanatory structures beside one another that no individual would otherwise hold together long enough for criticism to operate. It can help reveal hidden contradiction and generate alternative rational reconstructions. It can expose where a model depends on a category inherited from somewhere else, or where an explanation in one field quietly requires something another field says is impossible.

That is consilience as an engineering problem. You remain the epistemic locus; the machine enlarges the surface on which problems can appear.

The unpredictability of knowledge therefore suggests a research program. How can large bodies of objective knowledge be represented in ways that preserve explanatory structure rather than merely textual similarity? How can machines expose contradictions across fields? How can they generate criticizable rational reconstructions without converting those reconstructions into predictions? How can they preserve multiple candidate explanations without collapsing them into a probability distribution? How can they help you discover problems rather than merely answer inherited ones? How can they make conflicting evaluative criteria visible? How can they show where an apparently stable future depends on the assumption that nobody creates a new explanation?

These are technological questions, but they arise from the epistemology.

<a id="chapter-18--8-planning-without-possessing-the-future"></a>

#### 8. Planning Without Possessing the Future

The inability to know the future is not a new human problem. Traditions have located the future in fate, providence, prophecy, divine will, historical necessity, technological progress, economic law, and statistical expectation. The explanations differ enormously, but many can be reconstructed as responses to the same problem:

> How should you act when what happens next cannot be known?

One recurring response is to create an authority with privileged access to the future. The role can be occupied by the oracle, the priest, the ruler, the historian of destiny, the expert forecaster, the probabilistic model, or the algorithm. The forms differ, but the attraction is similar. If the future can be known by someone or something, uncertainty becomes governable.

The epistemic problem returns wherever future history depends upon explanatory knowledge not yet created. No authority possesses that knowledge in advance. An authority may still know more about some present causal structures, construct better models, or identify real constraints. None of these achievements converts open knowledge creation into a closed future.

This does not make expertise useless or planning incoherent. You still act. Institutions coordinate. Engineers design. Companies allocate resources. Governments build infrastructure. Parents make decisions. The openness of knowledge changes the epistemic status of those activities rather than eliminating them.

A plan is a tentative solution. A roadmap is a conjecture. A scenario is a model. A forecast is a representation. Each can be useful and each can be criticized. None contains the future.

Planning under openness therefore has a different architecture. Action proceeds from the best present explanation while alternatives remain available, assumptions and causal dependencies remain visible, and the structures carrying the plan remain revisable. Surprise then becomes a new problem for the plan rather than a failure of reality to obey it. The aim is not possession of the future. It is continued capacity for correction when the future becomes different from what was represented.

The same structure applies to the future self.

You can create a plan for your life, form an identity, decide what matters, and imagine who you will become. These can all be useful forms of objective knowledge. But when you later inhabit that future, you will know things you do not know now. You may encounter problems that do not yet exist or acquire concepts that make current goals look strange. You may create a criticism of an identity that presently feels obvious. You may invent a criterion by which today's success looks like failure, or become interested in something you cannot yet name.

Your future self therefore cannot be fully represented by your present self. This is not merely because life is uncertain. It is because you remain epistemically open.

The same mistake we make with history can be made with ourselves: compress the present self, project the compression, call the trajectory identity. Commitments need not disappear for that mistake to be avoided. They can remain tentative structures inside an open epistemic life. Your future remains available for surprise because you remain capable of creating knowledge that your present representation cannot contain.

<a id="chapter-18--9-you-cause-the-future"></a>

#### 9. You Cause The Future

You are not merely inadequately described by a trait, more complicated than a category, or difficult to measure. You are a source of new explanatory knowledge.

Your future therefore cannot be represented merely as the continuation of your present state. And because people create the objective knowledge from which institutions, technologies, norms, sciences, and later problems are made, their creations inherit the same openness.

The future is not open because reality lacks causes. It is open because some of those causes will be knowledge that does not yet exist.

That gives creativity its most consequential meaning. You can bring into the world an explanation that changes what happens next. You can create a problem that redirects a field or a criticism that destroys an inherited category. You can create a criterion that makes an old success irrelevant, a tool that changes which actions are possible, or an explanation of yourself that reopens a life.

The openness of knowledge is therefore not merely an epistemic limitation. It is the causal signature of personhood.

You cannot know every problem your future self will encounter or every criterion by which you will judge what matters. Yet you must still act, commit, choose, and explain why one direction is worth pursuing rather than another.

Some of those explanations become so important that you stop treating them as explanations at all. You call them values.

But if your values are guides to an open future, what happens when they begin protecting themselves from the criticism that could change it?

<a id="chapter-19"></a>

### XIX. The Value Bomb

You are not exhausted by your present explanations. A commitment does not specify the future you. New problems can become visible, new criticisms can arrive, and new explanations can be created. You can change what you think matters, what you count as progress, and even what you regard as the problem.

That open future creates a problem: Some explanations may become sufficiently general, important, and compressed that we stop experiencing them as explanations at all. We call them **values.

A value can sound like the place where explanation ends:

> I value liberty.
> I value truth.
> I value a natural childhood.
> I value equality.

The grammar is revealing. The value appears as an internal fact about you. You may feel it sincerely; it may organize your action and appear morally serious. Because it is called a value, asking for an explanation can begin to sound almost improper.

Why do you value liberty? Equality? Tradition? Technological abstinence?

At some point the answer may become:

> Because I do.

Or:

> Because it is right.

Or:

> Because those are my values.

The explanatory chain has stopped, but the value has not stopped doing explanatory work. The same unexplained value can now be used to explain why an action is good, why an institution is legitimate, why a technology is dangerous, why a child should be protected, why another person is immoral, why an opposing idea should be excluded, or why criticism itself has gone too far.

That inversion is the problem. A compressed explanation becomes an explanatory premise, and the premise can then be turned back upon its own criticism. The value begins by summarizing an explanation. It ends by protecting itself from explanation.

That structure can scale. It can help make religions and ideologies unusually difficult to criticize. It can turn rival values into pollution, people into viruses, objective knowledge into contamination, and technologies into villains. It can also turn a real liberal problem about tolerance into a blunt permission to exclude others.

The conclusion is not that values are inherently problematic. Some values may be useful precisely because they compress explanations with great reach. But useful compression is not explanatory foundation. If a value is to preserve explanatory knowledge rather than replace it, the road back to the explanation has to remain available.

<a id="chapter-19--1-values-are-compressed-explanations"></a>

#### 1. Values Are Compressed Explanations

Consider:

> I value liberty.

It appears to name a moral primitive. But epistemically, liberty is not treated that way. We arrived at freedom through explanation.

You are fallible. Knowledge grows through conjecture and criticism. Criticism requires alternatives. Coercion can remove alternatives, punish dissent, suppress communication, restrict experimentation, and narrow the problems you are permitted to pursue.

That gives an explanatory structure:

$$
\text{fallibility}
+
\text{criticism}
+
\text{open alternatives}
\rightarrow
\text{epistemic importance of freedom}.
$$

Only after constructing that structure do we obtain the compressed expression:

> liberty matters.

The explanation comes first. The compressed value comes later.

The same relation appears elsewhere. Truth is not valuable merely because the word *truth* has moral force. It begins with realism and from the possibility that explanations can be wrong. Error matters only if there is something for the explanation to be wrong about.

Creation is not valuable merely because creation sounds noble. You can create a cruel institution, a better weapon, or a more efficient propaganda system. What matters is the explanatory structure in which creation occurs and the problems it solves or creates.

Equality is not self-validating either. It can acquire explanatory force through deeper claims about persons, coercion, knowledge, authority, and the absence of any demonstrated epistemic caste entitled to rule the rest.

The general sequence is:

$$
P
\rightarrow
E
\rightarrow
V
$$

where $P$ is a problem, $E$ an epistemic structure, and $V$ a compressed value.

The value is shorthand. It is not the origin of the explanation.

The error appears when the sequence is reversed:

$$
V
\rightarrow
E.
$$

Now liberty asserts why something is good. Equality asserts why something is good. Tradition or nature does the same work. The compression is being used as though it were the structure that originally gave the compression meaning.

Compression itself is not a defect. You could not think or coordinate without it. A scientific term can compress an enormous body of explanation. A mathematical symbol can preserve relations that would otherwise require pages to restate. A technical interface can hide complexity while preserving access to the function built upon it.

Values can work similarly. When you say:

> I value truth,

that phrase may carry realism, fallibility, criticism, scientific practice, personal honesty, distrust of authority, and an understanding that false explanations can cause harm. The phrase is useful because you do not need to reconstruct that whole history every time you decide whether to conceal an error.

The problem begins when the compression becomes opaque to its own origin. Then *I value truth* stops meaning *this phrase is shorthand for a large explanatory structure* and begins to mean *my commitment to truth explains itself*.

The same danger applies to epistemic compressions. Consider:

> all life is problem solving.

That sentence could become a slogan repeated whenever difficulty appears. Instead, we decompressed it. What is a problem? How does a problem become a problem for you? How do tentative solutions arise? What counts as criticism? What happens between epistemic states? How can the future remain open if physical processes remain causally continuous?

Likewise:

> evil is the lack of knowledge

could become a moral slogan. We found it useful by asking what kind of knowledge is lacking, how harmful explanations persist, why intelligence can coexist with cruelty, how explanatory closure can stabilize suffering, and what it means for a corrigible person to preserve a morally destructive explanation.

The compressed phrase became useful because the explanation remained recoverable.

Values are often harder to decompress because they arrive already elevated: revealed, received, sacred, traditional, natural, self-evident, civilizational, constitutional, foundational. Their source may be theological, political, familial, or professional. A value may also be tied to identity so deeply that it appears older than any explicit explanation you can reconstruct.

That is unsurprising. Much of your epistemic life is inexplicit. You can know how to move, notice, trust, fear, prefer, reject, or anticipate without possessing an explicit account of how that knowledge is represented. Values can occupy the same hidden landscape.

You may not be able to say why something feels sacred, why a violation appears immediately disgusting, or where a distinction entered your epistemic mind. You may have reconstructed it from family life, stories, institutions, religion, law, schooling, peers, media, private experience, and countless small criticisms distributed over decades.

The resulting value can feel immediate. That immediacy does not show that the value is foundational. It may show that the explanatory road has become invisible. You experience the destination without seeing the route.

Your epistemic mind is vast enough to hide that route. It contains memories, skills, expectations, emotional associations, categories, perceptual habits, social knowledge, language, theories, inexplicit distinctions, unfinished problems, and objective knowledge reconstructed from outside you. These structures need not be consciously available, neatly organized, or mutually consistent.

You can retain contradictions for years without experiencing them as contradictions. A contradiction does not automatically become a problem; enough tension must become salient for reconstruction to begin. A value can therefore participate in circular explanation without the circle ever becoming visible.

The simple form is:

$$
V
\rightarrow
E
\rightarrow
V.
$$

The lived form may be distributed:

$$
V
\rightarrow
A_1
\rightarrow
A_2
\rightarrow
A_3
\rightarrow
E
\rightarrow
A_4
\rightarrow
A_5
\rightarrow
V.
$$

The route may pass through childhood assumptions, religious concepts, social categories, emotional salience, political vocabulary, historical narratives, remembered authority, and long-inexplicit distinctions. By the time the explanation returns to the value, no circle is felt. You simply experience: *of course creation requires a creator; of course truth is manifest; of course a good parent protects a child from corrupting influences; of course liberty requires intolerance of illiberalism.*

The phrase **of course** is epistemically interesting because it can mark a transition that no longer appears as a transition. A value can feel self-evident because the arrows supporting it have disappeared into the depths of your epistemic mind.

What happens when the invisible road is arranged so that criticism itself protects the value?

<a id="chapter-19--2-reflexivity-can-become-immunity"></a>

#### 2. Reflexivity Can Become Immunity

Circularity is often treated as a textbook logical defect. That description is too weak for what matters here. The more useful question is: **what does the circle do?**

Suppose you value creation and adopt an explanation in which creation requires a creator. The existence of creation becomes evidence of the creator, while the creator becomes the source of the value of creation. The value participates in an explanation that returns to establish the value.

Suppose instead that you value truth and possess a doctrine under which truth reveals itself to the properly oriented person. Your recognition of the doctrine becomes evidence that the doctrine is true, while failure to recognize it becomes evidence of distortion in the observer.

Or suppose you value liberty and possess an explanation under which illiberal views threaten the possibility of liberty. The existence of such views becomes a reason to restrict them, and the restriction becomes an expression of commitment to liberty. The value has authorized conduct that appears, at first glance, to oppose the value.

The contents differ. The reflexive form is similar:

$$
V
\rightarrow
E
\rightarrow
\text{interpretation of }V
\rightarrow
V.
$$

The problem becomes more severe when criticism itself enters the loop.

A doctrine says:

> doubt is temptation.

You doubt the doctrine. The doubt does not become criticism; it becomes evidence that temptation is operating.

An ideology says:

> members of the dominant class cannot recognize their own domination.

A member of the alleged class rejects the explanation. The rejection becomes evidence of the blindness being alleged.

A political doctrine says:

> intolerant people exploit tolerance in order to destroy tolerance.

Someone questions whether a particular opponent should be excluded. The question becomes evidence that the critic is naively tolerating intolerance.

Abstract it.

The operation is the same:

$$
C(V)
\rightarrow
\text{classification of critic}
\rightarrow
\text{dismissal of }C(V).
$$

The criticism is not answered. The critic is explained. The question has changed from *is this value or doctrine wrong?* to *what is wrong with the person who cannot see that it is right?*

That is an immunizing structure. It consumes possible falsifiers. A disagreement that might have generated a successor problem becomes confirmation that the existing problem was correctly formulated. Criticism could expose a hidden assumption and create a problem that did not previously exist. Here, criticism is prevented from becoming a problem at all.

Once criticism has been converted into evidence of moral defect, classification becomes easy. The critic can be called sinful, corrupted, impure, irrational, unenlightened, hateful, intolerant, decadent, brainwashed, extremist, or dangerous. The vocabulary changes; the structure does not:

$$
\text{criticism of explanation}
\rightarrow
\text{classification of person}
\rightarrow
\text{loss of standing of criticism}.
$$

A measured output became a trait, then the trait became the person. A social category became a causal explanation. A diagnosis became a mechanism. An institutional role became an ontology.

Now a retained value becomes the person.

The moral category absorbs the explanatory agent, and the move can feel rigorous from inside the insulated structure. If obedience is virtue, disobedience is vice. If purity is virtue, contamination is vice. If tolerance is virtue, intolerance is vice. The conclusion appears deductive because the protected value has already fixed the terms of the deduction.

Abstract the structure.

The structure is symmetric. A value system you reject can perform the same operation. Suppose one side has:

$$
V_A
\rightarrow
\text{critics of }V_A\text{ are corrupt},
$$

while the other has:

$$
V_B
\rightarrow
\text{supporters of }V_A\text{ are corrupt}.
$$

One side sees decadence where the other sees oppression; one sees moral collapse where the other sees authoritarianism. The same action is reconstructed inside different epistemic worlds, and each explanation predicts the other's response. The response therefore feels confirmatory:

$$
V_A
\rightarrow
\text{interpret }V_B
\rightarrow
V_A
$$

while:

$$
V_B
\rightarrow
\text{interpret }V_A
\rightarrow
V_B.
$$

The two systems become mutually immunizing. More observations need not create more criticism because the explanatory structures are already determining what the observations mean. A problem still has to become visible.

The same architecture can scale. A protected value can support another explanation, which supports another. One part explains moral authority, another history, another dissent, another insider insight, another outsider blindness, another the danger of rival explanations. Eventually the system may contain a theory of why criticism proves the critic's corruption:

$$
V
\rightarrow
E_1
\rightarrow
E_2
\rightarrow
E_3
\rightarrow
E_4
$$

while:

$$
E_4
\rightarrow
\text{protection of }V.
$$

A religion or ideology organized this way can contain enormous explanatory structure. The defect is not the presence of explanation. It is that criticism is interpreted from inside the system it is supposed to criticize.

Reflexivity has become immunity. Reflexivity itself is not the defect. This project is reflexive: if knowledge grows through criticism, then the epistemology must remain criticizable; if explanations have reach, the explanation of explanations must be allowed to create problems for itself; if you are fallible, so are the authors of the epistemology.

Abstract it.

Healthy reflexivity exposes the explanation to more criticism:

$$
E
\rightarrow
E(E)
\rightarrow
\text{new criticism}.
$$

Immunizing reflexivity protects it:

$$
E
\rightarrow
E(C(E))
\rightarrow
\text{dismiss criticism}.
$$

The relevant distinction is therefore not linear versus circular explanation. It is reflexivity that exposes versus reflexivity that protects.

Once a value can protect itself this way, its moral status can be transferred to whatever contains it.

<a id="chapter-19--3-the-logic-of-contamination"></a>

#### 3. The Logic of Contamination

Suppose a value has already been classified as morally bad. A further compression becomes possible: whatever contains the value inherits its status.

$$
V_{\text{bad}}\in X
\rightarrow
X_{\text{bad}}.
$$

The carrier disappears into the classification. A person who contains the value becomes a bad person. An artifact that contains it becomes a bad artifact. A technology that embodies or transmits it becomes a bad technology.

The same move can be written three ways:

$$
\text{person contains bad value}
\rightarrow
\text{reject person},
$$

$$
\text{artifact contains bad value}
\rightarrow
\text{reject artifact},
$$

$$
\text{technology embodies or transmits bad value}
\rightarrow
\text{reject technology}.
$$

In each case, the containing structure loses its complexity. A person becomes the explanation they presently retain. A book becomes the doctrine it contains. A platform becomes the worst idea transmitted through it. A technology becomes the harmful use made of it.

Once the objectionable value is detected, it detonates the moral standing of the whole. That transfer will be called the **value bomb**.

The name matters because the mechanism recurs. Suppose an artifact contains an explanation judged morally unacceptable. Under a pollution model, reconstruction of the whole artifact is unnecessary; the objectionable value is enough:

$$
V_{\text{bad}}
\rightarrow
K_{\text{bad}}.
$$

If you then encounter the artifact, the same model can treat the value as though it transfers directly:

$$
K_{\text{bad}}
\rightarrow
P_{\text{polluted}}.
$$

You become a carrier. If you speak, the value may spread further. An epistemic problem has been turned into a sanitation problem.

The vocabulary follows: exposure, contamination, corruption, toxicity, radicalization, dangerous content, unsafe ideas, harmful influence. Some of these words can refer to real causal processes. People can be manipulated. Propaganda can be destructive. Your epistemic mind can become worse. Bad explanations can spread.

The pollution model becomes misleading when those causal processes are replaced by passive transfer. You are no longer reconstructing, criticizing, misunderstanding, rejecting, modifying, or integrating objective knowledge. You are absorbing a substance. That is the old bucket theory in moral form.

The architecture predates digital technology. We encountered it in the history of media. A new medium gives people access to forms of objective knowledge that previous institutions did not fully control. Some of that knowledge is poor, manipulative, morally abhorrent, or merely unfamiliar. The status of the content is then transferred to the medium:

$$
\text{bad content}
\rightarrow
\text{bad medium}
\rightarrow
\text{restrict medium}.
$$

The same pattern can recur with books, popular music, television, games, the internet, smartphones, social media, and artificial intelligence. The surface changes, but the medium remains the moral carrier of the value.

Technological abstinence can therefore feel like an explanation: remove the carrier, remove the pollution, protect the person. That compression is already difficult to sustain.

<a id="chapter-19--4-technology-and-the-apparatus-of-preservation"></a>

#### 4. Technology and the Apparatus of Preservation

The category *technology* is already too broad to function within an explanation. Technology has appeared in several different relations: as objective knowledge embodied in artifacts; as a medium that extends memory, communication, coordination, and criticism; and as an instrument through which surveillance, manipulation, censorship, or ideological amplification can also occur.

Those are not contradictory descriptions. They are different uses and mechanisms carried by a broad technological substrate. The existence of malicious uses therefore cannot, by itself, settle the moral status of the category *technology*.

Artificial intelligence makes the symmetry unusually visible. AI can reinforce a value, restate it persuasively, help construct a coherent ideological explanation, classify speech according to an inherited framework, or suppress rival explanations. The same broad technology can also decompress a slogan, reconstruct assumptions, compare explanatory structures, expose circularity, retrieve criticism, and preserve a long explanatory surface that unaided memory would compress.

The category does not settle the local problem. The same system can participate in closure or decompression. Calling AI morally neutral in this limited sense does not imply that every system or use is equally good or bad. It means that the explanation cannot stop at *AI*.

The structure becomes especially visible when the person being protected is a child because the authority relation is already established.

A parent possesses some explanation of a good childhood. It may include physical play, direct relationships, attention, nature, books, local community, family continuity, protection from commercial manipulation, or protection from explicit content. Those concerns may be real and may support good local restrictions.

Once compressed, however, the explanation can become:

> I value a low-technology childhood.

That sentence can conceal many different causal claims. The problem begins when the value substitutes for the claims it compressed:

$$
\text{low technology is good}
\rightarrow
\text{technology is harmful}
\rightarrow
\text{restriction is good}.
$$

Now the distinctions that matter disappear. Which technology? Used how? For what problem? By which child? Under which social conditions? What knowledge becomes available? What criticism becomes unavailable? What changes when a restriction removes a harmful interaction, and what changes when it removes access to an explanation the parent does not possess?

Those questions reopen the compression.

A parent can lose epistemic overlap with a child as the child develops interests, relationships, vocabulary, and knowledge inside environments the parent does not understand. The parent's experienced problem may be:

> I no longer understand this part of my child's world.

Yet a restriction can be described as solving a different problem:

> this part of my child's world is dangerous.

Values can conceal that substitution. A parent who values a low-technology childhood may have a good explanation. The same restriction may also preserve an explanatory environment in which the adult's values remain comparatively uncontested.

That is not a universal diagnosis of parents. It identifies a structural question: does the restriction solve a demonstrated problem for the child, or does it also preserve the adult's preferred epistemic landscape by controlling which rival explanations become available?

The same structure produces a revealing symmetry at the level of technology. Technology is often described as the source of polluted values: the internet spreads extremist ideology, social media radicalizes, AI produces harmful content. Yet the proposed remedies are often technological too: filtering, content moderation, parental controls, automated classification, identity systems, surveillance, or AI safety systems.

So the same variable appears on both sides:

$$
T
\rightarrow
\text{pollution}
$$

and:

$$
T
\rightarrow
\text{purification}.
$$

The apparent contradiction disappears once the category is decompressed. Technology is not the polluter or the purifier. People are using objective knowledge to influence which objective knowledge other people encounter. The moral disagreement occurs through the technology rather than residing inside it as an essence.

Modern filtering systems are extensions of an older project. Human societies have long created objective knowledge that preserves values across generations: religious canons, schools, professional codes, constitutions, censorship regimes, curricula, rituals, libraries, archives, and institutions of interpretation. These structures can preserve good explanations. They can also preserve immunized values.

Digital systems alter the scale and responsiveness of the apparatus. A filter can operate continuously. A classifier can intervene before a rival explanation is encountered. A system can personalize what becomes visible. AI can increase the granularity further.

The underlying relation is older:

$$
V
\rightarrow
\text{objective knowledge}
\rightarrow
\text{preservation of }V.
$$

Preservation is not itself the defect. The problem begins when preservation becomes insulation from criticism.

Once rival values are treated as pollution, protecting people begins to mean managing exposure. Some cases involve concrete causal problems: a child can be protected from an adult attempting manipulation; a person can be protected from threats; an institution can establish boundaries needed for its function.

The pollution model expands when the rival explanation itself becomes the danger:

$$
\text{bad explanation}
\rightarrow
\text{bad objective knowledge}
\rightarrow
\text{restricted access}.
$$

Applied to adults, the model creates an old asymmetry. An authority is assumed competent to encounter the bad explanation and classify it, while the ordinary person is assumed to require protection from it. The authority may examine the poison; the public should not. That is the authority memeplex again.

The same problem reappears inside liberalism, where values created to preserve liberty can themselves become insulated from criticism.

<a id="chapter-19--5-liberal-values-after-the-explanation"></a>

#### 5. Liberal Values After the Explanation

We did not begin with liberal declarations: *liberty is a Western value*, *free speech is a liberal principle*, or *pluralism is good because liberal democracy says so*. Instead, we reconstructed their problems.

You are fallible. No authority possesses complete knowledge. Criticism requires access to alternatives. Coercion can prevent criticism from entering your problem situation. Objective knowledge also lets persons with very different internal worlds coordinate through relatively thin interfaces without requiring deep agreement. Political structures that permit criticism, exit, revision, dissent, and nonviolent removal of bad policies therefore solve important epistemic problems.

Only after that reconstruction do words such as *liberty*, *tolerance*, *pluralism*, *free speech*, and *democracy* become useful compressions. The labels are not the explanatory grounds. They are what remains after the explanation has been compressed. That matters because liberalism can become immunized in the same way as any other doctrine if its compressed values are allowed to reverse the explanatory sequence.

The phrase **paradox of tolerance** makes the danger visible. The familiar formulation is that a tolerant society may be destroyed if it tolerates people who would abolish tolerance, and therefore tolerance requires intolerance toward intolerance.

The problem described by the slogan is real. A society that permits open criticism may encounter people who advocate or undertake actions that would eliminate those conditions.

But the problem does not contain its own solution. A tentative solution still has to be created and exposed to criticism:

> How can institutions preserve the conditions of criticism when some people advocate or undertake actions that would destroy those conditions?

That formulation does not settle the case in advance. Different problems may support different tentative solutions: counter-speech, constitutional structure, exit rights, institutional boundaries, rules against coercive conduct, legal protections, procedural constraints, or further criticism.

A specific restriction may solve a specific problem. The phrase *paradox of tolerance* cannot perform that explanatory work by itself.

The danger appears when the problem is compressed into a rule:

$$
\text{intolerance}
\rightarrow
\text{must not be tolerated}.
$$

At once, another problem appears. What counts as intolerance? Who classifies it? Which actions are being prohibited? Which explanations are being excluded? What criticism would change the classification?

If those questions disappear, the slogan has ceased to identify a problem and has become a jurisdiction:

$$
\text{classified intolerance}
\rightarrow
\text{exclusion permitted}.
$$

The immunizing structure then returns. Someone questions whether exclusion is warranted, and the question is recoded as evidence of moral failure:

$$
C
\rightarrow
\text{tolerance of bad value}
\rightarrow
\text{bad critic}.
$$

The value bomb is now operating inside a doctrine meant to preserve criticism. To question whether the bomb has been correctly identified is treated as willingness to tolerate the explosion. That is precisely the structure liberal institutions were supposed to keep open to criticism.

The abstraction *intolerance* is too broad to settle local cases. Political campaigns try to change other people's values. Religious movements evangelize. Activists condemn institutions. Parents transmit moral beliefs. Editors reject submissions. Universities and professional associations impose standards. Friends tell one another that certain conduct is unacceptable.

Many of these activities can be called intolerant in an ordinary sense. The label alone therefore does not distinguish among them. The local explanation has to recover the causal problem: what action occurred, what constraint was imposed, what criticism became impossible, what institution is being protected, what harm is being prevented, and what alternative solution exists.

That distinction also separates explanation from conduct. Criticizing the pollution model does not entail that every action inspired by every value must be permitted. A person can threaten, use violence, advocate coercion, manipulate access to resources, or suppress criticism through force. Those are concrete causal problems.

The epistemic distinction is narrower:

$$
\text{bad explanation}
\neq
\text{permission for every conduct inspired by it}
$$

and:

$$
\text{bad explanation}
\neq
\text{automatic warrant to exclude every carrier of it}.
$$

The moral classification of an explanation does not by itself explain the causal problem created by an action, institution, artifact, or technology. Reconstructing that problem is less convenient than applying a value rule, but it preserves the fallibility that gave the liberal values their explanatory force in the first place.

If values are not foundations, what grounds the explanation that produced them?

<a id="chapter-19--6-no-final-ground"></a>

#### 6. No Final Ground

The demand for a ground has a familiar form. If values are not foundations, what grounds morality? Liberty? Criticism? The goodness of an explanation?

We encounter the same architecture in justificationism. The demand assumes that some deeper structure must convert a conjecture into an entitled belief. If values are not the ground, perhaps reason is. If not reason, perhaps evidence; if not evidence, consensus; if not consensus, probability; if not probability, the epistemology itself. The search moves the ground downward without changing the architecture.

The epistemology employed here rejects that architecture. A problem exists. A tentative solution is created. Criticism exposes errors. A successor problem appears:

$$
P_1
\rightarrow
TS
\rightarrow
EE
\rightarrow
P_2.
$$

No justification enters the sequence. That includes the epistemology itself.

It would be a mistake to exempt criticism from the argument:

> all values are conjectural, except the value of criticism.

Or:

> the supreme moral value is preserving error correction.

That would only install another sacred premise.
