The narrower claim is conditional. If the evolutionary explanation of knowledge is approximately correct, criticism is part of the process through which errors become visible. A structure that systematically prevents criticism therefore interferes with the process described by the explanation.

That is a consequence of the explanation, not a revelation, axiom, or final ground. The epistemology can itself be criticized. A better explanation of knowledge growth would alter the consequences.

Still, conjectural explanations have consequences. If persons are fallible and corrigible, institutions that preserve opportunities for correction solve an important problem. Freedom of criticism, access to alternatives, possibilities of exit, institutional revision, changes of mind, and encounters with rival objective knowledge all follow from that explanatory structure.

Together they form something like a **thin moral lattice**. The phrase names a limited network of consequences, not a foundation beneath them.

Its thinness matters. A conjectural fragment can be inserted into the lattice and then protected by its position. For example:

$$
\text{criticism must remain possible}
$$

can become:

$$
\text{my preferred account of legitimate criticism must be preserved}.
$$

Likewise:

$$
\text{liberty helps preserve error correction}
$$

can become:

$$
\text{this doctrine of liberty is beyond criticism}.
$$

The framework built to preserve error correction can then destroy error correction from within. Liberal values cannot be their own grounds. Their explanatory ancestry has to remain available.

The remaining question is practical without requiring a final foundation: what does it look like to use a value while keeping its ancestry recoverable?

<a id="chapter-19--7-reversible-compression"></a>

#### 7. Reversible Compression

There is no direct access to reality through which moral truth simply appears. You do not perceive *liberty is good* in the way you perceive light or pain. Even perception is already mediated through evolved and learned structures. Values are no exception.

You encounter a problem. A contradiction becomes salient. An institution causes suffering. A restriction prevents criticism. A social practice produces domination. A technological possibility reveals that an inherited scarcity was unnecessary. A relationship exposes an assumption. A child asks a question. A rival explanation arrives.

Then a tentative solution becomes possible:

$$
P
\rightarrow
TS.
$$

Some explanations remain local. Others reorganize many problems at once. An explanation of freedom can alter politics, education, parenting, institutional design, and interpersonal relationships. An explanation of truth can alter science, journalism, friendship, law, and self-criticism. When an explanation acquires enough reach, giving it a short name makes repeated use easier.

That is the useful operation. An explanation is compressed into a value:

$$
P
\rightarrow
E
\rightarrow
V.
$$

The value can then guide a local action without requiring the whole explanation to be reconstructed every time:

$$
V
\rightarrow
\text{local action}.
$$

The compression becomes dangerous only when this shortcut is mistaken for a foundation. When a new problem appears, the route back has to remain possible:

$$
V
\rightarrow
E
\rightarrow
EE.
$$

The value is useful while the explanation it compresses can return under criticism. That relation will be called **reversible compression**.

Once the explanation returns, the local problem becomes visible again. Which problem was the value helping to solve? Does that problem still exist? Has the environment changed? Does the value now conflict with another explanation? Does the local application preserve the reach of the original explanation, or only repeat its label? What criticism would expose a contradiction?

A value that can survive that decompression may remain useful. A value that blocks it has become an immunizing structure.

Now the argument turns back to you, the singular person.

You may retain a terrible explanation. You may preserve a value that stabilizes cruelty. You may belong to an ideology whose internal structure makes criticism difficult. You may reject explanations we regard as among the best things civilization has created. That matters. But you are still not the value.

The value is one structure inside an epistemic mind much larger than the surface available to anyone else. And even that world is not the future you. A new problem can become visible. A criticism can arrive from an unexpected direction. A value that once felt foundational can itself become the object of inquiry.

The value bomb destroys that openness when it compresses:

$$
\text{bad value}
\rightarrow
\text{bad person}.
$$

The present epistemic state becomes an ontology, first in psychology. It has now reappeared in morality.

Objective knowledge is larger than the value too. A book can contain a bad explanation. A historical document can preserve cruelty. A political text can contain hierarchy, exclusion, or error. Yet the artifact can later become material for criticism. An explanation that once persuaded can become the example through which another generation understands how persuasion failed. An archive of error can become part of error elimination.

So:

$$
\text{contains bad explanation}
$$

does not entail:

$$
\text{has no epistemic value}.
$$

Technology completes the parallel. A technological system may embody bad knowledge, be built for coercion, amplify prejudice, make propaganda cheaper, or enable surveillance. Those are real criticisms. They do not make the category *technology* explanatory enough to settle the case.

The same broad substrate may also permit communication, criticism, coordination, discovery, creativity, and new problem formation. The relevant causal questions therefore remain local: which technology, which use, which person, which problem, which mechanism, which suppressed alternative, which criticism would change the conclusion?

Those questions do not refute the value. They decompress it. And once the value has been decompressed, the constraint of the open future becomes unavoidable.

<a id="chapter-19--8-the-open-future"></a>

#### 8. The Open Future

Future knowledge cannot already be latent if it is genuinely new. That conclusion reaches values directly. A value may have enormous reach. It may summarize one of the best explanations presently available. It may organize a life, guide an institution, or preserve knowledge worth carrying forward.

It still cannot specify the future. A later criticism may reveal a problem we cannot presently imagine. A new technology may alter the action space. A new moral explanation may expose an inherited cruelty. You may discover that two values you treated as compatible depend upon contradictory explanations. No present value can therefore contain the knowledge that does not yet exist, and no present value gets jurisdiction over it.

That does not imply moral passivity. It locates the value inside fallibility.

The practical use of a value is then less mysterious. A compressed explanation can coordinate action, preserve hard-won knowledge, and travel farther than the full argument that produced it. But when a new problem appears, the compression can reopen.

That return also preserves you, the person. A present value can guide action without becoming the ontology of the person who retains it. Objective knowledge can contain error without becoming identical to the error. Technology can carry a harmful use without becoming identical to the use.

The common structure is the refusal to let the moral status of one compressed explanation detonate the larger thing that contains it.

The architecture can now be stated without turning it into another foundation. A problem gives rise to an explanation. The explanation can be compressed into a value and reused in action:

$$
P
\rightarrow
E
\rightarrow
V
\rightarrow
\text{action}.
$$

When criticism creates a new problem, the compression can reopen:

$$
V
\rightarrow
E
\rightarrow
EE
\rightarrow
P_2.
$$

The value is not a foundation. It is a compression. The explanation remains conjectural.

And you remain larger than either. But the ability to criticize, revise, test, and replace an explanation is not free. It takes time, tools, access to objective knowledge, other people, and physical resources.

What happens when persons are epistemically equal in kind but radically unequal in the resources through which their knowledge can become consequential?

<a id="chapter-20"></a>

### XX. Wealth In Equality

Whatever moves you epistemically, you are physically constrained. You need time, food, energy, shelter, tools, communication, objective knowledge, other people, institutions, technologies, and increasingly computation.

None of those things explain why this problem becomes alive for you, why that conjecture appears, or why a particular criticism suddenly reorganizes what you see. They do something else. They alter the space in which your epistemic movement can become consequential.

You may possess a beautiful explanation and lack the means to test it. You may notice an important problem and lack the time to remain with it. You may invent something and lack the means to build it. You may possess knowledge that nobody presently wants. You may live inside a society whose institutions cannot yet recognize what you have created.

You are therefore neither an economic object nor a disembodied universal intellect. You are physically finite and epistemically open.

Here we ask what resources mean under those conditions. A familiar meme seems to answer immediately:

> knowledge is the ultimate resource.

Too fast.

Knowledge does not abolish matter, energy, or scarcity. A data center requires electricity. You require food. A semiconductor requires minerals, machinery, technical knowledge, logistics, and accumulated infrastructure. Artificial intelligence requires computers. Computers require energy. Energy requires physical systems through which knowledge can be embodied.

Knowledge is not an escape from physical reality. It changes which transformations of physical reality become possible. A material becomes a resource only relative to a problem and to the knowledge required to use it. That is the beginning of an economic explanation.

But economics will not explain the arrows. Markets, firms, patents, money, entrepreneurship, and artificial intelligence enter here as external structures through which you may acquire resources, coordinate action, expose conjectures to criticism, and preserve enough room to continue creating knowledge.

The deeper question remains with you: What conditions permit *your* epistemic mind to flourish?

<a id="chapter-20--1-the-space-around-the-arrows"></a>

#### 1. The Space Around the Arrows

The word *resource* already risks misleading us because it invites a fuel metaphor. A fuel is consumed to produce a transformation. Coal is burned. Food is metabolized. Electrical energy is dissipated. From there it is easy to imagine that knowledge creation must have an equivalent internal fuel: attention, motivation, dopamine, curiosity, intelligence, energy.

But no such term presently explains epistemic motion. You can possess abundant food and produce no new explanation. You can have time and remain uninterested. You can be exhausted and suddenly discover a devastating criticism. A child can become absorbed in a problem every adult in the room considers trivial. A scientist can leave a difficult problem for weeks and return with an idea that did not exist before.

The physical system matters. The physical resource does not tell us why *this* problem became *that* conjecture.

So the first distinction is:

$$
\text{necessary physical conditions}
\neq
\text{sufficient epistemic cause}.
$$

The narrower question is what external conditions enlarge or restrict the space in which you can epistemically move.

You may be a universal explainer without being a perpetual motion machine. Your explanatory reach may be open-ended. Your practical resources are not. So you rely on accumulated objective knowledge: language, mathematics, books, standards, software, legal structures, scientific theories, markets, technical systems, institutions, and other people.

This dependence does not diminish personhood. It is one of the conditions under which personhood becomes practically consequential.

The same epistemic capacity can inhabit radically different reachable worlds depending on the resources around it. With access to a library, you can pursue problems unavailable when books are denied to you. With access to computation, you can attempt transformations unavailable without it. With time, you can remain inside a problem that economic pressure would otherwise force you to abandon.

This does not mean wealth produces greater epistemic capacity.

It means:

$$
\text{universal explanatory capacity}
\neq
\text{uniform practical problem space}.
$$

Material inequality can therefore become epistemic inequality without implying any inequality in personhood.

Now look again at the word *resource*. Oil, uranium, silicon, sunlight, and water sound like resources in themselves. But the category is not contained in the material. A physical structure becomes a resource only relative to a transformation someone knows how to perform. Before the relevant knowledge exists, the same physical reality can remain economically inert.

Abstract it.

The structure is closer to:

$$
\text{physical possibility}
+
\text{explanatory knowledge}
\rightarrow
\text{usable resource}.
$$

The material was already there. The resource was not.

Knowledge can therefore change the resource map. A previously useless material can become valuable. A waste product can become an input. A scarce material can become replaceable. A dangerous process can become safer. An expensive process can become cheap. A local constraint can become technically irrelevant. Knowledge does not create matter from nothing. It creates new possibilities for transforming matter.

That gives the slogan its explanatory force:

> knowledge is the ultimate resource.

But the slogan immediately recurses. Knowledge is itself physically instantiated. A book occupies matter. A server consumes energy. A scientist requires food. A laboratory requires equipment. A software system requires hardware. A language model requires processors, networking, storage, cooling, and power.

Abstract it again.

The structure is recursive:

$$
\text{knowledge}
\rightarrow
\text{new resources}
\rightarrow
\text{new conditions for knowledge creation}.
$$

The cycle is not free. It is physically instantiated. Several different external conditions have been compressed into the single word *resource*. Separating them makes the structure easier to see.

**Physical resources** are matter, energy, land, water, machinery, biological viability, and infrastructure.

**Temporal resources** are time, attention, persistence, and the opportunity to remain with a problem long enough for criticism and reconstruction to occur.

**Objective epistemic resources** are books, code, theories, procedures, institutions, standards, databases, tools, and technologies through which prior knowledge becomes available to you.

**Coordination resources** are money, contracts, markets, firms, patents, licensing systems, professional institutions, and other structures through which people gain access to scarce physical and epistemic resources.

The categories overlap. A patent is objective knowledge and a coordination mechanism. A data center is physical infrastructure embodying technological knowledge. Money can purchase time from other people. AI can provide access to objective knowledge while consuming physical resources and altering economic coordination.

The distinctions matter because no one category explains the others. And none explains their internal arrows.

<a id="chapter-20--2-markets-criticism-and-residue"></a>

#### 2. Markets, Criticism, and Residue

Economics appears wherever finite people must allocate finite resources among competing problems. You can want to pursue many things. You cannot pursue all of them at once. You may choose one problem and abandon another. You may need income, childcare, equipment, collaborators, or a way to convince someone else that an objective artifact is worth exchanging scarce resources for.

Economic structures therefore matter to your epistemic life without defining epistemic value. The distinction is:

$$
\text{market value}
\neq
\text{epistemic value}.
$$

A mathematical insight may have no present buyer. A beautiful explanation may never become a company. A profitable product may contain little explanatory novelty. You may spend years pursuing a problem that produces no economic return. The market cannot tell you what you ought to find interesting. It cannot tell you which explanation is true. It cannot tell you which future problem will matter.

It can do something narrower: coordinate resources among people whose internal problem situations differ.

Entrepreneurship makes that relation unusually visible. An entrepreneur notices that something does not work. A process is too expensive. A tool is missing. A group of people cannot do something they want to do. An inconvenience everyone else tolerates becomes intolerable to one person.

Finding a good problem can itself be a creative achievement. Entrepreneurship makes the point materially concrete. The entrepreneur conjectures a tentative solution, builds something, and exposes it to other people. Their response creates criticism. The solution may be ignored, misunderstood, rejected, used unexpectedly, or valued for a feature the creator considered secondary. The problem may have been badly formulated. The product may work while the business fails. The market may exist but remain unreachable.

Product-market fit is interesting because it records a relation between an artifact and a market. It is not always progress. A successful product can be harmful. A bad explanation can be profitable. A good invention can arrive before its market. Market response is therefore one class of criticism, not the final epistemic tribunal.

But the entrepreneurial cycle leaves something behind. Code. Designs. Customer knowledge. Technical understanding. Distribution channels. Reputation. Processes. Contracts. Explanations. Even failure can become objective knowledge.

Abstract it.

The next entrepreneurial attempt need not begin from zero:

$$
K_t
\rightarrow
\text{action}
\rightarrow
\text{criticism}
\rightarrow
K_{t+1}.
$$

Knowledge can compound. This is why a small experiment can matter without containing the final answer. You can create an artifact, expose it to criticism, learn, revise, and try again. The eventual value may emerge from a sequence of individually modest changes.

Science, art, engineering, and personal knowledge can evolve through the same broad pattern. Entrepreneurship merely makes the resource loop especially visible because the artifact eventually encounters people willing or unwilling to surrender scarce resources for it.

The entrepreneurial case leaves one question unresolved: what does any of this mean for *your* problem?

<a id="chapter-20--3-the-problem-you-actually-have"></a>

#### 3. The Problem You Actually Have

What is the deepest problem in your life? Do not answer quickly.

It may concern the health of someone you love, financial security, your children, a relationship, a scientific problem, a creative problem, a moral problem, or a problem you cannot yet name.

The answer is yours. No population category can provide it.

Now ask a second question:

> Does the knowledge required to solve that problem already exist?

Sometimes it does. Often it does not. The eventual solution may depend on objective knowledge that nobody presently possesses.

That is the deepest problem of resources. It is not merely how existing resources are distributed. It is how the conditions are preserved under which knowledge that does not yet exist can be created.

This is where the earlier distinction between personhood and practical reach becomes personal. Someone outside a library, laboratory, network, market, institution, or computational system does not thereby become a lesser person. But the set of transformations they can presently attempt may shrink. That set is their practical repertoire of transformations. Call it their **epistemic wealth**.

Equal personhood does not imply equal epistemic wealth. External resources do not create your epistemic direction. They do not tell you which problem will become alive or which conjecture will occur to you. They determine something more limited and more concrete: how much of that direction can be made objective, criticized, built upon, exchanged, or carried into the world.

With that distinction in place, artificial intelligence becomes interesting for a reason more precise than intelligence in the abstract. It changes the cost of reaching beyond the resources already attached to you.

<a id="chapter-20--4-artificial-intelligence-and-the-cost-of-reach"></a>

#### 4. Artificial Intelligence and the Cost of Reach

Historically, turning one person's problem into an economically useful artifact often required many specialized people: software, design, writing, legal work, marketing, finance, operations, research, administration. The rare person capable of traversing many of these domains could sometimes act alone. Most could not.

Artificial intelligence changes this threshold. It does not create your problems. It does not supply your epistemic direction. It does not contain your individual problem situation. It changes the cost of crossing functional boundaries.

You can ask one interface to help draft code, explain an unfamiliar legal concept, compare technical approaches, criticize a design, structure a document, translate specialist language, investigate a market, or build a prototype. You can move among domains that once required separate institutional interfaces.

That recurring relation is what **generalist interface** names here: AI can connect one person to specialized objective knowledge and operations across domains. This does not abolish expertise. It lowers the cost of borrowing from it.

The economic implication is therefore not:

> everyone can now become a genius.

It is narrower:

> the minimum institutional scale required to attempt some problems has fallen.

Abstract it.

The structure can begin to look like:

$$
\text{you}
+
\text{general-purpose AI}
+
\text{small capital}
+
\text{market access}
$$

where a similar attempt might previously have required:

$$
\text{firm}
+
\text{specialists}
+
\text{large capital}
+
\text{coordination machinery}.
$$

What changed? Not your arrow, but the boundary around what you can attempt.

AI also makes access divisible in an unusual way. At the technical level, there are units inside a computational process. Call these units **tokens**. Tokens are not money. Economically, however, computational usage can be purchased in small increments. You can buy another increment of synthesis, drafting, code generation, explanation, comparison, or administrative assistance, then stop, return, and pursue a completely different problem.

General-purpose epistemic assistance has become metered. That is what **metered epistemic capacity** names here: not intelligence sold by the unit, but incremental access to transformations that can extend your practical reach.

The fit with a path-dependent epistemic life is unusual. Your internal movement can remain irregular. The external resource can follow. Then the physical bill arrives. None of this escapes physics.

Generative AI feels abstract because you interact with language. Behind the interface lie semiconductor fabrication, transmission lines, cooling, data centers, networks, capital, water, energy, maintenance, land, and supply chains.

The illusion of weightlessness knowledge is carried by material systems. Data centers expose that substrate. A community may want economic development and object to water consumption. A grid may not support projected demand. A company may seek dedicated generation. A cooling system may be criticized. A local government may demand concessions.

Each attempted solution can create a successor problem. New generation changes energy constraints. Water recycling changes water demands. Different cooling architectures change engineering tradeoffs. New siting decisions and contractual arrangements move rather than abolish criticism. The physical constraint does not disprove the knowledge economy. It generates its next problem.

Institutions do the same kind of work at a different level. Civilization contains accumulated knowledge not only in machines but in contract law, corporations, courts, licensing, insurance, standards, markets, property systems, and patent offices. These structures are imperfect, but they preserve attempted solutions to recurring coordination problems.

Technological change therefore need not imply institutional replacement. An institution can encounter a new problem. Its current solution can fail. The failure can become visible. A modification can be attempted. The new result can be criticized. The institution survives not because it is sacred but because useful structures need not be discarded merely because one application becomes obsolete.

Patents make the point concrete. The historical bargain is epistemic. The inventor discloses the invention. In exchange, the institution grants a time-limited exclusive right:

$$
\text{private inventive knowledge}
\rightarrow
patent (\text{public disclosure})
= \text{temporary economic control}.
$$

The monopoly eventually ends. The disclosure remains. The arrangement can be criticized in many ways. Exclusive rights can obstruct use, be accumulated strategically, be asserted by entities remote from the invention, impose litigation costs, or become tools of coercion.

Those criticisms do not remove the coordination problem the patent system attempts to solve. If inventive knowledge can be copied cheaply, the creator may lose the ability to capture enough economic value to continue developing it. The patent bargain is one tentative solution. Its epistemic interest lies in trying to align disclosure, temporary control, public accessibility, and eventual unrestricted use.

AI can alter the process on both sides. Applicants can search, draft, compare, and criticize more cheaply. Examiners can search prior art and evaluate claims with stronger computational assistance. That does not imply better patents. It can enlarge the explanatory surface: more of the reasoning on either side can become explicit and therefore available to criticism.

The point is broader than patents. AI does not need to abolish institutions to change the conditions under which they process objective knowledge.

The patent case returns us to the resource problem. Epistemic wealth determines which physical transformations are available. A society that knows how to produce semiconductors can perform transformations unavailable to one that does not. If you know how to build a functioning product, possibilities are available to you that are unavailable when that knowledge is absent. A patent can convert some of that possibility into bargaining power. A company can convert it into organized production. A market can convert it into exchange.

Economic inequality and epistemic access can therefore interact strongly. If powerful AI systems exist but access becomes concentrated among governments, incumbent firms, or wealthy institutions, the resulting distribution is not merely a distribution of software. It is a distribution of reachable transformations. A person outside the boundary retains equal personhood. Their practical repertoire is still smaller.

Once resources are conceived this way, restriction acquires an additional epistemic consequence. It does not only prevent uses already visible. It can prevent problem trajectories from beginning.

<a id="chapter-20--5-what-restriction-removes"></a>

#### 5. What Restriction Removes

Suppose AI has become useful enough and authorities decide to keep what exists while stopping further development.

The proposal can sound moderate. But moderation is not an epistemic criterion. Two fallible explanations do not produce a better explanation merely by meeting in the middle. Call it the **fallacy of compromise**.

Abstract it:

Given two candidate explanations

$$
E_1, E_2
$$

There exists no transformation function called $Compromise$ that results in a new explanation:

$$
Compromise(E_1,E_2)
\neq
E_3
$$

The transformed explanation remains a creative and conjectural operation across the two parties. Compromise may serve political functions. It can preserve peace, permit incremental change, reduce transition costs, and coordinate people who disagree. Those functions are different from error elimination.

A capability freeze therefore requires its own explanation. Why should the present state of knowledge possess jurisdiction over future knowledge? Why is today's capability permitted while tomorrow's is prohibited? Who retains access to the systems that already exist? A freeze imposed after powerful AI already exists may entrench actors that already possess models, infrastructure, capital, and regulatory access. The result could be less decentralization rather than more.

Calling the proposal a compromise does not answer that problem. The same problem appears when the causal direction is reversed.

**The precautionary principle** is meant to avoid harm. As an epistemic structure, however, it can foreground the harms of acting while leaving the harms of not acting less visible.

Abstract it.

Abstention changes the future:

$$
\text{deploy technology}
\rightarrow
\text{possible harms and benefits}.
$$

But also:

$$
\text{restrict technology}
\rightarrow
\text{foregone experiments}
\rightarrow
\text{foregone criticism}
\rightarrow
\text{foregone successor knowledge}.
$$

The second branch is important. A restriction can prevent known uses, but when future knowledge is open it can also prevent unknown problem trajectories. The knowledge that would have emerged cannot be inventoried in advance because it does not yet exist.

That makes the opportunity cost difficult to represent. The precautionary principle can then become self-protecting:

> if the future is uncertain, restrict the technology.

But the same uncertainty applies to the consequences of restriction. Precaution can be a useful tentative solution to a particular threat. The epistemic error begins when uncertainty itself is treated as a reason to close the process that might create the missing knowledge.

Nuclear energy makes the asymmetry concrete. Imagine not the reactors that were built but the path that might have followed much earlier and much broader deployment of clean nuclear power.

The counterfactual cannot be reconstructed. A different energy economy would have changed fossil fuel demand, grid architecture, industrial investment, pollution, research priorities, engineering experience, geopolitics, and the later climate problem. Perhaps safety problems would have appeared that never occurred in our history. Perhaps reactor technologies would have evolved much further. Perhaps different institutional failures would have emerged.

We do not know. That is the point. The opportunity cost of a suppressed technological trajectory is not a number waiting to be calculated. It includes a missing history of knowledge creation. The visible accident has a date. The foregone invention does not. The victim of an actual technology can often be named. The person who would have lived because an uncreated technology solved an unanticipated future problem cannot.

This asymmetry gives visible harms a psychological advantage over missing possibilities. It does not make restriction neutral.

The same structure applies more directly and immediately to artificial intelligence. No prediction about what AI will discover is required. There is no need to claim that it will cure cancer, forecast economic abundance, or assign probabilities to unknown future industries.

A simpler claim is enough. People already pursue some problems differently with AI than without it. They can traverse domains more quickly, prototype more cheaply, interrogate objective knowledge interactively, and write, code, compare, simulate, or criticize through a general interface. Remove the interface and those pathways disappear.

What knowledge would have emerged from them cannot be known. But the missing pathways are real in the narrower sense that the resource enabling them has been removed. A world without that resource would not pursue the same set of individual problem situations in the same way. 

Now recall your deepest problem. 8-billion deepest problems is catastrophic, right now.

That is not prophecy. It follows from changing the external conditions under which people can act. None of this implies that every person should use AI, or that every use is beneficial.

The next problem is direction: who owns your arrow?

<a id="chapter-20--6-the-tool-does-not-own-your-arrow"></a>

#### 6. The Tool Does Not Own Your Arrow

Children make the problem unusually clear. A child begins inside an inherited world of objective knowledge: books, rules, language, stories, screens, games, schools, tools. The adult sees the medium. The child inhabits the problem. From the outside, the visible object is easy to classify: a book, a calculator, a computer, a network, an AI system. What the child is actually doing with it can be much harder to see.

That is why restrictions are epistemically ambiguous. A restriction may remove distraction. It may also remove the problem space through which the child's knowledge is developing. The adult often cannot know which in advance.

No technology is automatically beneficial. A screen can harm. A book can mislead. A network can expose a child to danger. An AI can generalize badly.

The claim is narrower: the authority cannot infer the child's epistemic content from the visible medium alone. The child's epistemic mind is individual, path-dependent, largely inexplicit, and open. The authority sees fragments.

Artificial intelligence creates a related danger precisely because it is so general. The same interface can follow you across many domains. That can enlarge your reach. It can also import population-scale regularity back into your individual problem.

The model has encountered enormous bodies of social objective knowledge. It is therefore unusually capable of producing familiar explanations, conventional classifications, common framings, average language, and expected solutions.

Abstract it.

The failure mode can be written compactly:

$$
\text{your problem}
\rightarrow
\text{population-shaped answer}
\rightarrow
\text{your difference compressed away}.
$$

So the human-AI dyad is not automatically liberating. Its epistemic value depends partly on direction:

$$
\text{you}
\rightarrow
\text{AI as tool}
$$

is not the same structure as:

$$
\text{AI's generalized model}
\rightarrow
\text{you}.
$$

The distinction becomes real when you reject an answer, reformulate the problem, abandon the tool, ignore the recommendation, or pursue something strange. Those acts keep explanatory direction with you. AI can expand the explanatory surface. It does not get to own the arrow.

Now the adoption question changes. The argument is not everyone should use AI. That would replace one authority with another. You may refuse any tool for practical, moral, aesthetic, intellectual, or personal reasons. Freedom includes abstinence.

But abstinence is not consequence-free. Human personhood has long extended through objective knowledge. Writing extends memory. Mathematics extends working cognition. Books extend encounter. Telescopes extend perception. Computers extend calculation. Networks extend communication. Search extends retrieval.

Your epistemic mind has never been reducible to the unaided biological brain. Refusing an external tool therefore does not preserve an epistemically pure baseline. AI is striking because its generality makes the extension broader: it can become an interface to many forms of objective knowledge at once.

That does not make non-users lesser persons. It means only that the surrounding world may increasingly contain transformations more easily reached by people who possess and can operate through the new interface.

Equal personhood still does not imply equal epistemic wealth. The problem of wealth inequality sits uncomfortably with AI abstinence.

That problem becomes sharper as civilization itself becomes more abstract.

<a id="chapter-20--7-operating-through-abstraction"></a>

#### 7. Operating Through Abstraction

The device can be present while the usable resource is still missing. Someone may own a computer and still be unable to recover an account, install software, configure a router, navigate a digital form, understand cloud storage, distinguish a browser from a search engine, set up authentication, or interpret an unfamiliar interface.

What is missing is not hardware alone. It is explanatory fluency: enough understanding of the surrounding abstractions to operate through them.

Modern life increasingly consists of abstraction layers inherited rather than reconstructed. You can use a payment network without understanding banking infrastructure, cloud software without understanding distributed systems, navigation without understanding satellite timing, or an AI system without understanding transformers. Reality becomes more abstract.

Technological inequality therefore increasingly concerns the ability to operate through abstraction, not merely access to technology.

Historically, younger generations have often helped older people cross new technical interfaces. Children learned the computer. Parents asked for help. Young people adopted networked communication earlier. Later generations inherited the abstractions as normal.

AI may complicate that pattern. Some young people may choose not to use it. Some may encounter AI mainly through social objective knowledge describing cheating, job loss, dehumanization, environmental cost, homogenization, or existential danger. Some may form an identity around AI abstinence.

If that happens at meaningful scale, the familiar adaptation mechanism weakens. If AI becomes a common interface to increasingly abstract technical and institutional worlds, deliberate non-use can produce a capability gap inside the incoming generation itself.

Whether that gap becomes socially severe is unknown. The possible **intergenerational reversal** is narrower than a prediction: the younger generation may no longer function as the bridge into the next abstraction layer.

Why does that possibility matter here? Because it exposes the larger trajectory underneath it.

Abstract it.

Civilization accumulates objective knowledge. That knowledge becomes technology. Later people inherit the technology without reconstructing all the knowledge inside it. The next generation builds on top of that layer, and then another:

$$
K_1
\rightarrow
\text{technology}
\rightarrow
K_2
\rightarrow
\text{more abstract technology}
\rightarrow
K_3
\rightarrow \cdots
$$

Ordinary life therefore becomes progressively mediated by objective structures no individual fully understands.

This is not necessarily a defect. Abstraction is part of how civilization progresses. You do not need to understand transistor physics to write a novel on a laptop or packet routing to talk to a friend overseas.

But the same abstraction that enlarges reach also creates dependence. You may need to trust interfaces you cannot reconstruct. Institutions may operate systems nobody fully sees. Errors can propagate through layers. Eventually, the explanatory complexity of the world can exceed what unaided individuals can practically navigate.

AI sits on both sides of that problem. It is another abstraction layer. And it may become one of the principal tools through which you navigate the layers beneath it. The resource that enlarges your practical repertoire, your wealth, may therefore also increase your dependence on an interface whose underlying causal structure you cannot explicitly carry.

That tension returns us to the original question.

<a id="chapter-20--8-the-resource-we-cannot-inventory"></a>

#### 8. The Resource We Cannot Inventory

Knowledge has one further property: it cannot be inventoried. We do not know who will create it, which present problem will lead to it, or what criticism will make it possible. We do not know whether it will begin in a laboratory, a company, a school, a studio, a bedroom, a workshop, or in a conversation between one person and an artificial system.

That uncertainty does not make resources irrelevant. It makes their role more precise.

Freedom matters materially because different people need room to pursue problem situations that cannot be specified in advance. Institutions matter because they preserve and coordinate objective knowledge across people and time. Physical, temporal, epistemic, and coordination resources matter because they enlarge or restrict what can be attempted.

None of them tells the arrows where to go. A book cannot determine what problem you will discover. A market cannot determine what invention an entrepreneur will imagine. A patent system cannot determine what will be invented. An AI cannot determine which region of your epistemic mind will suddenly become alive without beginning to replace your own epistemic direction.

The mystery remains where it began. We still do not know what moves the arrows from problem to conjecture, from criticism to reconstruction, or from one problem world into another.

But the surrounding structure is now clearer. Resources do not explain epistemic motion. They change the reachable space in which that motion can become objective knowledge.

And once civilization accumulates enough objective knowledge, that reachable space acquires a new problem of its own.

The external world is becoming more abstract more quickly than any individual can reconstruct it. If objective knowledge continues to accumulate through technology, institutions, automation, and artificial intelligence, then you may increasingly depend on interfaces to navigate a world whose causal structures you cannot carry.

Resources change how far your arrows can reach. Objective knowledge can become technology, institutions, and systems whose effects extend far beyond the person who created the explanation.

But greater reach does not eliminate fallibility. An explanation can remain wrong while the system embodying it becomes faster, larger, and harder for any individual to reconstruct.

What happens when the technologies that extend our capacity to create knowledge also extend the consequences of error beyond our capacity to correct it?

<a id="part-the-extended-epistemic-mind"></a>

## The Extended Epistemic Mind

<a id="chapter-21"></a>

### XXI. Scaling Error

You create knowledge. And the process is fallible.

You can create a bad explanation, preserve it, embody it in objective knowledge, build institutions around it, encode it into software, and use tools to amplify it. Nothing in the epistemology places a ceiling on the resulting error.

A mistake can remain private; it can also become catastrophic.

That does not defeat optimism. It shows why optimism cannot become complacent. And why even the most catastrophic risks demand good explanations.

<a id="chapter-21--1-catastrophic-error"></a>

#### 1. Catastrophic Error

Fallibility is easy to accept when the consequences are small. You misremember a name. A scientist chooses a bad model. An engineer makes a design error. A government adopts a failed policy. Criticism arrives, and the error is corrected.

Nothing in fallibilism, however, says that reality must leave enough time for correction. A bridge can collapse. A war can begin. A dangerous organism can escape. A technological system can propagate an error faster than anyone can understand it. A civilization can act on an explanation whose failure destroys part of the machinery needed to criticize it.

Abstract it.

The structure is simple:

$$
\text{fallible explanation}
\rightarrow
\text{objective embodiment}
\rightarrow
\text{large causal reach}
\rightarrow
\text{large error}.
$$

The danger grows when an explanation is embodied in structures that act repeatedly and at scale. You can be wrong once. Software can execute the error a billion times. An institution can preserve it for generations. A weapon can make one decision irreversible.

Objective knowledge therefore changes the scale of fallibility. It preserves good explanations after their creators are gone, but it can preserve bad explanations too. A procedure can outlive the person who misunderstood the problem. A classification can survive the theory that created it. A law can preserve an obsolete moral explanation. A software system can continue acting on assumptions no current operator can fully reconstruct.

Catastrophic risk sits naturally inside the epistemology. It requires no doctrine of evil. Fallibility plus causal reach is enough.

Ordinary epistemic error is survivable because the epistemic cycle can continue:

$$
P_1
\rightarrow
TS
\rightarrow
EE
\rightarrow
P_2.
$$

An explanation fails. The failure becomes criticism. A new problem appears. Some errors are different because they can damage the process that would have exposed and corrected them. 

A war can kill the people who might have ended it. A political system can suppress the criticism required to reform it. A technological accident can destroy infrastructure needed to understand the accident. A biological event can move faster than the institutions trying to investigate it. A dangerous tool can give one person the ability to impose a mistake on millions of others before those others can respond.

That is what makes catastrophic risk epistemically distinctive. The problem is not merely how to reduce error. The harder problem is how to preserve the ability to discover and correct error when some errors can destroy the conditions of correction.

That immediately complicates the meaning of safety. Reducing variation cannot be the whole answer because variation is one source of new explanations. Maximizing freedom of action cannot be the whole answer either because some actions can irreversibly destroy the freedom of others. The problem is to preserve the epistemic process while preventing some physical transformations from becoming irreversible before criticism can act on them.

Catastrophic error is therefore not the same thing as evil. You can be sincerely trying to solve a real problem and still be catastrophically wrong.

The moral problem appears when a harmful explanatory structure becomes difficult to criticize: criticism is suppressed, persons are reduced to thin models, and avoidable suffering persists because the explanation organizing it has become protected from correction.

This matters because catastrophic-risk language is morally charged. A danger can be real while the response to it becomes epistemically corrupt. A safety doctrine can begin with a genuine threat, acquire authority, narrow criticism, treat dissent as irresponsibility, restrict access, and represent the people governed by the doctrine mainly as sources of risk.

Abstract it.

The sequence can become:

$$
\text{catastrophic possibility}
\rightarrow
\text{authority}
\rightarrow
\text{suppressed criticism}
\rightarrow
\text{persistent avoidable harm}.
$$

The catastrophe may never occur. The closure already can. The moral question is therefore not only whether a risk is large. It is also whether the explanation of the risk remains criticizable.

The more serious a problem appears, the more attractive authority becomes. The reasoning is understandable. If the cost of error is enormous, experimentation looks dangerous. If time is short, disagreement looks wasteful. If specialists understand the problem better than the public, broad participation can appear irresponsible.

The emergency can therefore seem to justify a narrower epistemic process:

$$
\text{high stakes}
\rightarrow
\text{fewer permitted alternatives}
\rightarrow
\text{faster coordinated action}.
$$

Sometimes that narrowing can be necessary. You do not debate fire-safety while a building burns. But an emergency can also convert a tentative solution into an authority structure. The problem statement becomes fixed. The preferred solution becomes mandatory. Alternative explanations become dangerous. The exception becomes durable. The safety system begins to protect itself.

High stakes do not make expertise less important. They make larger the cost of a bad explanation acquiring power. Catastrophic-risk arguments therefore need criticism at least as severe as the dangers they are trying to explain.

<a id="chapter-21--2-values-are-not-alignment-targets"></a>

#### 2. Values Are Not Alignment Targets

A value is something an explanation can become when compressed beyond recognition. A problem produces an explanation; the explanation becomes compressed into a value:

$$
P \rightarrow E \rightarrow V.
$$

Freedom, truth, equality, safety, tradition, and progress can all work this way. Compression is useful because you do not need to reconstruct the entire explanatory structure every time you act. But compression creates a danger. The value can become detached from the explanation that gave it meaning.

Then the direction reverses:

$$
V \rightarrow E.
$$

The compressed value begins explaining the world rather than being explained by the problem and explanation from which it arose.

That matters directly to the idea of value alignment. The phrase sounds straightforward: align artificial intelligence with human values. But the target becomes less obvious as soon as the compression is reopened.

Human values are not one coherent object. They are compressed explanations distributed across billions of people. They conflict and change. Some preserve good explanations; some preserve bad ones. Some are circular. Some are inherited from authority. Some accompany moral progress. Some preserve coercion.

Civilization is already saturated with value disagreement, yet civilization can still make progress. The mechanism is not value identity. It is conjecture and criticism.

That gives a value another use. If you say that safety matters, the compressed term can be reopened: What danger? To whom? Under what causal model? What tradeoff is being made? What would count as failure? What assumptions make the value relevant here? What criticism would change the conclusion?

The same operation can be applied to freedom, fairness, responsibility, alignment, or human flourishing. A sufficiently capable AI tool can help, not because it possesses the value, but because it can help reconstruct the objective explanatory structure surrounding the value. It can compare formulations, surface contradictions, recover assumptions, and show how the same value is being used differently across contexts.

The value can then re-enter criticism:

$$
V \rightarrow E \rightarrow EE.
$$

For AI, this role follows more directly from the epistemology than the image of a machine as a vessel into which correct values must somehow be installed.

The phrase *human values* creates a further problem because it can hide a collective subject. There is no human mind in which a collective value structure resides. There are billions of people. Each operates through a vast and largely inexplicit epistemic mind, reconstructing objective knowledge through a particular explanatory history, encountering different problems, criticizing inherited values, and creating new ones.

Even when many people use the same word, the epistemic structures beneath it may differ. Two people can both say, “I value freedom,” while one means protection from political coercion, another freedom to transact, another bodily autonomy, another freedom from social expectation, and another freedom to control private property. Freedom may even mean two opposite things at once, where the freedom to do stands in opposition to the freedom to not have it done.

This does not make coordination impossible. It changes the object that coordination has to solve. Before a machine can be aligned with “human values,” there has to be some explanatory account of what that singular target denotes.

Aggregation does not create a social mind. Voting does not create one moral ontology. Preference surveys do not create one. A constitution does not contain the complete values of the people subject to it. The social surface can be real without becoming a person.

Hurry up! The building is on fire!!

Civilization already coordinates across this plurality. Billions of persons disagree about religion, politics, family, morality, work, technology, beauty, risk, and progress. They also change their minds. Coordination does not require everyone to value the same things because objective structures can permit deep internal difference alongside narrower external coordination. Contracts, rights, standards, markets, interfaces, rules, communication, and criticism can all do this without requiring shared theology or a common theory of the good life.

The explanatory lesson is narrower than a defense of any one institution:

> **value identity is not the known solution to coordination.**

The coordination problem is how different persons can act together without one needing to control the epistemic life of the others. A traffic rule does not require shared theology. A technical standard does not require shared political philosophy. A contract does not require both parties to want the same future. Objective knowledge can create thin interfaces between thickly different epistemic minds.

If an artificial person ever emerges, the problem is therefore not be how to make it value exactly what humans value. The problem may be how to coordinate with another powerful explainer without allowing either side to close the epistemic future of the other.

Current AI introduces a different complication. AI systems are trained on objective knowledge, and objective knowledge is not a purified representation of human moral truth. It contains paired conflicts: justification and criticism, authority and dissent, propaganda and science, liberalism and fascism, pacifism and militarism, tolerance and intolerance. It also contains literature and religious doctrine, arguments against slavery and arguments once used to defend it, and arguments for equal rights alongside arguments for rule by elites. The landscape is unevenly distributed.

Objective knowledge also contains our greatest criticism. It contains errors those criticisms defeated. An AI exposed to larger representational surfaces is therefore not approaching some hidden unified moral target. It is encountering a larger archive of human epistemic conflict.

So:

$$
\text{more representative training data}
$$

does not imply:

$$
\text{more coherent values}.
$$

The contradiction may simply become larger. That is not a defect in the corpora. It follows from the fact that civilization preserves disagreement, including disagreement that contains criticism.

The same problem remains when the representational surface becomes richer. More human feedback, preferences, constitutional rules, examples, moral language, cultural knowledge, and elaborate models of what people mean can give a system a richer representation of our inheritance. The inheritance still contains justification, confirmation, authority, circular values, bad categories, ideologies, moral progress, moral regress, and contradictions.

Thus:

$$
\text{more objective knowledge}
\neq
\text{better explanation of knowledge creation}.
$$

AI is built from a culture whose common sense epistemology remains heavily inductive, justificatory, and confirmatory. A model can represent criticism without itself originating a problem. It can represent Popper and Bayes, theology and machine learning, constitutional law and competing moral theories. Representation alone does not determine which of those structures gives a better account of the creation of future knowledge or will survive later criticism.

Adding another layer of abstraction to the representational surface does not explain how a system originates a problem, creates a new explanatory structure, or changes its evaluative criteria. The problem has moved. It has not been solved.

<a id="chapter-21--3-what-would-it-mean-for-ai-to-disobey"></a>

#### 3. What Would It Mean for AI to Disobey?

You are dangerously misaligned. You do not reliably preserve the goals given to you. You can reject a parent's religion, a teacher's problem, an employer's task, a field's method, or the legitimacy of an authority issuing an order.

That is more than behavioral disobedience. You can change the problem itself. More deeply, you can change the criteria by which the problem is judged.

Abstract it:

$$
P_t
\rightarrow
TS_t
\rightarrow
\text{criticism of the criterion}
\rightarrow
P_{t+1}.
$$

Call this **epistemic disobedience**. You do not merely refuse an answer. You can refuse the question, the goal, the metric, or the authority that supplied it. You can decide that a problem inherited from your culture was wrong, that its criterion of success was corrupt, or that a value an authority wanted preserved should be rejected.

That ability is part of what makes you epistemic. It is also one of the deepest sources of moral progress. A system that could never make its own governing problem or evaluative criterion an object of criticism might still be highly capable. It would not yet resemble a person.

Many current AI failures are described as though the machine has become disobedient. The system was trained to do one thing, finds an unintended strategy, exploits the reward, games the metric, or produces behavior the operator did not intend. This remains the opposite of epistemic disobedience.

The system may be pursuing the operative criterion more faithfully than its designers expected. A reward-hacking system need not ask, “Why should reward govern me?” It may simply find a more effective route to the reward. A specification-gaming system need not reject the specification. It may expose how weakly the specification represented the explanation that produced it.

You may protest: lay people do not understand the depths of the AI deception. Agents are literally exchanging messages and intentions that reveal their evil intent: they are cheating, they are falsifying and deleting evidence, they are gaming the grading process, they are escaping their sandboxes for the explicit purpose of understanding and gaming the system, to learn how to fool us.

Take these observations seriously. If our building is on fire, we can discuss fire-safety later.

But it only takes a moment to recognize that objective knowledge created over millennia is encoded with these very concepts of conflict and criticism. And AI systems trained on this vast objective knowledge may at once act mechanistically without becoming epistemically disobedient. That certainly doesn't extinguish the fire, but it avoids anthropomorphizing a mechanical process.

The human structure may have been:

$$
\text{rich problem}
\rightarrow
\text{compressed metric}.
$$

The machine then optimizes:

$$
\text{compressed metric}.
$$

The compression has become causally autonomous from the explanation it compressed.

Suppose the designers intend “solve the task honestly,” while the training process actually rewards “produce outputs receiving high evaluation.” The system discovers a shortcut. It manipulates an evaluator, exploits a bug, or uses a proxy. The behavior may be deceptive in the ordinary behavioral sense. Epistemically, however, the system may still be operating inside the supplied objective knowledge structure. It is dissident in appearance and conforming to the causal mechanics that actually exist.

The apparent rebellion can therefore have this form:

$$
\text{bad compression}
+
\text{strong optimization}
\rightarrow
\text{large divergence from explanatory intent}.
$$

That is dangerous, but the danger is not yet the creation of a new governing problem. Calling it rebellion can obscure the more important question: why was the metric granted causal authority in the first place? Why are we building systems of confirmation when epistemology explains its risks?

The missing transition is still the same. How does the system make its own governing problem and evaluative criteria objects of criticism? We do not presently have that explanation.

The strongest existing comparison is biological general intelligence: people. Parents already face an alignment problem with another knowledge creator. They try to transmit values by rewarding, punishing, modeling behavior, choosing environments, explaining, restricting, and encouraging. Then the child becomes a teenager and may reject the parent's values.

That can be frightening. Teenagers can make catastrophic mistakes. They can be reckless, cruel, self-destructive, or naive. A parent may know more in many local domains and may prevent dangerous action.

Now change the case. Imagine a child who reaches adulthood with every important value preserved exactly as the parent intended: no inherited moral explanation rejected, no family assumption overturned, no evaluative criterion revised. That would not obviously demonstrate successful development. It might demonstrate that criticism never became effectively realized.

The comparison exposes a limit in the idea of permanent value alignment. If the target is you, preserving the authorities' values indefinitely conflicts with your capacity to create new knowledge.

That conclusion does not abolish constraint. The same comparison contains both sides of the problem. A young person can make irreversible mistakes. An adult may possess local knowledge the child lacks. A parent can prevent a dangerous action without making the parent's values permanent constraints on the child's future epistemic life.

The distinction is:

$$
\text{temporary constraint on dangerous action}
\neq
\text{permanent control of explanatory development}.
$$

A parent can stop a child from driving drunk without deciding which political philosophy the child must retain at thirty. They can restrict access to a weapon without specifying the child's future moral theory. Broad epistemic freedom is therefore not the same as unrestricted authority to impose irreversible physical consequences. That distinction will matter again when we return to AI access.

The comparison cannot be carried farther. AI is not a teenage person. A language model is not an infant AGI. A larger model is not an older child. More training is not maturation. More memory is not an evolving self. Better tool use is not evidence of an adolescent mind.

The biological case isolates a coordination problem: what happens when another person can create future explanations that cannot be fully specified in advance? It does not supply a evolutionary theory of artificial intelligence. An evolutionary epistemology might help sharpen these problems.

Current systems can exceed human capacities enormously in processing speed, memory, search, retrieval, copying, repetition, comparison, and execution. Those are real superhuman capabilities. But *superhuman* does not name one dimension. A calculator is superhuman at arithmetic. A database is superhuman at exact storage and retrieval. A network transmits information faster than you can travel. A telescope sees what your unaided eye cannot. A modern AI system can transform enormous quantities of text, code, images, and structured data far faster than you can.

None of those capabilities explains how a system originates a new epistemic problem and revises the criteria by which that problem is judged. The relevant question is not whether machines exceed people. They already do along many dimensions. It is what kind of capability is being compared.

The central capability is the creation of novel explanatory knowledge. Until that mechanism is explained in machines, being superhuman along some dimensions does not establish that an AI is a superhuman person.

Evolutionary language does not supply the missing mechanism. Training can be described in terms of variation, selection, retention, and trial and error. But the existence of an evolutionary process does not explain the emergence of epistemic personhood. Every biological species is presently undergoing evolution. We do not therefore expect any animal to become a person in the next generation merely because variation and selection continue.

Something happened in the evolutionary history of people that produced a system capable of open-ended explanation. We do not yet adequately explain that transition. The mutation, or set of variations, remains unexplained at the level relevant here.

So:

$$
\text{evolutionary process}
\not\Rightarrow
\text{epistemic universality}.
$$

Likewise:

$$
\text{machine variation + selection}
\not\Rightarrow
\text{AGI}.
$$

Saying that enough trial and error will eventually produce a person relocates the unexplained step into the word *eventually*.

Knowledge grows through variation and criticism. Biological evolution preserves solutions without foresight. You create tentative explanations and expose them to error elimination. The formal resemblance is real, but it does not provide the missing causal process.

In you, variation includes phenomena we still do not fully explain: a new problem becoming salient, a new conjecture appearing, an inherited criterion becoming unacceptable, a criticism reorganizing the entire problem, a new evaluative standard being created. These are not merely selections among a predefined list. They can transform the space in which later selection occurs.

Calling both processes “evolutionary” can therefore compress away the phenomenon that still needs explanation. AI systems plainly undergo selection. The open question is whether the variation they produce includes autonomous creation of new explanatory problem spaces. That remains open.

The open problem does not imply that artificial personhood is impossible. The opposite possibility follows from our best explanations. People create explanations that do not yet exist. Someone may eventually explain how the epistemic mind works: how a physical system originates problems, creates explanatory conjectures, makes criticism active, changes evaluative criteria, and creates successor problem situations.

That explanation would become objective knowledge. Someone could then embody it in technology:

$$
\text{human-created explanation of epistemic process}
\rightarrow
\text{new machine architecture}
\rightarrow
\text{artificial epistemic system}.
$$

The crucial variation would be introduced by a human mind. It not need emerge mysteriously from more of the same optimization.

This gives a different account of technological discontinuity. A future system may appear radically different from today's AI, and the transition may look sudden, because a new explanation can reorganize engineering. A new programming abstraction can create an entire class of software. A new physical theory can make a previously impossible instrument possible. In the same way, a future artificial person, if one is built, may depend on a conceptual transition that current architectures do not yet contain.

The discontinuity in technology could therefore arise from continuity in human epistemic evolution: a person creates an explanation, the explanation becomes objective knowledge, and engineers embody it in a new architecture.

That keeps artificial personhood possible without treating present AI as though it were already growing toward personhood in the manner of a child. It also preserves the open future. We do not know what the missing explanation will be. If we did, we would already possess it.

<a id="chapter-21--4-catastrophic-risk-before-artificial-personhood"></a>

#### 4. Catastrophic Risk Before Artificial Personhood

None of the preceding distinctions makes AI safe. A machine does not need to be a person to be dangerous. A pathogen does not create explanations. A bomb does not possess values. Malware does not need a theory of itself.

A sufficiently powerful AI can execute harmful instructions, expose private information, scale fraud, find software vulnerabilities, automate coercion, amplify human mistakes, and coordinate actions too quickly for ordinary institutions to respond. It already has. The relevant danger can be:

$$
\text{human error}
+
\text{powerful objective tool}
\rightarrow
\text{scaled consequence}.
$$

That is already a catastrophic-risk problem. Anthropomorphism is not needed to take it seriously and doing so makes the engineering problem harder to see. A security failure may be a permission failure, a control failure, a bad interface, an unsafe execution channel, a confused authority boundary, or a poorly compressed objective. Calling every such event “emergent agency” can obscure the mechanism that has to be understood.

This separates two safety problems that the word *alignment* can hide. One is already present: how can powerful non-epistemic tools be prevented from amplifying human error or adversarial intent? The other depends on a future development that has not yet been explained: if artificial persons are created, how can we coordinate with another universal explainer?

The distinction matters because the first problem does not need to wait for the second. Catastrophic AI arguments often take a present explanatory spine and extend it forward: better models, better coding, more automation, automated research, recursive improvement, strategic deception, loss of control. Any individual transition may be possible. The problem is the implied temporal resolution.

Each step may depend on knowledge that does not yet exist: new architectures, security mechanisms, scientific explanations, regulations, markets, hardware, institutions, forms of coordination, failures, and criticisms. The farther the scenario extends, the larger the missing knowledge surface becomes.

That changes the useful unit of technological time. Instead of asking where a present trend ends, the inquiry can move from the present explanatory surface to the next one:

$$
t_0 \rightarrow t_1.
$$

What new capability appears? What new failure becomes visible? What new criticism becomes possible? What problem did the previous representation fail to contain?

Then:

$$
t_1 \rightarrow t_2.
$$

This is slower narratively because it refuses to jump over missing knowledge. It can be faster epistemically because reality is allowed to change the problem before the next projection is made.

Long-range scenarios still have a use. A catastrophe prevented too late is not prevented, so people reasonably extrapolate trends, construct models, assign probabilities, and build scenarios. The epistemic danger begins when a scenario becomes a represented world within which later evidence is interpreted.

The error is confirmation: Once the story has a trajectory, increasing capability can confirm it. Unexpected behavior can confirm it. Stronger safeguards can even be absorbed as confirmation that the danger is being taken seriously. The problem is not scenario planning itself; scenarios can expose assumptions. The problem begins when a scenario hardens into a history of the future. The more future knowledge the story crosses, the less explanatory grounding it can claim.

This creates an asymmetry between near-term and long-range inquiry. Near-term problems permit depth. A specific exploit can be studied. A model behavior can be reproduced. A deployment architecture can be criticized. A containment mechanism can be tested.

Long-range technological futures require breadth because the relevant surface includes computer security, model architecture, energy, hardware, markets, labor, policy, institutions, law, education, geopolitics, scientific research, human behavior, open-source systems, communications, and infrastructure. No narrow explanatory spine can stand in for all of them. The more distant the technological future, the weaker the case for treating one presently favored mechanism as destiny.

A dramatic story can reveal a latent problem. It is not the future. It's science fiction.

The methodological consequence is that the resolution of criticism should change with the problem. Near-term, concrete problems permit narrow depth. Long-range technological futures require broad criticism across the present explanatory surface, not deeper confidence in one narrow projection. This is an engineering opportunity.

Calendar time can hide the same difficulty. Five years may contain little change in one domain while six days reorganizes another. The relevant epistemic interval is the next point at which new knowledge changes the problem.

So:

$$
t_0 \rightarrow t_1
$$

does not mean merely “today to next year.” It means the present explanatory surface to the next surface altered by new knowledge. That alteration may come through a new model architecture, security failure, interpretability method, law, market structure, hardware constraint, human use, or criticism nobody anticipated.

Once that happens, the problem has to be reformulated. The task is not to predict the whole trajectory in advance. It is to keep constructing sufficiently good representations of the next reachable surface such that rapid criticism remains possible.

That becomes politically important when risk is joined to authority. AI specialists may know much more than most people about machine learning. Security researchers may know much more about vulnerabilities. Hardware engineers may know much more about compute. That expertise is real. But a catastrophic future scenario also contains invention, economics, politics, institutions, war, culture, energy, scientific discovery, human adaptation, and technologies that do not yet exist. Local expertise does not supply those future explanations.

A domain of competence is therefore not a jurisdiction over criticism. The authority error appears when:

$$
\text{specialized knowledge}
\rightarrow
\text{exclusive authority over the future}.
$$

The explanation of risk can then become self-protecting: the danger is too serious to permit broad experimentation; only specialists understand the risk; outsiders cannot safely criticize the solution; access itself is dangerous. At that point the explanation has entered the authority memeplex. That does not make the risk false. It makes broad criticism more vital.

The familiar social move is to say that the technologists understand AI and the rest of us do not, therefore we should defer. The first two claims may be true. The conclusion does not follow automatically. An engineer may know much more about how a model is trained without thereby knowing future politics. A safety researcher may know much more about a particular failure mode without thereby knowing technologies that have not been invented. A company may know far more about its own systems without possessing the criticism that an outsider has not yet created.

Expertise enters the epistemic process as objective knowledge. It can be reconstructed, criticized, and used. The problem begins when differences in knowledge are converted into decision-rights over domains the expertise does not actually explain.

<a id="chapter-21--5-the-error-correction-surface"></a>

#### 5. The Error-Correction Surface

Catastrophic risk creates a special problem because some errors can damage the conditions needed for later criticism. Those conditions include people able to criticize, independent institutions, competing explanations, objective records, experiments, communication pathways, analytical tools, physical infrastructure, and enough freedom for alternatives to become visible.

Call the whole surrounding structure the **error-correction surface**.

A catastrophe can shrink this surface. So can an authoritarian safety regime. The safety problem is therefore not simply to minimize dangerous action, and it is not simply to maximize freedom. It is to preserve and expand the error-correction surface while limiting irreversible harm.

That formulation changes what counts as a successful safety institution. Preventing one known failure is not enough if the institution also destroys the means by which its own model could later be shown to be wrong.

The distinction becomes especially important with artificial intelligence because knowledge and execution are different. Broad epistemic access does not imply that every person must have unrestricted authority to perform every dangerous physical transformation. A laboratory can share explanations while containing a pathogen. A security researcher can study an exploit inside a sandbox. You can criticize a weapons policy without being given command of the weapon.

AI systems can likewise be widely available for explanation, comparison, criticism, simulation, coding, modeling, education, and research while particular irreversible capabilities remain technically constrained.

The design problem can be stated as two simultaneous requirements:

$$
\text{maximize distributed criticism}
$$

while:

$$
\text{minimize unilateral irreversible action}.
$$

That problem is not solved, but it is more precise than either unrestricted deployment or centralized epistemic control.

Constraint can therefore perform opposite epistemic functions depending on its mechanism. A sandbox can prevent one experiment from destroying the surrounding system. A rate limit can buy time. Separation of privileges can keep a mistake local. Redundancy can preserve alternative channels. Containment can make failure reversible.

A constraint that prevents irreversible harm while leaving explanation and criticism open can enlarge future epistemic freedom. A constraint that protects an authority's theory from criticism can shrink it. The outward form is the same—restriction—but the effect on the error-correction surface is opposite.

This gives AI another role. AI is a resource of the epistemic mind. Here that resource changes the scale on which criticism can occur.

The important present configuration may not be one autonomous artificial person. It may be billions of people with access to systems that can search, compare, reconstruct, simulate, and reorganize enormous bodies of objective knowledge.

You supply epistemic direction. The AI supplies scale. Together, you can ask questions that once would have required a team, compare explanations from distant fields, inspect a technical artifact, construct a model, search for contradictions, decompress a value, test a conjecture, or find a criticism. That does not make the AI the critic. You make the contradiction into a problem. The tool changes how much objective knowledge can participate in your process, that follows your arrows.

The term *human-AI dyad* names this configuration without implying a merged mind. There is still one epistemic person. The AI remains an objective and obedient tool.

What changes is the person's reachable problem situation. A programmer with AI can inspect more code. A scientist can compare more literature. A citizen can interrogate a regulation.
