But the epistemology has produced a stranger conjunction. Every known person belongs to the same explanatory class. Every person is capable of creating explanatory knowledge. Yet every person's mind landscape is historically singular.

The universality is common. The individuality is not.

You and another person can share language, family, country, profession, religion, politics, childhood home, and decades of memory, yet still discover that the same event inhabits two radically different explanatory worlds. The overlap can be enormous. The divergence can be larger.

So perhaps:

> We are not the same

is not the threat. The threat appears when difference is forced into hierarchy.

$$
\text{difference}
\nRightarrow
\text{different moral worth}.
$$

That arrow must also be explained.

Earlier we described each person as a universe. Not a separate reality. There is one reality. But each person contains an enormous evolving abstraction of it.

Imagine two such universes. One contains knowledge you admire; the other, explanations you despise. One has produced great kindness; one, cruelty. One has encountered criticism and changed; one appears closed. One is brilliant in a domain you understand; one seems confused. One is a child; one is dying.

What unit would let you weigh their capacity to create the next explanation? There is none available.

The absence of such a unit does not prove moral equality. It removes an easy route to moral inequality. A demographic category cannot supply it. Neither can an intelligence score, a personality profile, a political identity, a diagnosis, or a reputation. None of these compressions contains the future epistemic trajectory of the person. The moral conclusion is still not forced. But some shortcuts have disappeared.

There are billions of people alive now. The number is easy to say; the thing it refers to is almost impossible to imagine. Billions of histories. Billions of partly inexplicit worlds. Billions of memories whose significance cannot be externally recovered. Billions of networks of salience, skill, expectation, and attachment. Fear, curiosity, resentment, humor, unfinished problems, half-formed distinctions, private contradictions. Billions of possible future explanations.

Some will never become objective. Some will become jokes, tools, criticisms, equations, acts of cruelty, acts of care, institutions, mistakes, or ideas that reorganize civilization.

The abstraction *humanity* is tiny beside what it compresses. We need it; no person can encounter everyone individually. But when the abstraction begins to feel complete, something has vanished.

Perhaps awe is the feeling produced when the compression briefly fails. Not mystery as an excuse. Not mysticism. Not reverence demanded by doctrine. The recognition that the object before you has more explanatory depth than your model can hold.

One person can sometimes do that. The class of all people is beyond imagination.

<a id="chapter-29--6-judgment-without-completion"></a>

#### 6. Judgment Without Completion

The word *evil* compresses too. That does not make it useless. Some people deliberately torture others. Some build institutions that preserve suffering. Some exploit vulnerability. Some kill. Some terrorize. Some knowingly block criticism because criticism threatens their power. The causal consequences can be terrible.

A moral framework that cannot condemn or stop such actions would be defective. But a second claim does not follow from the first:

$$
\text{this action must be stopped}
$$

does not entail:

$$
\text{we possess the final explanation of this person}.
$$

Earlier we described evil as something like persistent harmful closure:

$$
\text{harmful explanation}
+
\text{power}
+
\text{blocked criticism}
\rightarrow
\text{persistent avoidable suffering}.
$$

That remains useful. It identifies something we may need to oppose immediately without requiring an essence of evil inside the person. The person can be dangerous. The action can be intolerable. The institution can require dismantling. The ruler can require removal. And the explanation of the person can still remain incomplete.

This distinction is difficult because urgency compresses. Sometimes it must. If you are running from violence, you do not owe the attacker a complete epistemology. Again, the problem situation matters.

The harder danger appears when moral authority turns the compression into a closed system. The language is familiar:

> Any decent person knows this.
> No reasonable person could believe that.
> Only someone evil would disagree.
> The matter is settled.
> The science says.
> History is not on your side.
> Everyone knows what side you should be on.

Each statement may refer to something true. The problem is structural: a conjecture has become a condition of participation. Disagreement no longer arrives as criticism. It arrives as diagnosis. The dissenter is stupid, corrupt, brainwashed, dangerous, immoral, unfit. The original explanation may survive not because it is hard to vary, but because criticism has been reclassified as evidence against the critic.

Externally, this can produce authoritarian institutions. Internally, it can produce something stranger. The voice says:

> A good person would not think this.
> A rational person would not feel this.
> Someone like me cannot want that.
> If I doubt this, I am betraying who I am.

The ruler has crossed the border into your epistemic mind.

<a id="chapter-29--7-who-rules-you"></a>

#### 7. Who Rules You?

Ask the political question again:

> Who should rule?

This time do not imagine a parliament. Imagine your epistemic mind. Which explanation gets authority? Your parents? Your religion? Your politics? Your diagnosis? Your profession? Your reputation? A memory? A fear? A moral injury? A theory of yourself formed when you were sixteen? A person who hurt you? A person you loved? A sentence someone said once and never remembered?

The question is not whether these structures should disappear. Some may contain excellent knowledge. Some may have preserved you. Some may be true. Some may still solve important problems.

The question is which of them may become a problem. Which explanation is allowed to be contradicted? Which identity can survive revision? Which value may be inspected without the inspection itself being treated as betrayal? Which ruler can be removed?

A bad internal ruler need not be false. That makes the problem harder.

Suppose you are talented. The explanation may be true. Then:

> I am talented

can become:

> I must not fail.

Suppose you were harmed. That may be true. Then:

> I was harmed

can become:

> I can only understand myself through the harm.

Suppose your political opponents have made serious errors. That may be true. Then:

> they are wrong about this

can become:

> everything they say is evidence of corruption.

Suppose your parents loved you. That may be true. Then:

> they loved me

can become:

> therefore their explanation of my life must be right.

A ruler can begin as knowledge. The failure occurs when the knowledge acquires sovereignty. Criticism becomes forbidden not because the explanation has survived criticism, but because criticism threatens the structure around it.

This is how a self-conception can become manifest truth. You no longer experience:

> I currently understand myself this way.

You experience:

> this is what I am.

The difference is one word. The consequences can be enormous. It is easy to condemn the same closure in someone else. The compression is efficient: selfish, weak, narcissistic, irrational, lazy, broken, evil. Sometimes a compressed description solves the immediate problem. Sometimes you need distance, a legal category, an exit, or a way to stop someone. But understanding requires more work.

What problem were they solving? What did they know, and what did they not know? What structure made the action seem available? What criticism failed to enter? What harm did the explanation create? What power preserved it? What could change?

The same questions apply inwardly. What problem were you solving? What did this belief protect? Why did this feel obvious? What changed? What criticism are you routing around? What would you lose if this explanation failed?

There is no guarantee that asking produces wisdom. The questions can themselves become rituals. You can explain endlessly to avoid acting. A clever mind can rationalize anything. Criticism is not moral purity. It is an opportunity for movement. Political systems sometimes make rulers removable, not because the replacement will be perfect, but because permanence magnifies error.

The internal analogue should not be pushed too far. A mind is not a state. A thought is not a president. A memory is not a legislature. The metaphor works at one point: Sovereignty. A ruler becomes dangerous when there is no legitimate route by which the ruler can cease to rule. The same can happen to an explanation.

So perhaps the internal question is not:

> What is the correct belief that should rule my mind?

It is:

> What makes a bad explanation removable?

Contradiction may do it. So may conversation, time, humor, a book, a new friendship, an experiment, a loss, a tool, a therapist, a child, an enemy who notices something your friends do not, a question you cannot dismiss, or an explanation that reorganizes years of inexplicit knowledge.

No universal procedure decides which will matter. That would require knowing the next problem before it exists. The important structure is that movement remains possible.

<a id="chapter-29--8-do-not-clean-the-swamp"></a>

#### 8. Do Not Clean the Swamp

The epistemic landscape is a swamp. Not because knowledge is polluted, but because many forms of knowledge coexist there: biological feeling, social inheritance, objective explanation, memory, skill, habit, moral criticism, identity, contradiction. Some reinforce one another. Some conflict. Some never meet.

There is a temptation, especially in morality, to imagine the healthy mind as clean: no contradiction, no forbidden thought, no shame, no uncertainty, no wrong desire, no ideological contamination, no irrationality, no inherited error, no inconsistency.

But remove all variation and what remains? A perfectly coherent mind might be perfectly wrong. If you cannot think the forbidden thought, you cannot criticize the rule that forbids it. If you must remain consistent with a prior self, you have lost one route to becoming otherwise.

The point is not to celebrate confusion. Coherence matters. Consilience matters. Temporary equilibrium matters. You need to act. But the swamp must remain capable of moving. The goal is not the correct ruler. It is a landscape in which no ruler is beyond criticism.

Now the ought can return. Does any of this tell you what you ought to do?

Perhaps you feel that it does. Perhaps you feel the opposite. Perhaps the explanation of people as open epistemic minds makes freedom seem morally unavoidable. Perhaps it makes responsibility seem more important. Perhaps you think the entire structure smuggles liberal values into its premises. Perhaps you think it does not go far enough. Perhaps you reject the definition of a person. Perhaps you accept the epistemology but deny its moral reach.

Good. The transition is now visible enough to criticize. That is more useful than hiding it.

The claim is not:

$$
\text{person is epistemically open}
\therefore
\text{liberalism is proven}.
$$

The claim is narrower. Persons create explanatory knowledge. Future explanatory knowledge is not derivable from present compression. Coercion can suppress criticism. Authority can preserve its own error. Individual epistemic minds exceed external reconstruction. If those claims hold, then moral systems that permanently subordinate your capacity for criticism acquire a problem. They require explanation. So do systems that treat persons as fixed types, make dissent evidence of defect, or deny routes of correction.

That is criticism. It is not a command from outside the epistemic cycle.

<a id="chapter-29--9-the-tool-does-not-own-the-arrow"></a>

#### 9. The Tool Does Not Own the Arrow

Artificial intelligence makes the old political question unusually visible. Who should control it? Governments? Companies? Experts? Parents? Platforms? International institutions? Users? The public? Some actor will control some things. Models have owners. Infrastructure has operators. States regulate. Parents make decisions for children. Institutions establish rules.

But "who should rule AI?" can conceal several different problems. What harms require immediate restriction? What capabilities require technical containment? What forms of access expand individual capacity for criticism? What systems centralize explanatory authority? What categories of person are being compressed? A second cluster concerns reversibility: who can challenge an AI decision, recover the explanation behind an output, refuse the system, leave, or build an alternative? And who decides that the risk has become urgent?

The epistemic orientation does not supply one ruler. It supplies criticism of arrangements in which mistakes cannot become problems. An AI policy can be wrong. A safety theory can be wrong. A company can be wrong. A government can be wrong. A parent can be wrong. A child can be wrong. You can be wrong.

The problem is not how to construct a world without error. It is how to avoid making one error sovereign. AI can retrieve, compare, translate, generate candidate explanations, preserve histories, expose contradictions, and reopen objective knowledge at scales no unaided biological person could traverse. That can enlarge your epistemic surface.

It can also narrow it. A generalized model can return the population to you. A recommendation can become a profile. A profile can become an environment. An environment can shape your next choice. The tool can begin to own the arrows. The danger is not only that the answer is wrong. It is that the answer becomes difficult to refuse.

So moral AI policy may involve a surprisingly old concern. Not:

> Which machine gives the right answer?

But:

> Can you still make the answer a problem?

Can you reject it? Inspect it? Choose another tool? Act without the profile following you? Recover enough of the causal history to criticize what happened? Can institutions remove bad systems without first proving a final theory of intelligence?

These questions are not the whole of AI morality. They are one place where the older question about rulers has returned in technical form.

<a id="chapter-29--10-the-authority-of-a-life"></a>

#### 10. The Authority of a Life

We often say:

> The individual has authority over their own life.

The sentence feels liberal. Perhaps humanist. Perhaps obvious.

Then reality complicates it. A child does not exercise every adult authority. A suicidal person may be restrained. A violent person may be imprisoned. A patient under anesthesia delegates decisions. Contracts create obligations. Parents make choices. States tax. Courts compel. Emergency workers order evacuations. Institutions set conditions of participation. Authority over one's life is routinely limited.

Does that refute the principle? Perhaps the principle was compressed. Perhaps *authority* was carrying several relationships at once.

The epistemology suggests another way to inspect it. Who is the epistemic locus of your life? Who experiences the consequences? Who creates the future explanations through which that life changes? Who can reject the model from inside the problem situation? No external institution occupies that place. None can.

That does not abolish every external authority. It changes what external authority must explain. The stronger the intervention into your epistemic mind, the more explanatory work appears necessary. Not because autonomy is a sacred substance. Because the intervention acts upon a system whose relevant future state is not fully available to the intervener. The ignorance is structural.

There is another side to this. Suppose someone else says:

> You do not understand.

The reply arrives easily:

> I understand enough.

Sometimes you do. A court does not need to reconstruct every aspect of a person to determine whether a particular act occurred. A firefighter does not need your complete life story before moving you away from a collapsing wall. A friend may know enough to recognize danger. A doctor may know enough to treat an infection. Complete understanding is not required for every action.

But the sentence:

> I'm not like you

may contain knowledge too. Not magical private truth. Not immunity from criticism. A reminder of the asymmetry.

Think of someone you know well. Not an abstraction. One person. Perhaps you have known them for years. Name the problem occupying their mind at this exact moment. Not the topic. The problem.

Now name the explanation they will create next year. Name the memory that will become important after an event that has not happened yet. Name the criticism that will reorganize something they currently experience as obvious. Name the idea they will reject after defending it for twenty years. Name the person they will become impossible to imagine themselves becoming.

Perhaps you think you know. Perhaps you can guess. Perhaps your guess is excellent. Now do it for a stranger. Then for eight billion people. The exercise dissolves almost immediately, like sand between your fingers. 

The failure is not proof of sacredness, goodness, or future value. It suggests the scale of our common ignorance. A beginning of infinity.

<a id="chapter-29--11-morality-after-explanation"></a>

#### 11. Morality After Explanation

> Preserve the means of error correction.

Now the proposition can be stated more carefully. It is not an axiom imported from outside the epistemology. It is not a command proved by epistemology. It is a moral conjecture generated by an explanation of what the growth of knowledge appears to require.

If knowledge grows through criticism, systems that permanently block criticism threaten knowledge growth. If persons are where explanatory knowledge can be created, systems that permanently destroy or subordinate that capacity threaten something the epistemology treats as causally special. If authority can preserve error, removability matters. If compression can become identity, decompression matters. If one person's epistemic landscape cannot be fully reconstructed by another, coercion contains an ignorance problem.

These consequences fit. They have reach. They cohere with other aspects of the epistemology.

That does not make them untouchable. The truck is open now. Criticize them.

You have authority here that I do not. Not because whatever you think is true, not because your feelings cannot be criticized, and not because there is no shared reality. There is. The authority is narrower.

I do not know what problem, if any, the epistemology has become inside your mind. Perhaps it has confirmed something. If so, be careful. Perhaps it has irritated you. That may be useful. Perhaps you think the is-ought move fails, or that liberalism has been smuggled into the account. Perhaps freedom has been granted too much explanatory work. Perhaps people are less open than the epistemology suggests. Perhaps current AI already crosses the boundary into personhood. Perhaps the entire framework feels like a contraption, an elaborate compression protecting itself from criticism. Perhaps you have a better problem.

I cannot know which from here. That limit is not rhetorical. It is the subject.

What, then, is morality in this picture? Not a list of commands emitted by epistemology. Not subjective preference. Not whatever a culture happens to preserve. Not a final deduction from human nature. Not an algorithm that outputs the right action from sufficient facts.

Moral knowledge is explanatory. It identifies harms, conflicts, relations, constraints, consequences, and forms of authority. It can also identify conditions under which people can continue to criticize and create. Such explanations can be good or bad, inherited or invented, compressed or institutionalized, made manifest or used coercively. They can be reopened and improved. They can survive criticism. They can fail.

And when they reach you, they enter another epistemic mind. There they may become something else.

<a id="chapter-29--12-the-last-direct-application"></a>

#### 12. The Last Direct Application

One universal epistemology, applied repeatedly: to genes, personality, society, institutions, freedom, psychology, criticism, values, resources, children, media, artificial intelligence, love, madness, death, invention, knowledge, and now morality.

The epistemology can begin to feel like the answer to every question. It is not.

At best, it is an explanation with reach. It can make some problems visible, expose some category errors, preserve the role of criticism, and describe you without reducing you to the latest compression.

If it works, use it. If another explanation solves these problems better, the epistemology should fail. The explanation does not survive by being defended. It survives by remaining removable.

Before leaving, choose one explanation about yourself that feels obvious. It need not be important. Perhaps:

> I am bad at mathematics.
> I am an introvert.
> I am the responsible one.
> I do not get angry.
> I always choose the difficult path.
> I am not creative.
> I am the kind of person who forgives.
> I could never do that.

Do not reject it, replace it, or affirm the opposite. Ask instead:

> What problem was this explanation solving?

Then:

> What would have to happen for it to become a problem?

You do not need to tell anyone the answer. Perhaps nothing happens. Perhaps the explanation survives. Perhaps a memory moves. Perhaps another problem appears. That movement, if it occurs, belongs to you.

Now choose someone else. Someone you dislike may be more revealing: a political opponent, a colleague, a family member, someone whose behavior you have explained many times.

Notice the compression that arrives first. It may contain knowledge. The further question is:

> What does this explanation make invisible?

You are not required to forgive, agree, remain near someone who harms you, or turn danger into curiosity. The problem situation still matters.

But if another explanation appears, you may discover that the person changed without changing at all. Your model moved.

<a id="chapter-29--14-no-final-ruler"></a>

#### 14. No Final Ruler

We began with the question of moral authority:

> Who should rule?

Externally, the epistemology produced another problem:

> How do we remove bad rulers?

Internally, the question changed again. Not:

> Which explanation deserves permanent sovereignty?

But:

> Can the sovereign explanation become a problem?

This does not produce moral anarchy. Some explanations are better. Some actions are wrong. Some institutions should be stopped. Some rulers should be removed. Some emergencies require action before deliberation ends. Some commitments should survive enormous criticism.

Fallibilism is not indecision. It is the refusal to convert present success into immunity. No final ruler. Not the state. Not the crowd. Not the expert. Not the parent. Not the algorithm. Not the moral theory. Not the self-conception. Not this epistemology.

What remains? One reality. Many minds. Shared objective knowledge. Radically local reconstruction. Fallible explanations. Inexplicit histories. Institutions. Tools. Bodies. Memories. Arguments. Love. Power. Error. Criticism. Creation. Death.

The categories are compressions. The relations move. The future is open where knowledge has not yet been created. You enter that openness from somewhere different from everyone else. That much has become difficult to unsee.

What follows from it? Perhaps you already know.

If so, stop for a moment. Ask where the answer came from, what it compresses, and what would make it fail. Perhaps it survives. Perhaps not. Either way, the next problem is yours to choose.

At the beginning, *you* was hidden inside a population measure. Then you expanded. A genome. A body. An evolutionary history. A language. A society. An inexplicit landscape. A network of abstractions. Objective knowledge inherited from people long dead. Problems. Criticisms. Tools. Artificial intelligence. Love. Invention. Moral judgment.

Nothing in that expansion made you infallible. Nothing made you good. Nothing made every choice sacred. Nothing eliminated the need for institutions, authority, restraint, or criticism.

The opposite. You became more criticizable as the explanation became richer, and harder to finish. You can be wrong. You can cause harm. You can become a bad ruler or submit to one. You can mistake a compression for reality, block criticism, reopen it, create a problem no one else sees, and make something objective that did not exist before. Then another person can encounter it.

The future you is not hidden inside the present waiting to be measured. The arrow is still open. So is the problem.

<a id="part-closing"></a>

## Closing

<a id="chapter-30"></a>

### Beforeword: Inepistemic

I am an inventor, an entrepreneur, and a software architect. Those are ordinary categories. They are also compressions. They tell you something about the kinds of problems I have spent my career around. They do not tell you why one of those problems stayed with me for decades. Nor do they tell you why ideas from psychology, biology, computer science, philosophy, economics, physics, software architecture, and parenthood kept finding their way into the same problem situation. They do not tell you why I created this.

The story is harder to compress. It begins long before this project, with a problem I could not yet state. That has been one of the privileges of my life: to live with a problem long enough that the problem changes you. What first appeared to be one problem became several. Then the several seemed connected. Then the connection proved wrong. The error exposed another problem. Years later, an idea encountered somewhere else changed the terms in which the original problem could even be expressed.

I did not know what I was doing. For much of the time, I did not have the language. I still had the problem. That was enough.

<a id="chapter-30--1-the-earlier-machine"></a>

#### 1. The Earlier Machine

My early work involved knowledge processing. The phrase is broad enough to conceal almost everything interesting. The systems were primitive by present standards: slower machines, narrower interfaces, less objective knowledge available computationally. But the possibility was already extraordinary. A machine could hold structures that a person could not hold all at once. It could search, transform, compare, preserve, and return them. A representation could become operational. A relationship that once depended on a person remembering it could sometimes be embodied in a system instead.

The machine did not need to understand the problem in the way a person did. The explained part could leave the person.

Once outside, it could participate in the next part of the problem. That possibility stayed with me, not because I thought machines would replace thought, but because they might change its conditions. A notebook already does this. So do language, algebra, libraries, databases, compilers. Each moves some burden out of the biological mind and into objective structure. Then you encounter that structure again. The output returns as input, and the process changes.

I did not yet know a theory of this. I had an intuition: machines could do more than automate tasks. They could change the conditions under which problems were pursued. That distinction became important much later. At the time, it was simply exciting.

<a id="chapter-30--2-things-that-fit"></a>

#### 2. Things That Fit

At some point I encountered E. O. Wilson's *Consilience*. The details of what I retained from the book, and what I later rejected, matter less here than the problem it strengthened: what becomes possible when knowledge comes together. Not when one field conquers another, or when everything is reduced to one vocabulary, but when explanations developed for different problems meet and constrain one another.

That possibility felt enormous. It still does. The world is divided into disciplines for useful reasons. Reality is not. A problem does not care whether one of its causes belongs in computer science and another in psychology. Or whether an inventor, entrepreneur, or software architect belongs in any of it. A person does not stop being physical when thinking about morality. An institution does not stop having technical structure because lawyers rather than engineers maintain part of it.

The borders help us work. They can also hide the roads between the work. Consilience made a certain kind of intellectual restlessness feel less like a failure to specialize. Perhaps the problem really did cross the borders. Perhaps taking one explanation seriously meant following it somewhere else. Perhaps it meant taking it personally. That is our habit. Genetics could reach psychology, psychology epistemology, epistemology computation, computation the person, and the person morality and political institutions. Then the whole structure could turn around and criticize itself.

At the beginning, none of that existed. There were only things that seemed as though they ought to fit, and a problem in the spaces where they did not.

<a id="chapter-30--3-the-inexplicit-change"></a>

#### 3. The Inexplicit Change

Then I became a parent. There are changes whose importance becomes obvious before their explanation does. Parenthood was like that for me. I did not wake up with a new theory. Something changed in what mattered: time, risk, the future, other people, knowledge, the cost of not understanding certain problems. The desire to accelerate the creation of life-saving knowledge became less abstract. There was suddenly a person in the world whose future I cared about in a way that exceeded anything I could explain. Then there were more.

A parent can teach, protect, provide, explain, save. But a child is not an extension of the parent. The child's future cannot be filled in ahead of time. The problems they will face do not all exist yet, and the knowledge they will need may not exist yet either. That creates a strange kind of urgency. You want to give them something, yet the thing they may need most cannot simply be given. It has to be created—perhaps by them, perhaps by someone else, perhaps by a person not yet born. It may even come from an explanation produced for another problem and preserved long enough to become useful later.

The problem therefore widens. You cannot merely prepare one child for one predicted future. The future is not available for inspection. What you can hope for is a world in which knowledge can continue to be created and problems can become personal. Inherited explanations can be criticized, and tools can enlarge what people can do with objective knowledge.

I did not formulate the problem this way then. That came later. The purpose arrived before its explanation. Inexplicitly.

<a id="chapter-30--4-other-minds"></a>

#### 4. Other Minds

No solitary project is solitary in the strong sense. I have worked with many inventors, developers, researchers, entrepreneurs, lawyers, designers, scientists, and engineers whose ways of seeing problems changed mine. Sometimes the change came through conversation or disagreement. Sometimes the change came through an artifact or a failed attempt. Sometimes through a paper, a book, a diagram, a proof, a piece of software, or a sentence written by someone who died before I was born.

Call that objective knowledge. The term can sound bloodless. My experience of it has been anything but. There is something intimate about discovering that another person has already spent years inside a problem you have only just learned how to see. A person long dead can present a criticism. A notation can reveal a relationship. A programmer can leave behind a structure that changes how another programmer thinks. The person is gone from the encounter. The knowledge remains available—not perfectly, not without reconstruction or distortion, but enough.

That objective knowledge is one of the great facts of human life. Nothing I have made began with me. The languages, mathematics, machines, concepts, institutional forms, criticisms, and many of the problems were inherited. And then, occasionally, something in the inheritance became strange. That was where the interesting work usually began.

<a id="chapter-30--5-the-explanation-of-explanation"></a>

#### 5. The Explanation of Explanation

Then I encountered *The Beginning of Infinity*. This is not an appeal to authority. A book does not become true because its author wrote it. Its importance in this story is causal: it changed my problem situation.

I had spent years interested in knowledge processing, invention, intelligence, software, and the strange ability of people to produce things that did not exist before. Then explanations themselves became explicit as an object. An explanation could be judged neither by the confidence with which it was held nor by the quantity of observations arranged around it. The structure of the explanation itself mattered. That possibility sent me toward the philosophy of explanations, not for philosophy, but for inventive inspiration. I became interested in why some explanations reached across problems while others merely restated what had happened. Why could changing one part break the whole structure? How could explanations exist objectively, and how could encountering one make previously unavailable thoughts possible?

That looked increasingly relevant to artificial intelligence. AI was already being discussed as a machine for knowledge, reasoning, intelligence, perhaps one day explanation. I was trying to connect my still-fuzzy understanding of epistemology directly to that technological problem. At one point I wrote to David Deutsch and asked for his criticism. One correction stayed with me:

> "[Popper's] even bigger emphasis is on *problems*."

Problems. I had moved close to an epistemology of conjecture and criticism while underweighting the thing that gives both their structure. The error was productive. Explanations did not simply exist as structures awaiting criticism. They arose in problem situations. A conjecture was a tentative response to a problem. A criticism mattered because it changed the problem situation. After criticism, the important result was not merely a better answer. It was a different problem.

That correction gave me a reason to read Popper—deeply, repeatedly, across science, knowledge, politics, freedom, historicism, probability, objectivity, criticism, the open society, the logic of discovery. And, once I learned to see them, problems everywhere.

I did not simply read those explanations and acquire them. I misunderstood them, resisted them, reconstructed them, used them badly, forgot distinctions, recovered them, tried to build with them, found contradictions, returned to the texts, built again. 

This is a familiar condition in invention. You can know that a problem exists long before you know what would count as solving it. You can build a solution and discover that the solution has finally revealed the problem.

Eventually, epistemology started to feel like common sense. Fallibly, not easily. Common sense in the more literal sense that its distinctions became available before deliberate reconstruction. A request for evidence could make the justification problem visible. A statistical claim could trigger a question about causal explanation. A model could feel like a toy. A claim about a person could raise the problem of the person. An answer could make the problem behind the answer visible.

The framework had become partly inexplicit. That made it much more useful—and more dangerous. Any explanation that begins to feel like common sense can become difficult to see. This project is an exercise in remembering that too.

<a id="chapter-30--6-building-the-problem"></a>

#### 6. Building the Problem

I use software as a substrate for invention. That means, among other things, that I have spent a large part of my life turning conceptual distinctions into structures. A software architecture is full of claims: this thing is separate from that thing; this state must persist; this transition is allowed; this component should know this and remain ignorant of that. Architecture is objective knowledge about relationships made executable. When the relationships are wrong, the software shows you.

For years I kept returning to a question: could epistemic structure become architectural structure? Not a program that stores facts, a database of beliefs, a confidence-scoring machine, or an automated philosopher. Could a system represent the movement of explanation itself?

Eventually the pieces cohered enough to become an invention in the institutional sense. There were explanatory primitives and epistemic states, relations among explanatory objects, epistemic cycles, persistent histories of conjecture and criticism, and methods represented explicitly enough to be executed computationally. The software was organized not around final answers but around movement from problems through tentative solutions and criticism into successor problems.

The abstraction finally had a technical body. A tentative one, but real enough to run. I implemented it. The epistemic primitives became software objects; the explanatory states became operational states; the epistemic cycle became something a machine could participate in. Explanatory history could be persisted for criticism and revision.

That implementation matters because I used it. Not on a demonstration problem, but on problems I cared about. Like this one. The system became part of the machinery through which this project was researched, criticized, reorganized, rewritten, and preserved. The project did not merely describe the invention. The project ran through it. The tool became part of the problem situation that produced the explanation of the tool.

That changed the problem again.

<a id="chapter-30--7-the-other-participant"></a>

#### 7. The Other Participant

For most of the years I was thinking about knowledge processing, the machine remained comparatively rigid. It could store, retrieve, calculate, transform, execute. Then artificial intelligence changed the available surface. A machine could participate in natural-language transformations at a scale and flexibility earlier knowledge systems could not. It could generate variations, reorganize explanations, expose contradictions, compare formulations, and translate between levels of abstraction.

This obviously did not solve creativity. It did not turn the machine into the author of my problem. It changed the conditions under which I could remain with the problem. That distinction is the center of my experience with AI.

Previously, a problem of this scale would have entailed a large venture. I would have needed to persuade other people that the problem mattered, raise money, recruit, and coordinate. I would have had to translate a changing problem into tasks, preserve continuity across a team, and manage the organizational machinery around the inquiry. Such machinery can create extraordinary knowledge. It can also consume enormous quantities of the resource it is meant to support.

Some problems are especially difficult to institutionalize before they are explicated. The language, architecture, evaluative criteria, even the identity of the problem may still be moving. The person pursuing it does not yet know what should be delegated because discovering the problem is still part of the work.

Artificial intelligence changed that constraint. It made something closer to a solitary institution possible. Not solitary because nobody else contributed. Solitary because the coordination boundary became radically smaller. A conjecture could become objective in seconds. The objective form could be criticized. The criticism could generate alternatives. An old state could return. A method could be revised and immediately applied to the artifact that produced the criticism.

The machine was not merely helping me write. Writing was one surface. It was helping make a larger portion of the problem space accessible, and therefore available to me. The cost of moving between inexplicit structure and criticizable objective structure had fallen dramatically. Something inside could come out, then answer back.

There is a slogan I use for this relationship: **My AI and I are more clever than I.** It is often attributed to Einstein in another form, usually involving a pencil. The ancestry of the sentence may be unstable. That is almost more useful. The authority does not matter, and neither does the pencil. Replace it with chalk, a notebook, a blackboard, a compiler. The interesting structure survives.

The slogan is objective knowledge. It travelled; people reconstructed it; wording and attribution changed; different minds conjectured different meanings. That is the point. Objective knowledge can be inherited without preserving one private meaning. I encountered the structure and made a different conjecture from it.

This really is **my AI**. It is mine in the sense relevant to my problem situation. Objective knowledge was transformed into a novel architecture, and supplied a problem-specific epistemic environment that raw interaction alone did not. I used the integrated system on the problem that had produced it. Its outputs entered my explanatory history and changed subsequent problems. It became part of the machinery by which private and inexplicit knowledge could become objective enough to criticize. My AI is therefore not merely the model. It is the model as encountered through a technological and epistemic structure that itself belongs to the history of my problem.

The relationship is personal and objective at once. The dyad is not reducible to either participant. The machine gives me things I did not put into the prompt. Some expose a contradiction, recover something forgotten, show that I asked the wrong question, or make an inexplicit preference visible because I immediately dislike the result. I supply direction; the direction changes. The machine supplies variation; some of the variation changes me. The objective artifact enters the next problem situation.

Is the dyad more clever than I? There is no such scalar unit for cleverness. But I can describe the transformation. Problems that once exhausted my working surface can remain active outside it. Conjectures that would have disappeared can answer back. Criticism arrives faster. Revision is cheaper. The distance between an inexplicit intuition and a criticizable artifact has become dramatically shorter. By those measures that matter to the problem I have actually been living with, my AI and I are more clever than I.

<a id="chapter-30--8-the-project"></a>

#### 8. The Project

Something else changed. This became a project. That word is wonderfully modest, where venture is not. A project can be attempted, fail, remain unfinished, or simply continue. It does not need to become an institution before it deserves to exist, persuade a market before its problem can be pursued, or know its final form.

That mattered. There are explanations in this project I would have struggled to develop through ordinary organizational processes. Not because other people could not understand them, but because I did not understand them yet. It is difficult to coordinate a team around a problem whose terms are changing as quickly as the explanation. It is difficult to write a roadmap for an unknown abstraction, or assign a task whose completion may reveal that the task should never have existed.

The technological change made some of those constraints less decisive. I could pursue the problem before anyone else agreed that it deserved pursuit. That is freedom of a very practical kind.

It was not, however, continuously liberating. There were periods when the problem became too large to hold and every explanation exposed three more problems. A failed architecture could feel less like useful error elimination than evidence that years of work had been organized around the wrong problem. There was exhaustion and fear, and physical consequences to both.

Creativity is easy to romanticize from the outside because the surviving artifact compresses away the conditions under which it was made. The body does not disappear while the mind pursues an abstraction. Attention degrades. Sleep matters. Fear narrows. Obsession can create extraordinary persistence and make stopping feel like betrayal of purpose. The dark side of an open problem is that there is always another move available, including when the person making it should rest.

Those periods became part of the criticism too. A system for enlarging the epistemic surface that destroys the epistemic mind using it would be a bad method. The problem had to include the physical person pursuing it. Time, resources, and attention remained finite.

But a major class of coordination constraints had changed. The project became possible at the scale of one person with machines and access to the accumulated objective knowledge of other people. That is one of the things this series has been about—not only in theory, but in its own existence.

<a id="chapter-30--9-the-recursion"></a>

#### 9. The Recursion

At some point I noticed the embarrassment. I was building a system organized around explanatory knowledge while using the system to explain explanatory knowledge. I was trying to understand human-AI collaboration while collaborating with AI. I was writing about objective and inexplicit knowledge while repeatedly making private thought explicit, and about criticism while criticism changed the architecture. I was writing about invention while inventing.

The recursion became the project. Not as a trick, and not to persuade. A self-referential system can be wrong. A recursive system can amplify its own error. The recursion mattered because it made the claims materially criticizable. If explanatory primitives were useful, they should be useful here. If preserving problem histories mattered, it should matter to this project. If methods could be made computational, they should survive contact with the work that created them. If the human-AI dyad enlarged an epistemic surface, that enlargement should become visible in what the dyad could produce. If the person remained larger than the compression, the system had to remain criticizable by the person using it.

The project became one long adversarial test, and welcomingly, a new source of new problems.

<a id="chapter-30--10-the-artifact"></a>

#### 10. The Artifact

Now there is this. Thirty parts. An architecture underneath it. And one person trying to get something out.

It is objective knowledge. That does not make it good, true, or important. It means only that it has crossed a boundary. The problem is no longer present only in me. You can inspect it, misunderstand it, reject it, find a contradiction I missed, take one idea and combine it with a problem I have never encountered. The loss of control is part of the achievement.

For years, much of this existed as a structure I could feel more readily than explain. Pieces appeared in conversations, products, architecture, notes, code, failed companies, successful inventions, private frustrations. Now more of it is outside.

The object may be child's artwork. That possibility is not rhetorical modesty. Children make things whose significance to the maker exceeds their significance to everyone else. The drawing can be derivative, confused, technically poor, beautiful only to the parent. Still, something happened: an internal world became an objective artifact that can now be seen.

This project may be wrong in ways I cannot presently see. It may solve a problem nobody else has, or no problem at all for you. It may contain a useful distinction surrounded by unnecessary machinery. It may become interesting only when some future criticism breaks its central explanation.

Fine. It stands as a tentative solution to my problem. That is enough. I am grateful for the explanations and the people who made them, for the machines and the errors. I am grateful for the years in which the problem refused to disappear, and for the privilege of remaining with it long enough to get more of it out. It's just getting started.

<a id="chapter-30--11-other-people-are-not-like-you"></a>

#### 11. Other People Are Not Like You

When I have tried to explain some of these observations to people who know me well, one response has appeared more often than any other:

> "Yes, but other people are not like you."

The observation is true. Other people are not like me. No one is like another. That is one of the central claims of this project. A person is not an instance of an average mind. The path by which a problem becomes interesting, the inexplicit structures available, the inherited objective knowledge, the criticisms that land, and the future conjectures are different.

So I do not want to argue with the individuality. I want to protect it. The disagreement is elsewhere. 

Individuality does not cancel universality. The claim is not that everyone will care about my problems, use my vocabulary, or produce this project given the same books and machines. The claim is that the explanatory capacity that lets my particular mind become unlike yours is not evidence against personhood as a universal class. It is an expression of it. A universal explainer need not converge on my explanations. Universality permits divergence without a predetermined boundary on what may eventually be understood.

But I cannot ask another person simply to feel the distinction from inside my mind. If there is something here worth criticizing, I have to get enough of it out that another person can encounter it on their own terms. They can reconstruct a different problem, reject mine, find the hidden assumption, take one piece and leave the rest. That is the freedom objective knowledge creates between minds.

This became another motivation for the project. It is a legacy, though I hesitate over the word because legacy can sound like an attempt to control what remains after a person is gone. I mean almost the reverse. I want to leave something that can escape me. I want my children, family, friends, or a stranger to be able to encounter it without needing my presence to stabilize its meaning. They can disagree with it safely. A private structure can remain available without demanding that anyone inherit it as belief.

It is also, more simply, an effort to be known. You can love someone for decades and still have only fragments of the explanatory structures through which they encounter the world. Conversation, shared life, conflict, and work expose some of it, but much remains inexplicit. This project is an attempt to make one of those parts more explicit.

I want the people I love to understand something about why a statistical abstraction about a person can make me uneasy, and why a new explanation can feel beautiful. I want them to understand why an unanswered problem can remain alive for decades, why I am suspicious of certainty but not of truth, and why a tool that exposes error can feel liberating. I want them to understand why mistakes delight me. Above all, I want them to understand why their individuality is much more interesting than any category that describes them.

That love is not an exception to the epistemology. It is one of the experiences that made the problem impossible for me to leave alone. To love another person is, among many other things, to encounter a source of explanations that cannot be compressed without loss. They can continue to surprise you. You cannot possess their future knowledge in advance, and you can know them deeply without completing them.

So yes. Other people are not like me. Thank goodness. That is not where the explanation ends. It is where the more interesting one begins.

<a id="chapter-30--12-literacy"></a>

#### 12. Literacy

There is another way to describe what changed. Think about literacy. Reading is so deeply embedded in modern life that it is difficult for a literate adult to reconstruct the world before reading. Words appear everywhere. You do not decode each sign from first principles. Written instructions become available. A private thought can be externalized. A dead person's sentence can enter your present problem. Once literacy becomes inexplicit, the world itself seems full of readable structure.

Numeracy does something similar. Quantity becomes available through ratios, rates, scale, probability, compounding, orders of magnitude. A person who learns to think quantitatively does not merely acquire mathematical answers. New kinds of problems become visible. Logical and probabilistic concepts can likewise enter ordinary criticism: What is the denominator? Compared with what? Does that conclusion follow? Does this sample tell us about a population or this person?

Once a cognitive practice becomes ordinary, its concepts can disappear into the background. The fluent stop experiencing the fluency. They simply live through it. 

Cultures sometimes notice the absence of such fluencies before they notice the fluency itself, and coin labels for the supposed deficiency: illiterate, innumerate, technophobe. Some labels identify constraints; others compress away almost everything interesting about the person. The point is not to manufacture another taxonomy. It is that a medium or cognitive practice can become so ordinary that its conceptual machinery recedes from view.

For me, epistemology underwent a related transformation. At first it was a subject, then a body of arguments, then a set of distinctions, then a source of problems. Eventually it became difficult not to foreground questions such as: What problem is this explanation solving? What would criticize it? What did this measurement compress? What part is observation and what part explanatory structure? What does this model predict without explaining? What remains inexplicit? What would have to be different for this claim to fail? Is this disagreement about reality, the problem, the model, or the criterion being applied?

Once these distinctions become available, they become difficult to suppress. Epistemology moves from the background to the foreground. I do not mean possessing epistemology, being correct about it, belonging to a philosophical school, or knowing the answers. I mean living with epistemic concepts made explicit enough that they can participate in ordinary thought, the way literacy makes written structure available or numeracy makes quantitative structure available.

This is an individual account. Still, from inside this life, the difference feels real. There was a time before these concepts became foregrounded. There is a time after. The problems did not disappear. They became more interesting.

<a id="chapter-30--13-awe"></a>

#### 13. Awe

There is a temptation to make epistemology austere: problems, criticism, error, fallibility, refutation, no final authority, no guarantee. Read quickly, the vocabulary can sound almost hostile. My experience has been the opposite. The deeper the explanatory structure became, the more often it produced awe—not because everything fit permanently, but because sometimes things fit at all.

A problem in software architecture touches a problem in philosophy. A theory of knowledge changes how you think about parenting. A computational idea changes what can be externalized from one mind. A machine assembled from the objective knowledge of millions of people helps one person make a private problem public. For a moment, separate things stop appearing separate. The connections become visible. Then another criticism arrives and the equilibrium breaks.

Consilience can feel spiritual. No supernatural cause is required. The awe comes from reality becoming more connected through explanation than it appeared before. A physical thing like a person can understand something about the world, make that understanding objective, and leave it available for another person. Explanations created in different centuries can meet inside one present problem. A finite person can participate in explanatory structures whose reach may exceed a civilization. We can be wrong about all of it and continue.

The recursion continues. There is one conjecture in this project that I feel more than I can defend: we want to explain. Not every moment, not every person in the same way, not always explicitly. But the movement appears everywhere. Why? What happened? What does this mean? How does that work? Could this be different? Can I make it? Can I show you? Can you understand what I see?

Children ask why. Artists answer questions nobody noticed. Inventors build their conjectures. Lovers reconstruct one another. Programmers make abstractions executable. People argue, teach, draw, sing, design, write, build tools, raise children, create institutions, try again.

The forms vary. The movement outward does not. Something in a person becomes objective enough to enter another problem. Then reality answers back. Perhaps that is why being unable to explain can feel like confinement, and why getting something out can matter even if nobody else cares. Perhaps that is why the book nobody reads may still have needed to be written.

Perhaps that is why this one did.

<a id="chapter-30--14-a-word-i-needed"></a>

#### 14. A Word I Needed

Eventually I needed a word for this state. At first I formed it by analogy. We have words for lives constrained by the absence of forms of explicit cognitive equipment: illiterate, innumerate. I had come to feel something related about epistemology. Life before these distinctions became explicit had been harder in ways I could recognize only afterward.

So the first construction pointed toward a lack: an epistemic illiteracy. It named a state of living among explanations without sufficiently foregrounding what explanations are, where problems enter, how criticism works, why knowledge remains conjectural, and how objective knowledge changes what can happen next.

But epistemology itself broke the analogy. Literacy and numeracy can become so fluent that their machinery disappears. Epistemology did something stranger. The more deeply I absorbed it, the less plausible it became to treat epistemic competence as possession. The more explicit the structure became, the more ignorance became visible.

The positive state therefore contained the negative state. To become more explicitly epistemological was not to escape epistemic deficiency. It was to become increasingly capable of seeing it. The literate person is, in the relevant sense, not illiterate. The numerate person is not innumerate. But the epistemically explicit person cannot graduate from ignorance in the same way. Fallibility, problems, and the open future deny the graduation.

That is why the contradiction is not a defect in the word. It is the reason I kept it. The state is positive and negative at once: explicitly epistemological and fallible. It is equipped with tools for criticism and therefore less able to pretend that criticism can end. It can make knowledge objective and therefore expose more of what remained trapped, compressed, inherited, mistaken, or unseen. It can solve problems and therefore create problems.

Not *without epistemology*. Inside it. Not beyond ignorance. More intimately acquainted with it.

The word became useful in another direction too. To live with epistemic concepts foregrounded is to be *in* the epistemic process deliberately. Problems appear as problems, explanations as explanations, criticism as criticism, objective knowledge as objective knowledge. Fallibility is not an apology appended to a claim but part of the architecture through which the claim remains alive. Epistemology becomes an ordinary surface of thought. Its concepts become available, usable, criticizable, recursive—and therefore incapable of delivering the comfort promised by the original analogy.

This project is one artifact of that contradiction. Perhaps the artifact is wrong. Perhaps the architecture embodies a beautiful mistake. Perhaps the epistemic mind compresses away something important. Perhaps the human-AI dyad will look primitive very soon. Perhaps another explanation will displace the epistemology that now feels like common sense to me.

Good. Then there will be another problem. I do not want the final word to close that possibility. I want it to contain it: a word for lacking epistemic literacy and for foregrounding epistemology. A word for being inside the recursive process of problems, tentative solutions, criticism, and successor problems. A word for becoming more capable of creating knowledge and thereby making one's ignorance more explicit. More equipped and less finished; more able to explain and more able to see what has not been explained.

For the state in which epistemology has moved from an esoteric subject into the foreground of a life—into the tools, the questions, the criticism, and the making—the word I have is

**inepistemic**.

<a id="part-back-matter"></a>

## Back Matter

<a id="chapter-acknowledgements"></a>

### Acknowledgements

*"I am not a theoretician, and I don’t pretend to be a savant."*
— Thomas Alva Edison

I am an inventor by trade and temperament; software is the substrate. That matters here. The architecture for this project came before the book. The technical environment developed for the project is called *Explanata*, harnessed to GPT-5.6 Sol for the book's production. I operated the inquiry conversationally, posing problems, criticizing outputs, introducing distinctions, rejecting formulations, and deciding which successor problems were worth pursuing; the manuscript emerged from that process.

The underlying effort has been to treat epistemology as a first-class architectural abstraction: to ask what happens when aspects of epistemology are made explicit enough to be modeled, implemented, and processed. Software provides an environment where those abstractions can be explored. This book is one of many things that emerged when the resulting architecture was turned back upon the architect and the epistemology itself.

For that reason, the people I acknowledge as entrepreneurs, inventors, and engineers stand here as peers of those I acknowledge for their epistemic contributions. I have spent much of my career building things with other people. Problems found in companies, products, systems, interfaces, failed designs, working designs, arguments, and collaborations have shaped this inquiry as surely as books have. Many colleagues taught me that explanations are easy until something has to ship.

Steven Pinker, especially through *The Blank Slate*, *How the Mind Works*, and *The Stuff of Thought*, helped structure the cognitive-scientific and psychological landscape through which some of those problems became concrete. Scott Aaronson, through his explorations of computational complexity, quantum mechanics, and the nature of minds, sharpened questions at the intersection of computation, epistemology, and personhood. Richard Dawkins supplied evolutionary concepts and language that recur throughout the work, including the wonderfully dismissive phrase “Popperian heckle,” which seemed worth taking seriously.

Karl Popper and David Deutsch remain in the foreground of this project, but not in a straight line. I encountered Popper more deeply through Deutsch. Deutsch first made explanations themselves into a problem for me: not merely things philosophy talks about, but structures whose reach, consilience, constraints, and consequences could be investigated. That inquiry eventually led me further into Popper—into problems, conjecture and criticism, objective knowledge, fallibilism, and an epistemology much deeper than the familiar caricature of falsificationism.

Misunderstanding is catalytic. Explanations of explanation carried me through a wider philosophical landscape: Hempel, Kitcher, van Fraassen, Cartwright, Woodward, Strevens, and others working on causation, unification, models, realism, inference, probability, and what makes an explanation explanatory at all. Much of that work now stands for me more as a constructive foil. A parallel lineage also shaped my understanding of these problems: Miller, Bronowski, Lakatos, Shearmur, Bartley, Agassi, Corvi, Jarvie, Maxwell, Musgrave, and many others each deepened my understanding of Popper and the critical-rationalist tradition from different directions. Competing formulations exposed hidden assumptions, supplied counterexamples, and made the points of agreement and disagreement with Popper sharper.

The Conjecture Institute helped consolidate and sustain an intellectual environment in which these questions could remain live rather than settle into doctrine. Brett Hall has been a public teacher of record over many years, particularly through his podcasts and conversations about Deutsch, Popper, explanation, and the reach of ideas. His *The Farthest Reaches* occupies territory close enough to this work that the parallel deserves recognition, one pointing the person outward, the other inward. Ray Scott Percival’s *The Myth of the Closed Mind* occupies nearby Popperian territory, particularly in its treatment of human rationality, corrigibility, and the possibility of an open mind. Aaron Stupple's *The Sovereign Child* sharpened problems around children, authority, and epistemic sovereignty, and our conversations carried those problems beyond the book.

The movement was not from one authority to another. The inventive process navigated a landscape of competing abstractions, implemented some of them, collided them with one another, and retained what seemed to work. Deutsch has described his own work, in effect, as footnotes to Popper. I am comfortable placing this project in that lineage, though a builder needs a different metaphor: call them prototypes. I have inherited problems, explanations, vocabulary, and an epistemic attitude from them, and those ideas mutated inside problems they did not set for me. Where that process has produced errors, the errors are mine.

None of those acknowledgements should be read as warrants. The essay titles were constructed similarly: inherited memes, mechanically mutated to fit new problems. Their ancestry is part of the mechanism, not an assertion that the essays respond to the works whose language they inherit. A reference may identify ancestry, resemblance, disagreement, mutation, or simply another place where a problem has been encountered. I have therefore resisted using citations and parenthetical references throughout the manuscript as placeholders for explanations.

To everyone who built, argued, explained, criticized, listened, invented, funded, programmed, published, conversed, or otherwise altered the problem situation from which this work emerged: thank you. What survives here is one reconstruction among many possibilities, for your criticism.

<a id="chapter-endnotes"></a>

### Endnotes

<a id="chapter-endnotes--n-the-universality-of-you"></a>

#### N. The Universality of You

**1. Popper and Deutsch.** Popper's _Objective Knowledge_ (1972) and _Conjectures and Refutations_ (1963), and Deutsch's _The Fabric of Reality_ (1997) and _The Beginning of Infinity_ (2011), establish the book's principal intellectual ancestry: conjectural knowledge, criticism, explanatory reach, and universality. The distinctive application here is to the singular person.

**2. Objective knowledge and the growth of knowledge.** Popper's World 3 account in _Objective Knowledge_ distinguishes objective knowledge from subjective knowing, including objectively existing false theories. The schema $P_1 \rightarrow TS \rightarrow EE \rightarrow P_2$ adapts his $P_1 \rightarrow TT \rightarrow EE \rightarrow P_2$, replacing _tentative theory_ with _tentative solution_.

**3. Inexplicit knowledge.** Michael Polanyi's _Personal Knowledge_ (1958) and _The Tacit Dimension_ (1966) are predecessors for inexplicit knowledge; Gilbert Ryle's _The Concept of Mind_ (1949) distinguishes knowing-how from knowing-that. _Inexplicit_ additionally permits the creation of explicit, criticizable knowledge from previously unarticulated activity.

**4. Evolutionary and biological knowledge.** Charles Darwin's _On the Origin of Species_ (1859), Richard Dawkins's _The Selfish Gene_ (1976), and Donald T. Campbell's “Blind Variation and Selective Retention in Creative Thought as in Other Knowledge Processes” (1960) supply biological and evolutionary precedents. Popper's _Objective Knowledge_ links evolutionary adaptation with the growth of human knowledge.

**5. Abstraction, representation, and explanation.** Alfred Korzybski's _Science and Sanity_ (1933) is a source for the map–territory distinction. Deutsch's _The Beginning of Infinity_ distinguishes explanatory understanding from mere predictive or descriptive success; the chapter applies both distinctions to abstraction and compression.

**6. Explanatory reach and computational universality.** Deutsch's _The Beginning of Infinity_, particularly “The Reach of Explanations,” “The Reality of Abstractions,” and “The Jump to Universality,” and _The Fabric of Reality_ establish the general framework. His “Quantum Theory, the Church–Turing Principle and the Universal Quantum Computer” (1985) develops the physical claim concerning universal simulation. Scott Aaronson's “Why Philosophers Should Care About Computational Complexity” (2013) distinguishes abstract computability from computational feasibility, a constraint on what universal simulation makes practically reachable.

**7. Objective knowledge and recursive tools.** Popper's World 3 account provides the starting point for objective knowledge acting back upon knowers. Merlin Donald's _Origins of the Modern Mind_ (1991) describes how external symbolic representations expand human cognitive possibilities. The focus here is the recursive return of created artifacts to later problem situations.

**8. Ancestry, derivation, and explanatory creativity.** Popper's _The Poverty of Historicism_ (1957) argues that future knowledge cannot be scientifically predicted in advance; Deutsch's _The Beginning of Infinity_, especially “The Spark,” “Creation,” and “Artificial Creativity,” examines explanatory creativity. Historical ancestry is not a procedure for deriving a new explanation.

<a id="chapter-endnotes--i-you-are-not-a-geneget"></a>

#### I. You Are Not A Geneget

**1. Title.** _You Are Not A Geneget_ mutates Jaron Lanier's _You Are Not a Gadget_ (2010), replacing the technological referent with a genetic one. The reference is to the title, not an adoption of Lanier's argument.

**2. Personality genetics.** See Priya Gupta and colleagues, “A Genome-Wide Investigation into the Underlying Genetic Architecture of Personality Traits and Overlap with Psychopathology” (2024), and Ted Schwaba, Michel Nivard, and Elliot Tucker-Drob, “Personality Genomics” (2026), for the population-level personality-genetics research considered here.

**3. Heritability and causal explanation.** Richard Lewontin's “The Analysis of Variance and the Analysis of Causes” (1974) distinguishes explaining population variation from identifying the causes of a trait. A cause shared across a population can be important without explaining measured differences within it.

**4. Personality dimensions and individuality.** Dan P. McAdams's “The Five-Factor Model in Personality: A Critical Appraisal” (1992) and “What Do We Know When We Know a Person?” (1995) distinguish comparative traits from understanding a person. His phrase _psychology of the stranger_ is especially pertinent.

**5. Trait reification and causal structure.** Simon Boag, “Explanation in Personality Psychology: ‘Verbal Magic’ and the Five-Factor Model” (2011), examines circular trait explanations; Borsboom, Mellenbergh, and van Heerden, “The Theoretical Status of Latent Variables” (2003), distinguish measurement models from causal claims. See also Michael P. Grosz, “Why the Big Five Personality Traits Are Composites, Not Common Causes” (2026).

**6. Different causal histories, similar outcomes.** Dante Cicchetti and Fred A. Rogosch's “Equifinality and Multifinality in Developmental Psychopathology” (1996) describes distinct developmental pathways producing similar outcomes, and similar starting conditions producing divergent ones. A shared personality measurement need not imply a shared explanatory history.

**7. Cultural knowledge and historical development.** Joseph Henrich's _The Secret of Our Success_ (2015) and _The WEIRDest People in the World_ (2020) examine cultural knowledge, institutions, and their historical effects on human development, including effects that do not depend on changed genetic inheritance.

<a id="chapter-endnotes--ii-populations-fast-and-slow"></a>

#### II. Populations, Fast and Slow

**1. Title.** _Populations, Fast and Slow_ mutates Daniel Kahneman's _Thinking, Fast and Slow_ (2011). The contrast shifts from cognitive processing styles to rapid population classification versus the slower work of explaining a particular individual.

**2. Between-person and within-person explanation.** Peter C. M. Molenaar's “A Manifesto on Psychology as Idiographic Science” (2004) identifies conditions under which between-person findings could describe within-person dynamics. Fisher, Medaglia, and Jeronimus, “Lack of Group-to-Individual Generalizability Is a Threat to Human Subjects Research” (2018), develops the empirical challenge.

**3. Transportability and the limits of population inference.** Judea Pearl and Elias Bareinboim, “External Validity: From Do-Calculus to Transportability Across Populations” (2014), formalize conditions for transferring causal findings. Nancy Cartwright and Jeremy Hardie's _Evidence-Based Policy_ (2012) examines the assumptions needed for such transfer. Neither provides an explanation of an individual merely from population fit.

**4. The looping effects of classification.** Ian Hacking's “The Looping Effects of Human Kinds” (1995), in _Causal Cognition_, describes how classifying people can change their subsequent behavior and thus the phenomenon classified. Classification can be part of a person's causal history, not simply a report about it.

<a id="chapter-endnotes--iii-the-anxious-authorities"></a>

#### III. The Anxious Authorities

**1. Title.** _The Anxious Authorities_ mutates Jonathan Haidt's _The Anxious Generation_ (2024), transferring the focus of anxiety from children to the authorities interpreting and managing their media use. It is a title allusion, not a reply to Haidt's empirical thesis.

**2. Social knowledge and memes.** Richard Dawkins introduced _meme_ in _The Selfish Gene_ (1976); Susan Blackmore's _The Meme Machine_ (1999) develops the idea of mutually reinforcing _memeplexes_. These supply the cultural-inheritance vocabulary for recurring claims about epistemic and parental authority.

**3. Children and epistemic sovereignty.** Aaron Stupple's _The Sovereign Child_ (2025), within the Popperian Taking Children Seriously tradition, distinguishes children's knowledge creation from adult claims to authority over their judgment.

**4. The bucket theory of mind.** Popper's “The Bucket and the Searchlight: Two Theories of Knowledge,” in _Objective Knowledge_, opposes passive accumulation of inputs to active, expectation-guided learning. This underlies the distinction between children as interpreters and children as receptacles for media content.

**5. Children, media, and epistemic control.** danah boyd's _It's Complicated_ (2014) examines adolescents' participation in networked media and adult misreadings of it; Eli Pariser's _The Filter Bubble_ (2011) examines technological selection of informational exposure. Both concern the conditions of a person's next epistemic encounter.

<a id="chapter-endnotes--iv-the-wisdom-between-the-crowd"></a>

#### IV. The Wisdom Between The Crowd

**1. Title.** _The Wisdom Between The Crowd_ mutates James Surowiecki's _The Wisdom of Crowds_ (2004). _Between_ locates the relevant knowledge in relations, institutions, and shared artifacts rather than positing a collective knowing subject.

**2. Methodological individualism and social explanation.** Max Weber's _Economy and Society_ (1922) provides a classical statement of methodological individualism: social phenomena can be explained through individual actions without denying institutions or other social structures.

**3. Distributed knowledge and coordination.** Friedrich Hayek's “The Use of Knowledge in Society” (1945) examines coordination of dispersed knowledge; Leonard E. Read's _I, Pencil_ (1958) illustrates productive cooperation without comprehensive understanding by any participant.

**4. Freedom and error correction.** John Stuart Mill's _On Liberty_ (1859) defends free discussion as a means of discovering error; Popper's _The Open Society and Its Enemies_ (1945) makes institutional criticism and corrigibility central to political openness.

**5. Media and the conditions of knowing.** Marshall McLuhan's _Understanding Media_ (1964) examines how media alter the conditions of human activity; Neil Postman's _Amusing Ourselves to Death_ (1985) examines the structure imposed on public discourse by its medium. Neither is invoked as an alternative epistemology.

**6. Human–computer interaction and externalized cognition.** J. C. R. Licklider's “Man-Computer Symbiosis” (1960) anticipates interactive intellectual augmentation. Andy Clark and David Chalmers's “The Extended Mind” (1998) is a philosophical comparison concerning external cognitive resources; AI responsiveness alone does not establish a new knowing subject.

<a id="chapter-endnotes--v-the-popperian-heckle"></a>

#### V. The Popperian Heckle

**1. Title.** _The Popperian Heckle_ comes from Richard Dawkins's “Hall of Mirrors” (2000), later “What Is True?” in _A Devil's Chaplain_ (2003). The phrase is redirected from an objection about conjectural scientific truth to the unexplained creative arrows in Popper's schema.

**2. Theory-laden observation without relativism.** Norwood Russell Hanson's _Patterns of Discovery_ (1958) examines theory-laden observation; Thomas Kuhn's _The Structure of Scientific Revolutions_ (1962) describes historical changes in scientific problems. These are comparisons, not an endorsement of paradigm-relative truth: the governing epistemology remains Popperian realism.

**3. Epistemic action and recursive agency.** Albert Bandura's _Social Foundations of Thought and Action_ (1986) describes reciprocal relations among persons, actions, and environments. Kirsh and Maglio's “On Distinguishing Epistemic from Pragmatic Action” (1994) distinguishes actions that improve cognition from actions directly achieving an external result.

**4. Naturalistic agency, not a borrowed theory of freedom.** Daniel Dennett's _Freedom Evolves_ (2003) offers a naturalistic account of agency. It is a neighboring treatment of the physical possibility of freedom, not the chapter's explanation of creativity or its source of epistemology.

**5.
